title: Beyond the Quantum Promise: A Security Analysis of Classical Control in Quantum Key Distribution
summary: Quantum Key Distribution (QKD) protocols provide information-theoretic security by using quantum mechanical principles. Yet QKD is fundamentally a hybrid protocol: its security depends on the correct integration of the quantum phase with classical post-processing. While ETSI and ITUT specifications standardize QKD architectures and interfaces, they evaluate protocol security in isolation, leaving cross-layer interactions as an underexplored attack surface. This paper introduces a formal verification framework that holistically models QKD protocols based on ETSI and ITUT QKD specifications. Our model is the first hybrid QKD protocol model that supports automated analysis of protocollevel security focusing on how classical operations influence the security guarantees provided by the quantum phase of the QKD protocol. We formalize a comprehensive symbolic model of QKD protocols, based on ETSI and ITU-T QKD specifications, in Tamarin, an automated protocol verifier. Applying this framework, we obtain formal evidence of three specification-level vulnerabilities in ETSI- and ITU-T-grounded protocol models under adversary Eve+: subverted entanglement injection, basis-deferred measurement, and message reflection. Each arises from a classical control-plane omission in the procedure text and is established under a symbolic abstraction rather than as a claim about all practical deployments. We introduce two protocol improvements: measurement commitment and identitybound message authentication codes (MACs). Tamarin verification confirms that these countermeasures eliminate the identified vulnerabilities under Eve+. We have communicated our results and recommendations to relevant standardization organizations.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces the first formal verification framework that holistically models hybrid QKD protocols based on ETSI and ITU-T specifications in the Tamarin verifier, discovering three specification-level vulnerabilities (subverted entanglement injection, basis-deferred measurement, message reflection) and proposing two countermeasures (measurement commitment and identity-bound MACs) that eliminate these vulnerabilities.
AI.motivation: QKD protocols are fundamentally hybrid (quantum + classical), but existing standards like ETSI and ITU-T evaluate protocol security in isolation, leaving cross-layer interactions between the quantum phase and classical post-processing as an underexplored attack surface.
AI.method: The authors formalize a comprehensive symbolic model of QKD protocols based on ETSI and ITU-T specifications using Tamarin, an automated protocol verifier, enabling automated analysis of protocol-level security focusing on how classical operations influence quantum-phase security guarantees.
AI.result: The framework revealed three specification-level vulnerabilities under an adversary called Eve+: subverted entanglement injection, basis-deferred measurement, and message reflection—each stemming from classical control-plane omissions in the procedure text. Two protocol improvements (measurement commitment and identity-bound MACs) were verified in Tamarin to eliminate these vulnerabilities.
AI.conclusion: The vulnerabilities and countermeasures have been communicated to relevant standardization organizations, providing formal evidence and improvements for securing the classical components of standardized QKD protocols.

title: Readout-Rank Laws for Isotropic Quantum Tangents
summary: Deep parameterized quantum circuits may remain sensitive to a parameter change while the observables retained by a learning model barely respond. We study this separation for a fixed computational-basis measurement. For a pure-state tangent, we compare the quantum Fisher information $F_Q$, the Fisher information $F_{\rm full}$ in the complete bitstring distribution, and the largest variance-normalized response $\mathcal I_{\mathcal A}$ available to a diagonal readout space $\mathcal A$. If the joint state--tangent frame is Haar random, we prove that the two successive information fractions are independent Beta variables whose means are $1/2$ and $r/(2^n-1)$, where $r$ is the centered dimension of the readout. Consequently, even the joint span of all computational-basis Pauli strings through any fixed weight $k$ retain only $O(n^k2^{-n})$ of the full-record information. Exact-statevector experiments across six circuit families show increasing finite-size agreement with this hierarchy in five nonconserving ensembles as the circuit depth grows. A number-conserving family departs strongly from the isotropic prediction even after correcting the support and readout rank, showing that rank alone is insufficient without tangent isotropy.

AI.tldr: This paper studies the information gap between quantum Fisher information and classically accessible Fisher information for parameterized quantum circuits with fixed computational-basis measurements. Under Haar-random joint state-tangent frames, the two successive information fractions are independent Beta variables with means 1/2 and r/(2^n-1), where r is the centered readout dimension. This implies that even the joint span of all computational-basis Pauli strings up to weight k retains only O(n^k 2^-n) of the full-record information. Exact-statevector experiments across six circuit families confirm the hierarchy in five nonconserving ensembles, while a number-conserving family deviates strongly, showing rank alone is insufficient without tangent isotropy.
AI.motivation: Quantum parameterized circuits may remain sensitive to parameter changes while the observables retained by a learning model barely respond, creating a gap between potential information and accessible information. Understanding this separation for fixed computational-basis measurements is crucial for designing effective quantum machine learning models.
AI.method: The authors analytically prove that for Haar-random joint state-tangent frames with computational-basis measurement, the two successive information fractions follow independent Beta distributions with means 1/2 and r/(2^n-1). They compare quantum Fisher information, full bitstring-distribution Fisher information, and largest variance-normalized response for diagonal readout spaces, then validate via exact statevector simulations across six circuit families.
AI.result: The two information fractions are independent Beta variables with means 1/2 and r/(2^n-1). Joint spans of computational-basis Pauli strings up to weight k retain only O(n^k 2^-n) of full-record information. Five nonconserving circuit families show increasing agreement with the hierarchy as depth grows, while a number-conserving family strongly deviates from isotropic predictions, indicating rank alone is insufficient without tangent isotropy.
AI.conclusion: There is a fundamental information hierarchy in quantum circuits under computational-basis measurements: quantum Fisher information is typically double the accessible classical Fisher information in the full bitstring distribution, and diagonal readouts capture only exponentially small fractions of the full-record information. Circuit ensembles must possess tangent isotropy for rank-based predictions to hold, as number-conserving families demonstrate.

title: Storage, Scrambling, and Loss of Information in the Quantum Reservoir Computing Paradigm
summary: The suitability of a quantum reservoir computing (QRC) platform for a given time-series processing task is closely tied to the dynamical properties of its computational substrate and design. Information is injected into, processed by, and read from this substrate, and finally passed to a linear readout layer which is trained to perform a specific task. In this work we introduce a classical-quantum state derived from the process tensor representing the dynamical part of this process for typical QRC protocols found in the literature. Using this object, mutual informations between physical subsystems and subsets of past inputs can be written as Holevo quantities, which we then use to numerically investigate information saturation in the substrate, fading memory of past inputs, and the local accessibility of injected information for a commonly used QRC platform. We then extract two diagnostics that characterise the nonlocal scrambling of information within, and loss of information from the substrate, and compare these to QRC performance across Hamiltonian parameters and measurement strengths. Finally, we comment on future directions that the framework introduced here opens up for the study and extension of the QRC program.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces a classical-quantum state derived from the process tensor to analyze quantum reservoir computing (QRC) platforms, using Holevo quantities to quantify mutual information between physical subsystems and past inputs. Two diagnostics characterize nonlocal information scrambling and information loss in the substrate, which are compared to QRC performance across Hamiltonian parameters and measurement strengths.
AI.motivation: QRC performance is closely tied to the dynamical properties of its computational substrate, but there is a lack of systematic tools to characterize how information flows, saturates, and is lost within the reservoir substrate.
AI.method: The authors construct a classical-quantum state from the process tensor representing the dynamical part of QRC protocols. Mutual informations between physical subsystems and subsets of past inputs are formulated as Holevo quantities, enabling numerical investigation of information saturation, fading memory, and local accessibility of injected information. Two diagnostics are extracted to characterize nonlocal information scrambling and information loss.
AI.result: The framework numerically characterizes information saturation, fading memory, and local information accessibility in a commonly used QRC platform, and establishes connections between the two extracted diagnostics (nonlocal scrambling and information loss) and QRC performance across Hamiltonian parameters and measurement strengths.
AI.conclusion: The process-tensor-based framework opens new avenues for studying and extending quantum reservoir computing, providing principled diagnostics linking substrate dynamics to task performance.

title: Emergent Problem-Graph Alignment in RL-Discovered Entanglement Topologies for QAOA
summary: In the Quantum Approximate Optimization Algorithm (QAOA), the entanglement topology, where qubit pairs are connected by two-qubit gates, is conventionally set equal to the edge set of the problem graph. This coupling ties circuit design to explicit problem knowledge and may not yield the most trainable circuit under limited optimization budgets. We investigate whether a reinforcement learning (RL) agent can discover more effective entanglement topologies for QAOA-based MaxCut optimization without direct access to the problem graph. A Masked Proximal Policy Optimization agent sequentially places IsingZZ gates to construct a circuit topology, while a variational inner loop optimizes the resulting QAOA parameters and returns the approximation ratio as a sparse terminal reward. The agent's observation contains only the edges placed so far and the current approximation ratio; graph structure can only be inferred indirectly through the optimization reward. On Erdős--Rényi instances with up to $10$~qubits, the agent consistently converges to topologies that are strict subsets of the problem graph, achieving overlap ratios approaching $1.0$, despite receiving no explicit information about the graph structure in its observations. These sparse, problem-aligned topologies outperform the full graph topology and several structural baselines when the optimization budget is limited ($50$~gradient steps), but are overtaken by denser topologies given sufficient optimization budget. Our results reveal a trainability--expressibility trade-off governed by topology density and suggest that the variational optimization landscape implicitly encodes structural information about the problem Hamiltonian.

AI.tldr: This paper uses a Masked Proximal Policy Optimization (PPO) agent to discover entanglement topologies for QAOA-based MaxCut optimization without direct access to the problem graph. The agent learns to place IsingZZ gates sequentially, receiving only the approximation ratio as a reward. On Erdős–Rényi graphs up to 10 qubits, it converges to sparse topologies that are strict subsets of the problem graph (with overlap ratios near 1.0), which outperform the full graph topology under limited optimization budgets (50 gradient steps) but are beaten by denser topologies with sufficient budget.
AI.motivation: The entanglement topology in QAOA is conventionally fixed to the problem graph's edge set, which couples circuit design to explicit problem knowledge and may not be trainable under limited optimization budgets. The authors investigate whether RL can discover more effective topologies without direct graph access, revealing a trainability–expressibility trade-off governed by topology density.
AI.method: A Masked PPO agent sequentially places IsingZZ gates to construct a circuit topology, while a variational inner loop optimizes the resulting QAOA parameters and returns the approximation ratio as a sparse terminal reward. The agent's observation contains only the edges placed so far and the current approximation ratio, meaning graph structure is inferred only indirectly through optimization reward.
AI.result: On Erdős–Rényi instances with up to 10 qubits, the agent consistently converges to topologies that are strict subsets of the problem graph, achieving overlap ratios approaching 1.0 despite no explicit graph information in observations. These sparse, problem-aligned topologies outperform the full graph topology and structural baselines when the optimization budget is limited (50 gradient steps), but are overtaken by denser topologies given sufficient optimization budget.
AI.conclusion: The results reveal a trainability–expressibility trade-off governed by topology density and suggest that the variational optimization landscape implicitly encodes structural information about the problem Hamiltonian, enabling RL agents to discover problem-aligned sparse topologies without explicit graph knowledge.

title: Composite-State Localization Beyond the External Landscape in Non-Hermitian Quasicrystals
summary: A composite excitation need not inherit the localization behavior of its constituents. We show that an interacting non-Hermitian quasiperiodic ladder realizes a controllable and reversible localization inversion between composite and unbound excitations, where internal configuration, rather than only the external potential, becomes a control parameter for localization. Opposite complex potentials on the two legs cancel at first order for a same-rung pair but act directly on separated particles, allowing extended composite states to persist while the unpaired sector becomes localized. A strong-coupling theory identifies the composite state as an emergent weakly modulated non-Hermitian quasicrystal generated by virtual unpaired configurations. Breaking the potential antisymmetry restores a direct modulation of the composite band and reverses the localization hierarchy. Engineering configuration-space pathways further stabilizes an extended composite band embedded within a localized continuum, the inverse of the conventional bound-state-in-the-continuum scenario. Our results establish internal configuration as a reversible control parameter for localization.

AI.tldr: This paper demonstrates that in an interacting non-Hermitian quasiperiodic ladder, composite excitations can remain extended while unbound excitations become localized, controlled by internal configuration rather than just external potential. The authors achieve a reversible localization inversion via opposite complex potentials on two legs and strong-coupling theory, and further engineer configuration-space pathways to embed an extended composite band within a localized continuum.
AI.motivation: To establish that internal configuration of composite excitations can serve as a reversible control parameter for localization, extending beyond conventional external-potential-based control in non-Hermitian quasiperiodic systems.
AI.method: The authors study an interacting non-Hermitian quasiperiodic ladder with opposite complex potentials on its two legs. They use a strong-coupling theory to analyze the composite state, showing that first-order potential cancellation for same-rung pairs allows extended composites while separated particles localize. They break potential antisymmetry to reverse the hierarchy and engineer configuration-space pathways to stabilize extended composite bands within localized continua.
AI.result: The composite state emerges as a weakly modulated non-Hermitian quasicrystal generated by virtual unpaired configurations. Extended composite states persist while the unpaired sector localizes. Breaking antisymmetry restores direct modulation and reverses the localization hierarchy. An extended composite band can be embedded within a localized continuum, inverse of the conventional bound-state-in-continuum scenario.
AI.conclusion: Internal configuration is established as a reversible control parameter for localization in non-Hermitian quasiperiodic interacting systems, offering a new knob beyond external potential for controlling localization phenomena.

title: State Preparation Protocols for Entangled States via Open Quantum Walks
summary: Open quantum walks couple transitions on a graph to quantum operations on an internal degree of freedom. We use this structure to formulate protocols for quantum state preparation with nonunitary Kraus operators. We construct a ring-shaped OQW preparing an ensemble of Dicke states, with W states appearing as the single-excitation case, from which any individual Dicke state is recovered by postselecting the walker position; its convergence is governed by the spectral gap of the underlying Markov chain, for which we obtain a closed-form approximate expression. For GHZ states we present a two-node protocol using Kraus operators built from projective measurements that prepares them deterministically without requiring a measurement of the walker, and analyze how unsharp measurements affect the results and the convergence of the walk. We also show that the quantum trajectories method embeds naturally in the OQW framework as a graph-structured collision model.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes quantum state preparation protocols using open quantum walks (OQWs), constructing a ring-shaped OQW to prepare Dicke states (with W states as the single-excitation case) via postselection of the walker position, a two-node protocol for deterministic GHZ state preparation using Kraus operators from projective measurements, and showing quantum trajectories embed naturally in the OQW framework as graph-structured collision models.
AI.motivation: The authors aim to leverage the inherent structure of open quantum walks, which couple graph transitions to quantum operations on an internal degree of freedom, to formulate new protocols for quantum state preparation. The work addresses the need for effective state-preparation strategies for entangled multi-partite states like Dicke and GHZ states.
AI.method: The method involves constructing OQW protocols with nonunitary Kraus operators. For Dicke states, a ring-shaped OQW is designed whose convergence is controlled by the spectral gap of the underlying Markov chain, and a closed-form approximate expression for this gap is derived. For GHZ states, a two-node protocol uses Kraus operators built from projective measurements for deterministic preparation, and the effects of unsharp measurements on results and convergence are analyzed. The quantum trajectories method is also embedded into the OQW framework as a graph-structured collision model.
AI.result: A ring-shaped OQW prepares an ensemble of Dicke states, with W states as the single-excitation case, and any individual Dicke state can be recovered by postselecting the walker position. A two-node protocol deterministically prepares GHZ states without measuring the walker, with the impact of unsharp measurements analyzed. The quantum trajectories method is shown to embed naturally in the OQW formalism.
AI.conclusion: The OQW framework provides a versatile platform for quantum state preparation of entangled states, offering both postselective (Dicke states) and deterministic (GHZ states) preparation protocols, with convergence governed by Markov chain spectral properties, and unifying quantum trajectory methods within a graph-structured collision model.

title: Clustered Attractor Manifolds and Dynamical Condensation in Self-Attention
comment: 6 pages, 3 figures. Supplemental Material: 25 pages, 9 figures
summary: Transformer layers generate state-dependent interaction networks: token representations determine the attention matrix, which in turn updates the representations. We study this feedback in a minimal normalized self-attention dynamics and identify the overlap gap as the central quantity governing its attractor structure in the thermodynamic limit. When tokens form internally aligned clusters and their similarity to members of the same cluster exceeds that to every other cluster by a nonvanishing amount, inter-cluster attention is exponentially suppressed as the dimension increases. This mechanism produces a high-dimensional manifold of clustered fixed points, ranging from a few macroscopic clusters to extensive microscopic fragmentation, and also controls their stability against perturbations. Starting from an unstructured Gaussian state, we find that clustered states nucleate from the diffuse background only above a finite threshold in attention sharpness, giving rise to a dynamical attention-condensation transition.

AI.tldr: This paper analyzes minimal normalized self-attention dynamics as state-dependent interaction networks, identifying the "overlap gap" as the central quantity governing attractor structure. It shows inter-cluster attention is exponentially suppressed at high dimensions when intra-cluster similarity exceeds inter-cluster similarity, producing a high-dimensional manifold of clustered fixed points. Clustered states nucleate only above a finite attention-sharpness threshold from a diffuse Gaussian state, yielding a dynamical attention-condensation transition.
AI.motivation: Transformer layers form feedback loops where token representations determine attention weights, which in turn update the representations. Understanding this state-dependent feedback is fundamental to characterizing how transformers organize information, yet its attractor structure in the thermodynamic limit was not well understood.
AI.method: The authors study a minimal normalized self-attention dynamics in the thermodynamic limit, introducing the overlap gap as the key order parameter. They analyze clustered attractor states—ranging from few macroscopic clusters to extensive microscopic fragmentation—and examine their stability against perturbations.
AI.result: The overlap gap governs the attractor structure. When tokens are internally aligned with intra-cluster similarity exceeding all inter-cluster similarities by a nonvanishing margin, attention between clusters decays exponentially with dimension. Clustered states nucleate from an unstructured Gaussian state only above a finite threshold in attention sharpness, indicating a dynamical attention-condensation transition.
AI.conclusion: The self-attention dynamics exhibits a rich phase structure in high dimensions, with the overlap gap controlling cluster formation, stability, and the existence of a condensation transition. This provides a principled characterization of how attention organizes token representations.

title: Preparing approximate $N$-fold cat states with the phase space instruction set
summary: The phase space instruction set is a continuous-variable universal gate set involving single-qubit rotations and qubit-dependent displacements on a single boson. Using these gates, we prove that a circuit depth $\mathrmΩ(\varphi(N))$ is necessary to approximately prepare a large $N$-fold rotationally invariant Schrödinger cat state; here $\varphi(N) \gtrsim N/\log\log N$ is the Euler totient function. A protocol saturating this asymptotic bound on circuit depth is obtained for every prime number $N$. This protocol has an asymptotically optimal runtime, when the gates are generated by Hamiltonian evolution. Our results provide a sharp example where a universal gate set is surprisingly inefficient at preparing a simple family of states, and further imply that converting bosonic circuits between different universal gate sets can be extremely inefficient.

AI.tldr: A proof that the phase space instruction set (a continuous-variable universal gate set) requires Ω(φ(N)) circuit depth to prepare large N-fold rotationally invariant Schrödinger cat states, with an optimal protocol for prime N, revealing surprising inefficiency of this universal gate set.
AI.motivation: To investigate the computational complexity of preparing simple quantum states (rotationally invariant Schrödinger cat states) using a specific continuous-variable universal gate set, and to demonstrate that universal gate sets can be surprisingly inefficient for simple state preparation tasks.
AI.method: The authors prove a lower bound Ω(φ(N)) on circuit depth for preparing N-fold rotationally invariant Schrödinger cat states using the phase space instruction set, where φ(N) is the Euler totient function. They also construct a matching optimal protocol for every prime N, which saturates the asymptotic bound and achieves asymptotically optimal runtime when gates are generated by Hamiltonian evolution.
AI.result: A circuit depth of Ω(φ(N)) ≳ Ω(N/log log N) is necessary and sufficient (for prime N) to prepare large rotationally invariant Schrödinger cat states using the phase space instruction set. This also implies that converting between different universal bosonic gate sets can be extremely inefficient.
AI.conclusion: The phase space instruction set, while universal for continuous-variable quantum computation, is asymptotically inefficient at preparing rotationally invariant Schrödinger cat states, providing a sharp example of a universal gate set failing at simple tasks and showing that gate-set conversion in bosonic circuits can be prohibitively costly.

title: Quantum Relaxometry Under Continuous Wave Excitation
summary: Quantum relaxometry is one of the most successful applications of nitrogen-vacancy (NV) centers in diamond and, more broadly, solid-state spin qubits, enabling ultrasensitive detection of magnetic noise and paramagnetic species via measurements of the spin-lattice relaxation time $T_1$. Conventional pulsed protocols, however, probe $T_1$ efficiently only over a limited temporal range, which restricts the scope and throughput of the technique. Here we introduce a continuous-wave quantum relaxometry protocol that operates in the frequency domain. By measuring the frequency response of the optically detected magnetic resonance signal under low-frequency microwave amplitude modulation, we extract $T_1$ from the characteristic response time of the spin system. The method enables efficient $T_1$ measurements spanning more than three orders of magnitude -- directly demonstrated from 60 $μ$s to 200 ms in our experiments -- across a broad temperature range and under substantial ensemble inhomogeneity. We further show that this protocol enables quantitative relaxometry-based sensing in nanodiamonds, achieving a substantial speed-up over the pulsed methods and offering a practical approach to optimizing nanodiamond size for enhanced sensitivity.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces a continuous-wave quantum relaxometry protocol for nitrogen-vacancy (NV) centers in diamond that operates in the frequency domain, enabling efficient T1 measurements spanning over three orders of magnitude (60 μs to 200 ms) across a broad temperature range and under ensemble inhomogeneity. The method also enables faster relaxometry-based sensing in nanodiamonds compared to pulsed protocols.
AI.motivation: Conventional pulsed protocols for measuring spin-lattice relaxation time T1 in NV centers are efficient only over a limited temporal range, restricting the scope and throughput of quantum relaxometry as a sensing technique.
AI.method: The protocol operates in the frequency domain by measuring the frequency response of the optically detected magnetic resonance (ODMR) signal under low-frequency microwave amplitude modulation. T1 is extracted from the characteristic response time of the spin system.
AI.result: The method enables efficient T1 measurements spanning more than three orders of magnitude, demonstrated from 60 μs to 200 ms, across a broad temperature range and under substantial ensemble inhomogeneity. It achieves a substantial speed-up over pulsed methods for quantitative relaxometry-based sensing in nanodiamonds.
AI.conclusion: The continuous-wave frequency-domain protocol offers a practical approach to optimizing nanodiamond size for enhanced sensitivity and provides a more efficient, broadly applicable alternative to conventional pulsed T1 measurement techniques.

title: The Case for the Everett Multiverse
summary:
I give a non-technical presentation of the argument that quantum mechanics, in the form in which it is currently used, needs to be understood in many-worlds (Everettian) terms; the alternatives that have been discussed are at present not able to reproduce the full empirical content of the theory.
  This is a draft of a chapter for the forthcoming \emph{Blackwell Companion to Philosophy and the Multiverse (Klaas Kraay and Daniel Rubio, eds.) }

AI.tldr: A non-technical argument that quantum mechanics, as currently used, must be understood in many-worlds (Everettian) terms because all alternative interpretations fail to reproduce the full empirical content of the theory.
AI.motivation: To present a non-technical case that the many-worlds interpretation is the only viable interpretation of quantum mechanics capable of reproducing the full empirical content of the theory, challenging alternative interpretations.
AI.method: A non-technical philosophical argument presenting the case for Everettian quantum mechanics by systematically showing that alternative interpretations are unable to reproduce the full empirical content of quantum mechanics as currently used.
AI.result: The paper argues that alternatives to the many-worlds interpretation are currently unable to account for the complete empirical content of quantum theory, thereby supporting the Everettian reading as the necessary interpretation.
AI.conclusion: Quantum mechanics, in its current form, needs to be understood in many-worlds (Everettian) terms, since the available alternatives fail to reproduce the full empirical content of the theory.

title: Implicit Differentiation for Measurement-Efficient Bilevel Quantum-Classical Optimization
summary: Quantum optimization has shown promising results for quadratic unconstrained binary optimization (QUBO) problems. Real-world applications, however, often involve polynomial coefficients that depend on tunable external factors - such as demand forecasts or risk preferences - giving rise to bilevel optimization structures. We show how variational quantum algorithms (VQAs) can efficiently handle such parametric problems, making three contributions. First, we propose a bilevel optimization model for diagonal cost Hamiltonians where coefficients depend on a tunable outer parameter: an outer loop adjusts this parameter - reshaping the cost landscape - while an inner VQA optimizes circuit variables. Second, since derivative-free probing methods incur a multiplicative overhead when each outer evaluation requires a complete inner solve, we develop correlator-reuse implicit differentiation (CR-ID), which obtains outer gradients by reusing quantum measurements already collected during inner energy estimation, requiring essentially no additional circuit executions. Experiments across three coefficient families show that CR-ID consistently improves budget-normalized efficiency by ~4\% in 1D and over 14\% in multi-dimensional settings, showing a significant performance advantage compared to finite-difference methods. Third, we show that this property is architecture-dependent: VQE admits exact reuse gradients, whereas QAOA introduces a state-dependent term that creates a cost-bias trade-off.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes a bilevel optimization framework for parametric QUBO problems using variational quantum algorithms, introduces correlator-reuse implicit differentiation (CR-ID) to obtain outer-loop gradients without additional circuit executions, and demonstrates ~4-14% efficiency improvements over finite-difference methods, while showing the gradient reuse property is architecture-dependent (exact for VQE, bias-inducing for QAOA).
AI.motivation: Real-world QUBO problems often have coefficients that depend on tunable external parameters (e.g., demand forecasts, risk preferences), creating bilevel optimization structures. Existing variational quantum approaches do not efficiently handle such parametric dependencies; derivative-free probing methods incur multiplicative overhead since each outer evaluation requires a complete inner solve.
AI.method: The paper makes three contributions: (1) proposes a bilevel optimization model for diagonal cost Hamiltonians where an outer loop tunes a parametric coefficient reshaping the cost landscape while an inner VQA optimizes circuit variables; (2) develops correlator-reuse implicit differentiation (CR-ID), which reuses quantum measurements already collected during inner energy estimation to compute outer gradients with essentially no additional circuit executions; (3) analyzes how this gradient-reuse property depends on the VQA architecture, showing VQE admits exact reuse gradients while QAOA introduces a state-dependent term creating a cost-bias trade-off.
AI.result: Experiments across three coefficient families show CR-ID consistently improves budget-normalized efficiency by ~4% in 1D settings and over 14% in multi-dimensional settings, demonstrating a significant performance advantage over finite-difference methods.
AI.conclusion: Variational quantum algorithms can efficiently handle parametric QUBO problems with bilevel structure via CR-ID, which reuses inner-loop quantum measurements for outer gradients. The approach is architecture-dependent, with VQE providing exact reuse gradients while QAOA faces a cost-bias trade-off.

title: Randomized product formulas beyond optimal deterministic scaling
summary: Product formulas, also known as Trotter formulas, are among the most widely used and practical methods for simulating quantum systems on quantum computers. Here we introduce two new classes of randomized product formulas for simulating Hamiltonians with separated energy scales, $H=A+αB$, where $α$ is small. In the standard access model, where one can implement exponentials of $A$ and $B$ separately, our randomized formulas achieve $\mathcal O(α^2)$ error scaling at the cost of only doubling the gate depth of the corresponding deterministic formula. We further prove an $Ω(α)$ lower bound for deterministic product formulas. In a stronger access model, allowing exponentials of $A+αB_\ell$ for $B = \sum_{\ell}B_\ell$, our randomized formula, based on Trotter Heuristic Resource Improved Formulas for Time-dynamics (THRIFT)~[J. L. Bosse et al., Nat. Commun. 16, 2673 (2025)], achieves $\mathcal O(α^3)$ error scaling with only constant-factor expected gate overhead. We also establish an $Ω(α^2)$ lower bound for deterministic product formulas in this access model. Numerical simulations confirm gate-count reductions for simulating physically motivated systems.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces two new classes of randomized product formulas (Trotter formulas) for simulating quantum systems with separated energy scales, achieving improved error scaling (O(α²) and O(α³)) at low gate overhead, with matching lower bounds for deterministic formulas.
AI.motivation: Product formulas are the most practical methods for quantum simulation, but when Hamiltonians have separated energy scales (H = A + αB with small α), standard deterministic formulas suffer from poor error scaling. The authors seek randomized approaches that achieve better error scaling with minimal additional gate overhead.
AI.method: Two new classes of randomized product formulas are introduced: (1) in the standard access model (exponentials of A and B separately), randomized formulas achieve O(α²) error with only doubling the gate depth of the deterministic formula; (2) in a stronger access model (exponentials of A + αB_l for B = Σ B_l), a THRIFT-based randomized formula achieves O(α³) error with constant-factor expected gate overhead. Deterministic lower bounds of Ω(α) and Ω(α²) are proven for the two access models, respectively.
AI.result: The randomized formulas achieve O(α²) and O(α³) error scaling in the two access models, respectively, with minimal gate overhead (doubling and constant-factor, respectively). Lower bounds Ω(α) and Ω(α²) for deterministic product formulas are established, demonstrating the advantage of randomization. Numerical simulations confirm gate-count reductions for physically motivated systems.
AI.conclusion: Randomized product formulas provably outperform deterministic ones for simulating Hamiltonians with separated energy scales, achieving quadratically (or even cubically) better error scaling in α with only constant or doubling gate overhead, validated numerically on physical systems.

title: Emergent Non-Markovian Nonlinear Qubit From Collective Spin Interactions
summary: Open-system descriptions are typically introduced by coupling a quantum system to an external environment. Here we show that a closed interacting many-body system can itself generate a controlled non-Markovian quantum channel acting on a reduced nonlinear qubit through finite-size corrections to a nonlinear mean-field limit. We demonstrate this using the Kitagawa-Ueda one-axis twisting model, $H=χJ_z^2$, a paradigmatic model of collective spin dynamics, spin squeezing, and two-component Bose-Einstein condensates. Although the large-$N$ regime of this model has been extensively studied, the conventional fixed-$χ$ scaling does not yield a nontrivial dynamical large-$N$ limit. In this paper, we investigate a complementary large-$N$ formulation obtained from the double limit $N\rightarrow\infty$ and $χ\rightarrow O(g/N)$, where $g$ is a coupling constant. We derive the leading finite-$N$ corrections to this limit and show that they correspond to an emergent non-Markovian dephasing process, producing a Gaussian decay of the Bloch-vector coherence with characteristic timescale $t_\varphi\geq\sqrt{N}/(2g)$. Exact finite-$N$ calculations demonstrate that this effective open-system description becomes quantitatively accurate for systems containing on the order of one hundred qubits. The resulting framework provides a microscopic realization of non-Markovian dephasing generated intrinsically by a closed many-body system and enables efficient simulation of collective quantum dynamics beyond unitary mean-field theory. These results link the long-studied phenomenon of phase diffusion in atomic ensembles and Bose-Einstein condensates to the growing effort to characterize non-Markovian, beyond-Lindblad noise in quantum computing hardware, providing a rare case in which such a noise channel is derived from microscopic dynamics rather than fit phenomenologically.

AI.tldr: A closed many-body system (Kitagawa-Ueda one-axis twisting model) can intrinsically generate a controlled non-Markovian quantum channel acting on a reduced qubit, arising from finite-size corrections to a nonlinear mean-field limit. The leading finite-N corrections produce non-Markovian dephasing with Gaussian Bloch-vector coherence decay on timescale t_φ ≥ √N/(2g), quantitatively accurate for systems of ~100 qubits.
AI.motivation: To provide a microscopic derivation of non-Markovian noise from closed many-body dynamics, rather than phenomenological fitting, linking phase diffusion in atomic ensembles to beyond-Lindblad noise characterization in quantum computing.
AI.method: The authors study a complementary large-N formulation of the Kitagawa-Ueda model H=χJ_z² via a double limit N→∞ and χ→O(g/N). They derive leading finite-N corrections to the nonlinear mean-field limit and identify them as an emergent non-Markovian dephasing process, validated by exact finite-N calculations.
AI.result: The effective open-system description produces Gaussian coherence decay with timescale t_φ ≥ √N/(2g) and becomes quantitatively accurate for systems with ~100 qubits, providing efficient simulation of collective quantum dynamics beyond unitary mean-field theory.
AI.conclusion: This work demonstrates that closed interacting many-body systems can intrinsically generate non-Markovian quantum channels, providing a rare microscopic origin for beyond-Lindblad noise and connecting phase diffusion phenomena in BECs to quantum computing hardware noise characterization.

title: A Quantum-Enhanced Feedback Oscillator
summary: Feedback oscillators, such as lasers and masers, serve as time references in modern computing, communication, and measurement. Quantum fluctuations ultimately limit their phase stability and ability to keep time precisely; in the absence of quantum engineering, their phase stability is bounded by a standard quantum limit (SQL). Techniques to improve the frequency stability of feedback oscillators beyond the SQL have been theorized, but have not yet been demonstrated. We demonstrate an opto-electronic oscillator (OEO), a type of feedback oscillator, with phase stability approaching the SQL. We then engineer the OEO's quantum state to improve its phase stability, thereby demonstrating the essential principle quantum-enhancement of feedback oscillators. Similar techniques may be employed to evade the SQL in other feedback oscillators such as masers and lasers.

AI.tldr: This paper demonstrates an opto-electronic oscillator (OEO) with phase stability approaching the standard quantum limit (SQL), and then engineers its quantum state to surpass the SQL, marking the first experimental demonstration of quantum-enhanced phase stability in a feedback oscillator.
AI.motivation: Feedback oscillators (lasers, masers) underpin modern timing and communication systems, but their phase stability is fundamentally bounded by the standard quantum limit (SQL) due to quantum fluctuations. While techniques to surpass the SQL have been theorized, none had been experimentally demonstrated, so this work aims to achieve and validate quantum-enhanced phase stability in a feedback oscillator.
AI.method: The authors built an opto-electronic oscillator (OEO) and first characterized its phase stability, showing it approaches the SQL. They then engineered the quantum state of the OEO to improve its phase stability beyond the SQL, demonstrating the principle of quantum-enhanced feedback oscillators.
AI.result: The OEO achieved phase stability approaching the standard quantum limit, and through quantum state engineering, its phase stability was improved beyond the SQL—providing the first experimental demonstration of quantum-enhancement in a feedback oscillator.
AI.conclusion: The demonstrated quantum-state engineering technique can be applied to evade the SQL in other feedback oscillators such as masers and lasers, paving the way for higher-precision timekeeping and measurement in practical systems.

title: Multistage Rewinding Decoder for QLDPC Codes
comment: Accepted for presentation at the 2026 IEEE International Conference on Quantum Computing and Engineering (QCE 2026)
summary: In this paper, we propose a multistage decoding framework that leverages internal information produced by an underlying message-passing decoder. The proposed method targets the failure dynamics caused by both classical trapping sets and degenerate errors supported on symmetric stabilizers, which are among the primary limitations of iterative decoding for QLDPC codes. To identify unreliable variable nodes, we introduce a heuristic metric that combines several dynamical features of the decoder, including variable-node log likelihood reliabilities, hard-decision oscillations, the number of adjacent unsatisfied checks, and the soft information contributed by unsatisfied checks. Based on this ranking metric, the decoder performs guided rewinds by selectively forcing the initial log likelihood ratio values of the most suspicious variable nodes and restarting the message-passing decoder under the corresponding forced configuration. To manage the combinatorial growth of candidate configurations, the search is formulated within a beam- search framework with controlled beam width. In addition, we introduce a pruning metric based on the combination of the residual syndrome weight and a posteriori reliability of the decoder output, thereby retaining only the most promising search paths. Logical error rate results demonstrate that the proposed decoder significantly outperforms the normalized min- sum decoder and achieves competitive performance with belief propagation enhanced by order-10 ordered statistics decoding.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes a multistage decoding framework for QLDPC codes that uses a heuristic metric to identify unreliable variable nodes based on message-passing decoder dynamics, then performs guided rewinds via selective LLR forcing within a beam-search framework with pruning metrics to tackle classical trapping sets and degenerate symmetric stabilizer errors.
AI.motivation: Iterative decoding of QLDPC codes suffers from failure dynamics caused by classical trapping sets and degenerate errors supported on symmetric stabilizers, which are primary limitations limiting decoding performance.
AI.method: The method introduces a heuristic ranking metric combining variable-node log likelihood reliabilities, hard-decision oscillations, adjacent unsatisfied checks count, and soft info from unsatisfied checks. Decoder performs guided rewinds by forcing initial LLRs of most suspicious variable nodes and restarting message-passing decoding under forced configurations, within a beam-search framework with controlled beam width and a pruning metric based on residual syndrome weight and a posteriori reliability.
AI.result: The proposed decoder significantly outperforms the normalized min-sum decoder and achieves competitive performance with belief propagation enhanced by order-10 ordered statistics decoding.
AI.conclusion: The multistage decoding framework with beam-search-guided rewinds and informed pruning effectively addresses both trapping sets and degenerate errors in QLDPC codes, offering strong logical error rate performance.

title: A Universal Entanglement Witness Generator
summary: Entanglement witnesses are essential for certifying entanglement, yet constructing ones that are both noise-robust and economical in measurement settings remains challenging - particularly beyond qubits and for non-stabilizer ("magic") states. We present a machine-learning method that, given a target state and a user-specified number of measurement settings, generates an entanglement witness optimized for noise tolerance in the neighborhood of that state, requiring only local measurements. The approach is fully general, applying to multipartite qubit and qudit systems alike, including non-stabilizer states. For N qudits of dimension d, we train on the fully-separable eigenstates of each qudit's SU(d) generators to find a prototype witness, then tune the witness's bias term via gradient descent to maximize noise tolerance. Adversarial training further strengthens the witnesses, delivering greater noise tolerance with even fewer settings; critically, under this scheme the required training-set size becomes independent of system size. We package the entire pipeline as an automated script that, in every case we tested, produces witnesses surpassing all existing methods in noise tolerance and/or number of measurement settings. We demonstrate the method on Bell, GHZ, W, and hypergraph states, along with a range of qudit states, spanning 2-6 qubits, bipartite qudits up to d=10, and tripartite qutrits. Our witnesses achieve perfect accuracy across both physical experimental test states and large numerical sets of separable mixed states-including 30 million test states for a 3-qubit W-state witness and 10 million for a 4-qubit hypergraph-state witness-and we experimentally confirm the noise tolerance of Bell- and hypergraph state witnesses on both photonic and superconducting platforms, respectively.

AI.tldr: A machine-learning method that generates noise-robust entanglement witnesses with user-specified numbers of measurement settings, applicable to multipartite qubit and qudit systems (including non-stabilizer states), outperforming existing methods across all tested cases and validated experimentally on photonic and superconducting platforms.
AI.motivation: Constructing entanglement witnesses that are both noise-robust and economical in measurement settings is challenging, especially beyond qubits and for non-stabilizer ("magic") states. Existing methods struggle to balance these competing requirements, motivating a general and automated approach.
AI.method: The method uses machine learning: given a target state and a user-specified number of measurement settings, it trains on fully-separable eigenstates of SU(d) generators to find a prototype witness, then tunes the witness's bias term via gradient descent to maximize noise tolerance. Adversarial training further strengthens the witnesses, making the required training-set size independent of system size. Only local measurements are required.
AI.result: The method produces witnesses surpassing all existing methods in noise tolerance and/or number of measurement settings across all tested cases. Demonstrated on Bell, GHZ, W, and hypergraph states, spanning 2-6 qubits, bipartite qudits up to d=10, and tripartite qutrits. Achieved perfect accuracy on up to 30 million test states, with experimental confirmation on photonic and superconducting platforms.
AI.conclusion: The proposed fully general, automated ML-based approach delivers superior noise-robust entanglement witnesses with minimal measurement settings across a wide range of systems, including magic states, and is validated both numerically at scale and experimentally, offering a practical tool for entanglement certification.

title: Playing Nonlocal Games with Little to No Shared Randomness
summary: Bell nonlocality reveals correlations that cannot be explained by classical models and plays a central role in quantum information theory. In this work, we investigate classical models of Bell nonlocality under restrictions on shared randomness. For bipartite scenarios with bounded shared randomness, the set of classical correlations becomes nonconvex. We characterize the correlations achievable without shared randomness through the simultaneous evaluation of multiple linear Bell functionals. We then extend our analysis to quantum networks by relaxing the standard assumption of source independence. In this setting, the feasibility constraints derived for the bipartite case can be used to certify source dependence, and we further construct nonlinear inequalities that distinguish classical models with correlated sources from correlations achievable in standard quantum networks. As an application, we show that these nonlinear network inequalities give rise to an entropic Bell inequality for bipartite scenarios with limited shared randomness.

AI.tldr: This paper studies Bell nonlocality under restricted shared randomness and relaxed source-independence assumptions in quantum networks, deriving feasibility constraints and nonlinear inequalities that certify source dependence and lead to entropic Bell inequalities.
AI.motivation: Standard Bell nonlocality assumes unlimited shared randomness and independent sources in networks. The authors aim to characterize classical correlations when these assumptions are relaxed—either bounded shared randomness in bipartite scenarios or correlated (non-independent) sources in quantum networks—since these constraints arise naturally in practical implementations.
AI.method: The authors characterize the nonconvex set of classical correlations with bounded shared randomness by simultaneously evaluating multiple linear Bell functionals. They extend this framework to quantum networks by relaxing source independence, deriving feasibility constraints for the bipartite case to certify source dependence, and constructing nonlinear inequalities to distinguish correlated-source classical models from standard quantum network correlations.
AI.result: The derived nonlinear network inequalities are shown to yield an entropic Bell inequality for bipartite scenarios with limited shared randomness, providing a practical tool for certifying source dependence in quantum networks.
AI.conclusion: Restrictions on shared randomness and source independence lead to new, more refined classical correlation sets whose characterization enables the certification of source dependence in quantum networks and yields entropic Bell inequalities as applications.

title: Biorthogonal-only Floquet Dynamical Quantum Phase Transitions
summary: Non-Hermitian dynamical quantum phase transitions (DQPTs) are intrinsically sensitive to the choice of inner product under nonunitary time evolution. Although the biorthogonal formulation based on associated states provides a normalized Loschmidt echo with a probabilistic interpretation, previous studies have found biorthogonal and self-normal DQPTs to occur in the same parameter regimes, suggesting that the two forms of dynamical criticality are concomitant. Here we demonstrate that this is not the case. In an exactly solvable periodically driven non-Hermitian Su-Schrieffer-Heeger chain, we uncover a finite biorthogonal-only Floquet DQPT regime, where the biorthogonal Loschmidt rate becomes nonanalytic while the self-normal Loschmidt rate remains smooth. The critical conditions are obtained analytically, showing that the onset of biorthogonal Floquet DQPTs is locked to the exceptional lines of the effective Floquet Hamiltonian, whereas self-normal criticality has no corresponding spectral boundary. Moreover, for each critical momentum, the biorthogonal DQPT exhibits a pair of critical times within every driving period, whereas the self-normal DQPT exhibits only one. Our results establish a fundamental distinction between biorthogonal and self-normal DQPTs, thereby opening a route toward new nonequilibrium quantum phenomena in non-Hermitian systems.

AI.tldr: In an exactly solvable periodically driven non-Hermitian Su-Schrieffer-Heeger chain, the authors discover a finite regime where biorthogonal Floquet dynamical quantum phase transitions (DQPTs) occur while self-normal ones remain absent, demonstrating a fundamental distinction between the two formulations of non-Hermitian DQPTs.
AI.motivation: Previous studies suggested that biorthogonal and self-normal DQPTs in non-Hermitian systems always occur in the same parameter regimes, implying they are concomitant. The authors aim to test whether this apparent universality holds or whether the two forms of dynamical criticality can be separated.
AI.method: The authors analyze an exactly solvable periodically driven non-Hermitian Su-Schrieffer-Heeger chain. They analytically derive the critical conditions for biorthogonal Floquet DQPTs and compare them to self-normal criticality, examining the Loschmidt rate nonanalyticities and their spectral origins.
AI.result: The authors uncover a finite biorthogonal-only Floquet DQPT regime where the biorthogonal Loschmidt rate becomes nonanalytic while the self-normal rate stays smooth. Biorthogonal criticality is shown to be locked to exceptional lines of the effective Floquet Hamiltonian, whereas self-normal criticality has no spectral boundary. Additionally, biorthogonal DQPTs exhibit a pair of critical times per driving period, while self-normal DQPTs exhibit only one.
AI.conclusion: The results establish a fundamental distinction between biorthogonal and self-normal DQPTs in non-Hermitian systems, opening a route toward new nonequilibrium quantum phenomena and clarifying the role of inner-product choices in non-Hermitian dynamical criticality.

title: Breaking the Curse of Dimensionality in Quantum PDE Solvers via Gevrey Regularity
summary: We connect different degrees of smoothness of real-valued periodic functions to the cost of preparing their high-precision Fourier-basis amplitude encodings as quantum states. Our central observation is that the Gevrey hierarchy, which stratifies the space between smooth and analytic functions, provides a natural class for high-precision quantum algorithms. We then specialize to solving general linear partial differential equations (PDEs), showing how our Fourier methods do so efficiently at varying target precisions on a quantum computer. This also demonstrates how our framework enables passage from query-complexity results to explicit elementary gate counts. As an application, we introduce a hierarchy of many-body quantum simulation pipelines that harness these high-precision algorithms to probe the linear response of atomistic systems in first quantization. Each level of the hierarchy unlocks a further polynomial-degree quantum speedup, yielding a gradual improvement in simulation efficiency as quantum computers scale.

AI.tldr: This paper connects the smoothness of real-valued periodic functions (stratified by the Gevrey hierarchy) to the quantum cost of preparing high-precision Fourier-basis amplitude encodings, applies this to efficient quantum algorithms for general linear PDEs with explicit elementary gate counts, and introduces a hierarchy of many-body quantum simulation pipelines for linear response of atomistic systems in first quantization that yield progressive polynomial quantum speedups.
AI.motivation: The authors aim to establish a principled relationship between function smoothness and the quantum resource cost of high-precision amplitude encoding, and to translate query-complexity results into explicit gate counts for practical quantum algorithms, particularly for solving linear PDEs and simulating many-body systems.
AI.method: The paper leverages the Gevrey hierarchy—a stratification between smooth and analytic functions—as a natural class for high-precision quantum algorithms. It develops Fourier-based amplitude encoding methods whose cost depends on the Gevrey order, applies these to general linear PDE solvers, and builds a hierarchy of first-quantized many-body quantum simulation pipelines for probing linear response of atomistic systems.
AI.result: The paper shows that different smoothness levels in the Gevrey hierarchy lead to varying quantum costs for high-precision Fourier encodings, enables explicit elementary gate counts from query-complexity results, and demonstrates that each level of the proposed simulation hierarchy unlocks a further polynomial-degree quantum speedup for many-body linear response computations.
AI.conclusion: The Gevrey hierarchy provides a natural framework for analyzing and achieving high-precision quantum algorithms, yielding efficient linear PDE solvers with explicit resource estimates and a scalable hierarchy of quantum simulation pipelines that progressively improve efficiency as quantum hardware matures.

title: Quantum Chinese Remainder Clock
summary: The Chinese remainder theorem is used in metrology for extending the range of quantum clocks/radar/interferometry, where the phase of a signal is known relative to a set of oscillators with different periods. This paper investigates the performance of a quantum-mechanical Chinese remainder clock, consisting of atoms/oscillators with pairwise coprime periods. We provide the optimal initial state and the optimal Heisenberg-limited quantum measurements for measuring time up to the product of the periods. We introduce a novel fault-tolerant post-processing protocol that allows reconstruction of the correct time even in the presence of errors in the remainders.

AI.tldr: This paper investigates a quantum-mechanical Chinese remainder clock—a system of atoms/oscillators with pairwise coprime periods that extends the measurement range of time beyond individual period limits. It derives the optimal initial state and Heisenberg-limited quantum measurements for time measurement up to the product of periods, and introduces a fault-tolerant post-processing protocol that reconstructs the correct time despite errors in the remainders.
AI.motivation: The Chinese remainder theorem is a fundamental tool in metrology for extending the range of quantum clocks, radar, and interferometry. However, the quantum-mechanical implementation of such systems—particularly the optimal quantum states and measurements—and the robustness to errors in remainder measurements had not been fully explored.
AI.method: The authors formulate a quantum-mechanical Chinese remainder clock using atoms/oscillators with pairwise coprime periods. They identify the optimal initial (entangled) state and Heisenberg-limited quantum measurements for time estimation up to the product of all periods. They also develop a novel fault-tolerant post-processing protocol capable of recovering the correct time even when some remainders contain errors.
AI.result: The optimal initial state and optimal Heisenberg-limited measurements are provided, achieving the fundamental quantum limit for time estimation over the extended range. The proposed fault-tolerant post-processing protocol successfully reconstructs the correct time in the presence of errors in the remainders, addressing a practical robustness concern.
AI.conclusion: The work provides a complete quantum-theoretic treatment of the Chinese remainder clock, including optimal states and measurements, and introduces error-resilient decoding that makes the protocol practically viable despite imperfect remainder measurements.

title: Stable three-dimensional solitons in spin-orbit-coupled atomic-molecular condensates
summary: We elaborate a mechanism for the creation of stable three-dimensional (3D) solitons in spin-orbit-coupled (SOC) atomic-molecular Bose-Einstein condensate, modeled by the mean-field equations with the quadratic three-wave interaction, characterized by mismatch $α$. The planar (effectively two-dimensional) SOC is applied to the soliton's atomic component, structuring it as a mixed mode (MM) or semi-vortex (SV). The molecular component of the SV soliton is shaped as a 3D vortex, while the molecular component in the MM soliton is an MM too. The solitons exist up to a critical value of $α$. The system demonstrates a relatively large norm share of the vortex components, exceeding $50\%$ of the total norm, which is an essential feature of SOC-supported solitons. This is scheme for realizing stable vortex solitons in free space with the quadratic nonlinearity.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes a mechanism for creating stable 3D solitons in a spin-orbit-coupled (SOC) atomic-molecular Bose-Einstein condensate with quadratic three-wave interactions. The system supports two types of solitons — mixed modes (MM) and semi-vortices (SV) — with the molecular component forming a 3D vortex in the SV case. These solitons exist up to a critical momentum mismatch α, and exhibit a large vortex-component norm share (over 50% of total norm). The scheme enables stable vortex solitons in free space using quadratic nonlinearity.
AI.motivation: To realize stable three-dimensional vortex solitons in free space, which are generally difficult to stabilize without external traps or nonlocal nonlinearities, by leveraging spin-orbit coupling in an atomic-molecular Bose-Einstein condensate with quadratic three-wave mixing.
AI.method: The system is modeled by mean-field equations with quadratic three-wave interaction characterized by a mismatch parameter α. Effective 2D SOC is applied to the soliton's atomic component, structuring it as either a mixed mode (MM) or semi-vortex (SV). The molecular component of SV solitons is shaped as a 3D vortex, while for MM solitons the molecular component is also an MM. Stability is analyzed via soliton existence up to a critical α value and norm-share diagnostics.
AI.result: Stable 3D solitons exist in the SOC atomic-molecular BEC up to a critical value of the mismatch parameter α. The solitons feature a large norm share of vortex components exceeding 50% of the total norm, an essential signature of SOC-supported solitons. Both MM and SV soliton types are realized with corresponding molecular-component structures.
AI.conclusion: The scheme provides a viable route to realizing stable vortex solitons in free space with quadratic nonlinearity, enabled by spin-orbit coupling in an atomic-molecular condensate, with the vortex-component fraction dominating the soliton norm.

title: Near-Optimal Gap Amplification for Nonnegative Unentangled Quantum Proofs
summary:
We study gap amplification of the class $\mathsf{QMA}^{+}(2)$ characterized by unentangled quantum proofs whose amplitudes are nonnegative in the computational basis. This class was recently introduced by Jeronimo and Wu (STOC 2023), and its behavior depends sharply on the completeness-soundness gap: although it captures the power of $\mathsf{NEXP}$ for some small constant gap, it is equal to $\mathsf{QMA}(2)$ for larger constant gap. This is in stark contrast to $\mathsf{QMA}(2)$ where strong gap amplification is known due to the product test by Harrow and Montanaro (FOCS 2010, JACM 2013).
  In this paper, we prove for every completeness $c$ and soundness $s$ with $c-s=1/\mathrm{poly}(n)$, \[
  \mathsf{NEXP}
  = \mathsf{QMA}^{+}(2,c,s)
  =
  \mathsf{QMA}^{+}\left(2,1-\frac1{\mathrm{poly}(n)},\frac14+\frac1{\mathrm{poly}(n)}\right). \] Our result gives a clean complexity phase transition for $\mathsf{QMA}^{+}(2)$ since we have \[
  \mathsf{QMA}^{\mathbb R}(2)
  =
  \mathsf{QMA}^{+}\left(2,1-\frac1{\mathrm{poly}(n)},\frac14-\frac1{\mathrm{poly}(n)}\right), \] where $\mathsf{QMA}^{\mathbb R}(2)$ denotes $\mathsf{QMA}(2)$ with witnesses restricted to real amplitudes. Our amplification is thus optimal in the sense that a slight improvement of our soundness would have the collapse \[ \mathsf{QMA}^{\mathbb R}(2)=\mathsf{NEXP}. \]
  Our proof combines symmetric-subspace projections with the relation $\mathsf{QMA}^{+}(1)=\mathsf{NEXP}$ of Bassirian, Fefferman, and Marwaha (ITCS 2024). The main technical ingredient is a dimension-independent de Finetti theorem in Hilbert-Schmidt norm that applies when the number of registers under consideration grows logarithmically.

AI.tldr: This paper proves that for QMA⁺(2) — the class with nonnegative-amplitude unentangled quantum proofs — any gap of 1/poly(n) can be amplified to completeness 1-1/poly(n) and soundness 1/4+1/poly(n), and that this amplification is optimal since slight improvement would collapse QMA^R(2)=NEXP.
AI.motivation: Unlike QMA(2), where Harrow-Montanaro's product test provides strong gap amplification, the recently introduced QMA⁺(2) class (with nonnegative amplitudes) was poorly understood in terms of gap amplification. Its behavior depends sharply on the completeness-soundness gap, and understanding this sharp transition is crucial for characterizing its power.
AI.method: The proof combines symmetric-subspace projections with the known relation QMA⁺(1)=NEXP (from Bassirian, Fefferman, and Marwaha). The key technical ingredient is a dimension-independent de Finetti theorem in Hilbert-Schmidt norm applicable when the number of registers grows logarithmically.
AI.result: For every completeness c and soundness s with c-s=1/poly(n), NEXP = QMA⁺(2,c,s) = QMA⁺(2, 1-1/poly(n), 1/4+1/poly(n)). This reveals a clean complexity phase transition, since QMA^R(2) = QMA⁺(2, 1-1/poly(n), 1/4-1/poly(n)), demonstrating the amplification is optimal.
AI.conclusion: The paper establishes an essentially optimal gap amplification theorem for QMA⁺(2), showing it equals NEXP for inverse-polynomial gaps, while remaining distinct from QMA^R(2) — the amplification cannot be pushed further without causing the collapse QMA^R(2)=NEXP.

title: Quantum Decision Theory for Displacement Detection with Finite-Energy GKP States
summary: We develop a quantum-decision-theoretic framework for detecting phase-space displacements with finite-energy, $d$-level Gottesman-Kitaev-Preskill (GKP) probes. For single-mode and entanglement-assisted architectures, we derive the Bayesian minimum-error probability, the optimal Neyman-Pearson receiver-operating characteristic, and the corresponding minimum detectable displacement. Finite-energy effects are treated through exact theta-series displacement kernels, while pure loss followed by quantum-limited amplification is mapped to an effective Gaussian random-displacement channel. Entanglement removes preparation-dependent blind directions and preserves both logical displacement labels, although it does not surpass the pointwise optimized single-mode strategy in the noiseless pure-state setting. We benchmark the resulting protocols against coherent-state, direction-matched squeezed-vacuum, and twin-beam schemes at equal nominal squeezing. Numerical results identify finite-squeezing and lossy regimes in which GKP probes achieve both a lower Bayesian error and a smaller minimum detectable perturbation than the selected Gaussian receivers.

AI.tldr: This paper develops a quantum-decision-theoretic framework for detecting phase-space displacements using finite-energy, d-level GKP probes. It derives Bayesian minimum-error probability, Neyman-Pearson ROC, and minimum detectable displacement for both single-mode and entanglement-assisted architectures. Finite-energy effects are treated via exact theta-series displacement kernels, and loss followed by amplification is mapped to an effective Gaussian random-displacement channel. GKP probes are benchmarked against Gaussian receivers, showing advantages in finite-squeezing and lossy regimes.
AI.motivation: To establish a rigorous quantum decision-theoretic framework for GKP-based displacement detection, addressing finite-energy effects and lossy channel behaviors that previous ideal-GKP treatments neglected, and to benchmark these quantum-correction-code probes against conventional Gaussian-state receivers.
AI.method: The framework derives Bayesian minimum-error probability and Neyman-Pearson receiver-operating characteristics for GKP-probe displacement detection. Finite-energy corrections are handled via exact theta-series displacement kernels. Pure loss followed by quantum-limited amplification is mapped to an effective Gaussian random-displacement channel. Both single-mode and entanglement-assisted (twin-beam style) architectures are analyzed and compared to coherent-state, direction-matched squeezed-vacuum, and twin-beam Gaussian schemes at equal nominal squeezing.
AI.result: Entanglement removes preparation-dependent blind directions and preserves both logical displacement labels but does not surpass the pointwise optimized single-mode strategy in the noiseless pure-state setting. Numerical results reveal finite-squeezing and lossy regimes where GKP probes achieve both lower Bayesian error and smaller minimum detectable perturbation than the selected Gaussian receivers.
AI.conclusion: GKP probes offer practical advantages over Gaussian receivers for phase-space displacement detection in realistic finite-energy and lossy conditions, with single-mode strategies generally outperforming entanglement-assisted ones in the noiseless regime.

title: Time-reparameterisation invariant quantum evolution law: the lack of absolute time does not imply a stationary global state
summary: We challenge the common belief that if there is no absolute time parameter in physics, a quantum system described without reference to an external clock can be assumed to be in a stationary state of its Hamiltonian. We present a time-reparameterisation invariant quantum evolution law, which for a given initial condition predicts the same trajectory in state space as the Schrödinger equation, except that for nontrivial trajectories it does not predict the speed at which the trajectory is traversed. The solutions of this evolution law are all time-reparameterised solutions of the Schrödinger equation. We show how the predictions of the Schrödinger equation are recovered relative to an internal clock in this framework. In contrast to the Page-Wootters formalism or Dirac's quantisation of the Hamiltonian constraint, here the global sate is not stationary. We discuss the assumptions leading to the common conclusion that the state can be taken stationary and suggest that they need to be revisited.

AI.tldr: The paper challenges the assumption that quantum systems without an external clock must be in stationary states of their Hamiltonian, presenting a time-reparameterisation invariant evolution law that predicts the same state-space trajectory as the Schrödinger equation but not the traversal speed, with all solutions being time-reparameterised Schrödinger solutions.
AI.motivation: The authors aim to question the widely held belief that in the absence of absolute time, a closed quantum system must be described by a stationary state. This has implications for quantum gravity and relational quantum mechanics where external clocks are unavailable.
AI.method: The paper constructs a time-reparameterisation invariant quantum evolution law. It demonstrates that its solutions correspond to all time-reparameterised solutions of the Schrödinger equation, recovering Schrödinger predictions relative to an internal clock, while contrasting with the Page-Wootters formalism and Dirac quantization where the global state is stationary.
AI.result: For a given initial condition, the proposed evolution law predicts the same trajectory in state space as the Schrödinger equation for nontrivial trajectories, but does not determine the speed of traversal. Schrödinger predictions are recovered relative to an internal clock, and the global state is shown to be non-stationary, contrary to common assumptions.
AI.conclusion: The assumption that a clockless quantum system must be in a stationary Hamiltonian eigenstate is flawed and needs to be revisited, as there exists a consistent time-reparameterisation invariant evolution law that permits non-stationary global states.

title: Bell nonlocality with directly generated telecom-band spin-photon entanglement
summary: Quantum nonlocality, typically revealed through entanglement distribution across quantum networks, is a cornerstone of quantum information science. Long-distance distribution of entanglement requires the information carrier, i.e. flying photons, to operate in the minimum-loss telecom band of optical fiber. While extensive efforts have been devoted to the direct generation of entanglement between C-band telecom photons and various stationary spins, the verification of quantum nonlocality remains an outstanding challenge. Here, utilizing a dipole transition in rubidium atoms with a wavelength of 1530 nm and a cavity-assisted protocol, we achieve resonant excitation and direct emission of C-band telecom photons from a single atom, generating spin-photon entanglement with a measured Bell state fidelity exceeding 91.4%. We then verify Bell nonlocality by observing a Bell inequality violation of 2.455(77) > 2 using this high-quality entangled pair. These results extend the wavelength of a single-atom quantum emitter to the telecom C-band, achieving sufficiently high-fidelity spin-photon entanglement to finally verify Bell nonlocality. This work thereby provides a promising building block for a large-scale atom-based quantum network capable of distributed quantum metrology and long-distance quantum communication.

AI.tldr: This paper demonstrates the generation of high-fidelity spin-photon entanglement from a single rubidium atom emitting C-band telecom photons at 1530 nm, achieving a Bell state fidelity exceeding 91.4% and verifying Bell nonlocality with a Bell inequality violation of 2.455(77) > 2. This work extends single-atom quantum emitters to the telecom C-band, providing a building block for large-scale atom-based quantum networks.
AI.motivation: Long-distance entanglement distribution requires photons operating in the minimum-loss telecom C-band of optical fiber. While entanglement between C-band telecom photons and stationary spins has been generated, the verification of quantum nonlocality remained an outstanding challenge.
AI.method: The authors utilize a dipole transition in rubidium atoms at 1530 nm with a cavity-assisted protocol to achieve resonant excitation and direct emission of C-band telecom photons from a single atom, generating spin-photon entanglement that is then used to verify Bell nonlocality.
AI.result: Measured Bell state fidelity exceeding 91.4% for the spin-photon entangled pair, and observation of a Bell inequality violation of 2.455(77) > 2, thereby verifying Bell nonlocality.
AI.conclusion: This work extends single-atom quantum emitter wavelengths to the telecom C-band with sufficiently high entanglement fidelity to verify Bell nonlocality, providing a promising building block for large-scale atom-based quantum networks supporting distributed quantum metrology and long-distance quantum communication.

title: Gravitational Casimir-Polder interaction in a thermal bath
summary: We have investigated, by separating the contributions from thermal fluctuations (tf) and the radiation reaction (rr), the gravitational Casimir-Polder interaction between a gravitationally polarizable two-level object and an infinite gravitational Dirichlet boundary in a thermal bath at a temperature $T$. The results indicate that the rr-contribution to the interaction potential is independent of the temperature, whereas the tf-contribution is generally governed by a nontrivial interplay between the thermal corrections and the polarization effect. Here, the object-to-boundary distance, the characteristic transition wavelength of the object and the thermal wavelength of gravitons are denoted by $L$, $λ$ and $β$, respectively. In contrast to the vacuum case, where the interaction potential scales as $L^{-5}$ for $L\llλ$ and $L^{-6}$ for $L\ggλ$, corresponding to an always repulsive force, qualitatively new behaviors emerge at high temperatures. Particularly, when $\sqrt[4]{βλ^3}\ll L\llλ$ and the object is polarizable within the plane perpendicular to the boundary, a novel scaling of $TL^{-1}$ arises; when $\sqrt{βλ}\ll L\llλ$ and the object is polarizable along the vertical-to-boundary axis, the interaction force becomes surprisingly attractive. At extremely high temperatures and large distances, i.e. when $β\ll λ\ll L$, the potential oscillates with the distance $L$ and thus an attractive or repulsive and even vanishing force can be resulted, depending on the exact values of $L$.
