Our work demonstrates that thermal gravitons can act as an active control mechanism for quantum gravitational interactions, and temperature, polarization configuration, and object-to-boundary distance jointly determine the magnitude, scaling law, and even the attractive or repulsive nature of the interaction force.

AI.tldr: This paper theoretically investigates the gravitational Casimir-Polder interaction between a gravitationally polarizable two-level object and an infinite gravitational Dirichlet boundary in a thermal bath, separating contributions from thermal fluctuations and radiation reaction. It reveals temperature-dependent new behaviors including novel scaling laws, attractive forces, and oscillating potentials at high temperatures.
AI.motivation: To understand how thermal gravitons affect quantum gravitational interactions, extending the known vacuum Casimir-Polder results (which always produce repulsive forces with L^-5 and L^-6 scaling) to finite-temperature regimes where qualitatively new phenomena may emerge.
AI.method: The interaction potential is decomposed into two contributions: thermal fluctuations (tf) and radiation reaction (rr). Analytical calculations are performed for an infinite gravitational Dirichlet boundary, analyzing the distance and temperature dependence across different regimes defined by the object-to-boundary distance L, the characteristic transition wavelength λ, and the thermal wavelength of gravitons β.
AI.result: The rr-contribution is temperature-independent, while the tf-contribution depends on a complex interplay between thermal corrections and polarization. At high temperatures: (1) for sqrt[4]{βλ^3} ≪ L ≪ λ with in-plane polarizability, a novel TL^-1 scaling arises; (2) for sqrt{βλ} ≪ L ≪ λ with vertical polarizability, the force becomes attractive (unlike the vacuum case); (3) for β ≪ λ ≪ L, the potential oscillates with L, producing distance-dependent attractive, repulsive, or vanishing forces.
AI.conclusion: Thermal gravitons can serve as an active control mechanism for quantum gravitational interactions. Temperature, polarization configuration, and object-to-boundary distance jointly determine the magnitude, scaling law, and attractive/repulsive nature of the interaction force.

title: Preserving Heisenberg-Limited Metrological Information during Storage via Correlated-Noise Correction
summary: Quantum error correction has become an indispensable tool for restoring Heisenberg-limited precision in noisy quantum metrology. Existing protocols, however, almost exclusively focus on correcting noise during the signal-encoding stage and implicitly assume that the probe is measured immediately after sensing. In many quantum information processing tasks, the encoded probe must instead be stored before subsequent quantum operations, during which environmental noise can significantly degrade the accumulated metrological information. Here, we propose a correlated-noise correction (CNC) protocol for protecting quantum probes during the storage stage. By correlating probe errors with auxiliary qubits through fixed two-body entangling gates, memory errors are converted into measurable syndromes that are extracted only once after storage. We show that the protocol naturally extends from single-qubit to multi-qubit probes and protects the stored quantum Fisher information against dephasing, bit-flip, and amplitude-damping noise. Furthermore, we demonstrate that preserving the quantum Fisher information does not necessarily require restoring the entire quantum state when the probe is measured immediately after storage, whereas full state recovery becomes essential for subsequent rounds of quantum signal processing. Our results establish correlated-noise correction as a practical framework for protecting metrological information during quantum memory and provide a useful building block for sensing-enabled quantum information processing.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes a correlated-noise correction (CNC) protocol that protects quantum probes from environmental noise during the storage stage of quantum metrology, using fixed two-body entangling gates to correlate probe errors with auxiliary qubits and extract syndromes after storage.
AI.motivation: Existing quantum error correction protocols for noisy quantum metrology focus almost exclusively on correcting noise during the signal-encoding stage, implicitly assuming immediate measurement after sensing. However, in many quantum information processing tasks, the encoded probe must be stored before further operations, during which environmental noise degrades the accumulated metrological information.
AI.method: The CNC protocol correlates probe errors with auxiliary qubits through fixed two-body entangling gates, converting memory errors into measurable syndromes extracted once after storage. The protocol extends from single-qubit to multi-qubit probes and handles dephasing, bit-flip, and amplitude-damping noise.
AI.result: The protocol protects stored quantum Fisher information against dephasing, bit-flip, and amplitude-damping noise. It also reveals that preserving quantum Fisher information does not require full state recovery when the probe is measured immediately after storage, but full state recovery is necessary for subsequent rounds of quantum signal processing.
AI.conclusion: The results establish correlated-noise correction as a practical framework for protecting metrological information during quantum memory, providing a useful building block for sensing-enabled quantum information processing.

title: Hamiltonian spectra in quantum computers through the generalized eigenvalue method
summary: Quantum computers can generate real-time correlators of field theories. By adapting the generalized eigenvalue problem to these correlators, energy eigenvalues can be extracted directly. The method is tested using both classical simulations and quantum hardware, successfully resolving several low-lying energy levels in agreement with exact diagonalization. Comparison with an alternative spectrum determination based on the Fourier transform of correlators shows that the proposed approach is substantially more efficient.

AI.tldr: Quantum computers are used to compute real-time correlators of field theories, and a generalized eigenvalue problem (GEP) method extracts energy eigenvalues directly from these correlators. The method is validated on both classical simulations and quantum hardware, resolving low-lying energy levels consistent with exact diagonalization, and is shown to be substantially more efficient than Fourier-transform-based spectrum extraction.
AI.motivation: Extracting energy eigenvalues from quantum-computed real-time correlators is a fundamental challenge in simulating field theories on quantum hardware. Traditional Fourier-transform approaches are inefficient, motivating the need for a more efficient spectrum extraction method.
AI.method: The approach adapts the generalized eigenvalue problem (GEP) to real-time correlators generated by quantum computers, allowing direct extraction of energy eigenvalues without needing Fourier transforms.
AI.result: The GEP-based method successfully resolves several low-lying energy levels on both classical simulations and quantum hardware, matching exact diagonalization results. It is substantially more efficient than the alternative Fourier-transform-based spectrum determination approach.
AI.conclusion: The generalized eigenvalue problem applied to quantum-generated real-time correlators is a highly efficient and accurate method for extracting energy spectra of field theories, outperforming Fourier-transform approaches while remaining suitable for current quantum hardware.

title: Opposite post-processing orders of fermionic horizon channels and their quantum-resource monotonicity
summary: Relativistic quantum-information studies in noninertial and black-hole settings often determine resource behavior through explicit calculations for particular input states and state functionals, leaving unclear whether the recurring monotonic trends originate from those choices or from a common underlying structure. In this work, we formulate the effective single-mode fermionic horizon transformation as a pair of complementary exterior and interior quantum channels, corresponding respectively to the physically accessible and inaccessible sectors, and establish exact post-processing orders in opposite directions. As the relativistic channel parameter $q$ increases, the exterior channel becomes progressively degraded, whereas the interior channel is ordered in the reverse direction. These relations extend to arbitrary multipartite settings. Consequently, every state functional that is non-increasing under the corresponding intermediate maps is non-increasing in homogeneous exterior sectors and non-decreasing in homogeneous interior sectors. The framework therefore applies to broad classes of quantum resources and correlations, including entanglement and occupation-basis coherence monotones, optimized Bell-functional quantities, and contractive-divergence correlation measures. We further numerically evaluate collective coherence based on the quantum Jensen-Shannon divergence (QJSD) in the Garfinkle-Horowitz-Strominger (GHS) dilaton-black-hole spacetime, illustrating the predicted homogeneous monotonicity. The recurring trends are therefore traced to a common channel-ordering structure, while the physical setting determines the parameterization of $q$ and the resource-theoretic monotonicity determines which output-state quantities inherit the order.

AI.tldr: This paper reformulates the effective single-mode fermionic horizon transformation in relativistic quantum information as a pair of complementary exterior and interior quantum channels with opposite post-processing orders. As the relativistic channel parameter q increases, the exterior channel degrades while the interior channel improves. This channel-ordering structure implies that any functional non-increasing under intermediate maps is monotonic in homogeneous exterior/interior sectors, unifying previously observed resource trends in noninertial and black-hole settings. The framework is applied to entanglement, coherence, Bell-functional, and divergence-based correlation measures, with numerical confirmation of collective coherence via quantum Jensen-Shannon divergence in a GHS dilaton black hole.
AI.motivation: Previous relativistic quantum-information studies in noninertial and black-hole settings relied on explicit calculations for specific input states and state functionals, leaving unclear whether recurring monotonic trends stem from particular choices or from a deeper common structure. The authors seek to identify the underlying unifying mechanism driving these trends.
AI.method: The authors formulate the effective single-mode fermionic horizon transformation as two complementary quantum channels (exterior/accessible and interior/inaccessible). They establish exact post-processing orders in opposite directions as the relativistic parameter q increases, show these extend to multipartite settings, and use this channel-ordering framework to derive general monotonicity results for any state functional that is non-increasing under intermediate maps. They numerically test collective coherence via QJSD in the GHS dilaton-black-hole spacetime.
AI.result: The exterior channel is progressively degraded with increasing q, while the interior channel is ordered in the reverse direction. The framework applies to entanglement and coherence monotones, optimized Bell-functional quantities, and contractive-divergence correlation measures. Numerical evaluation of QJSD-based collective coherence in the GHS spacetime confirms the predicted homogeneous monotonicity.
AI.conclusion: Recurring monotonic trends in relativistic quantum-information settings are traced to a common channel-ordering structure rather than to ad hoc state or functional choices. The physical setting dictates the parameterization of q, while resource-theoretic monotonicity determines which output-state quantities inherit the order.

title: Millisecond optical coherence and strong collective coupling in an integrated telecom rare-earth photonic platform
summary: Long-range quantum network nodes require the combination of strong light-matter coupling, long coherence times and in situ spectral control at telecom wavelengths. The coherence of erbium in integrated devices is held back by its hosts, which do not simultaneously provide the weakly magnetic nuclear-spin environment and the well-defined substitutional sites found in coherence-optimised bulk crystals. Here we bring such an optimised crystal onto a photonic chip, by bonding an Er${^{3+}}$:CaWO${_{4}}$ host without an adhesive interlayer to a high-${Q}$ electro-optically tuneable thin-film lithium niobate microring resonator. At an effective temperature of ${75}$ mK and a field of only ${0.2}$ T, the bonded ensemble retains an effective homogeneous linewidth of ${289\pm34}$ Hz (${T_\text{M}=1.10\pm0.13}$ ms), with spectral diffusion proceeding at ${86\pm18}$ Hz and saturating at ${1.5\pm0.2}$ kHz. Electro-optically tuning the resonator through the erbium optical transition resolves an avoided crossing with a collective cooperativity of ${C=6.7\pm0.4}$. Exploiting superhyperfine coupling to the host's ${^{183}}$W nuclear spins, we store and retrieve optical phase information over ${5}$ s with a visibility of ${0.935\pm0.015}$. Strong collective coupling, millisecond coherence and in situ spectral tuning in a single device thus establish heterogeneous integration leveraging coherence-optimised hosts as a route to scalable telecom quantum networks.

AI.tldr: The paper demonstrates heterogeneous integration of an Er3+:CaWO4 crystal (a coherence-optimised host) onto an electro-optically tunable thin-film lithium niobate microring resonator without an adhesive interlayer, achieving millisecond coherence, strong collective coupling (C=6.7), and 5-second optical memory at telecom wavelengths.
AI.motivation: Long-range quantum network nodes require simultaneous strong light-matter coupling, long coherence times, and in situ spectral control at telecom wavelengths. However, erbium in integrated devices is limited by its hosts, which fail to provide both the weakly magnetic nuclear-spin environment and well-defined substitutional sites found in coherence-optimised bulk crystals.
AI.method: The authors bond an Er3+:CaWO4 crystal directly (without adhesive interlayer) to a high-Q electro-optically tunable thin-film lithium niobate microring resonator, enabling integration of the coherence-optimised host onto a photonic chip.
AI.result: At 75 mK and 0.2 T, the bonded ensemble retains a homogeneous linewidth of 289±34 Hz (TM=1.10±0.13 ms), with spectral diffusion at 86±18 Hz saturating at 1.5±0.2 kHz. Electro-optical tuning reveals an avoided crossing with collective cooperativity C=6.7±0.4. Using superhyperfine coupling to 183W nuclear spins, optical phase information is stored and retrieved over 5 s with 0.935±0.015 visibility.
AI.conclusion: Strong collective coupling, millisecond coherence, and in situ spectral tuning in a single device establish heterogeneous integration leveraging coherence-optimised hosts as a viable route to scalable telecom quantum networks.

title: Catching Transpilation Drift with a CI/CD Workflow in Quantum Software Development
comment: Accepted for publication in the Q-SET Workshop at IEEE QCE 2026
summary: Quantum software workflows rely on compiler and provider toolchains that evolve independently of application source code. Consequently, an unchanged quantum circuit may transpile into a different target-specific realization after changes in SDK versions, optimization settings, basis gates, coupling maps, or backend descriptions. Such transpilation drift can affect circuit depth, gate composition, qubit mapping, and execution behavior, yet it is rarely monitored in CI/CD pipelines. This paper proposes a Quantum DevOps workflow for detecting transpilation drift before execution. The workflow transpiles source circuits against configured target profiles, computes structural drift metrics, records provenance and artifacts in MLflow, and raises configurable warnings or failures in GitHub Actions. Using representative circuits and target profiles, we show how drift checks can expose toolchain-induced changes and support reproducibility audits. The contribution is a practical CI/CD guardrail for making quantum compilation behavior observable, testable, and auditable.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes a Quantum DevOps workflow that detects transpilation drift in quantum software—where unchanged circuits compile differently across SDK/compiler toolchain changes—by running transpilation checks in CI/CD pipelines, recording provenance and artifacts in MLflow, and raising warnings/failures in GitHub Actions.
AI.motivation: Quantum compiler and provider toolchains evolve independently of application source code, causing unchanged quantum circuits to transpile into different target-specific realizations. This transpilation drift can affect circuit depth, gate composition, qubit mapping, and execution behavior, yet it is rarely monitored in CI/CD pipelines, making quantum compilation behavior opaque and difficult to audit.
AI.method: The workflow transpiles source circuits against configured target profiles, computes structural drift metrics, records provenance and artifacts in MLflow, and raises configurable warnings or failures in GitHub Actions as part of a CI/CD pipeline.
AI.result: Using representative circuits and target profiles, the authors demonstrate that drift checks can expose toolchain-induced changes and support reproducibility audits.
AI.conclusion: The contribution is a practical CI/CD guardrail that makes quantum compilation behavior observable, testable, and auditable, enabling detection of transpilation drift before execution.

title: Quantum-classical crossover in noisy monitored oscillators
comment: Main text: 12 pages, 8 figures. Appendices: 5 pages, 4 figures
summary: The quantum first-passage problem involves stochastic trajectories conditioned on measurement outcomes. The timing statistics of such trajectories remain largely unexplored in open quantum systems. Here, we investigate the first-passage time to an energy threshold for a ubiquitous model: a harmonic oscillator driven by classical additive noise. We find that projective measurements and energy quantization lead to substantial differences between the quantum and classical first-passage-time distributions at low thresholds, while these differences gradually diminish as the threshold energy increases. We treat the problem using both ensemble-averaged conditioned density-matrix dynamics and trajectory-resolved stochastic pure-state dynamics. The two descriptions yield indistinguishable timing statistics. Quantization effects appear in the ensemble-level phase-space distributions of the surviving states and vanish at larger threshold energies. Individual trajectories reveal emergent quantum signatures from the repeated measurements, such as persistent Wigner negativity. Our results provide a framework for using first-passage processes to create measurement-induced nonclassical resource states and to study the quantum-classical crossover of monitored systems.

AI.tldr: This paper studies the quantum first-passage problem in an open quantum system—a harmonic oscillator driven by classical additive noise—and finds that projective measurements and energy quantization cause notable differences between quantum and classical first-passage-time distributions at low energy thresholds, which diminish with increasing threshold. Both ensemble-averaged conditioned density-matrix dynamics and trajectory-resolved stochastic pure-state dynamics produce identical timing statistics. The work reveals quantized features in phase-space distributions and persistent Wigner negativity in individual measurement trajectories, offering a framework for generating nonclassical resource states via first-passage processes.
AI.motivation: The timing statistics of conditioned stochastic trajectories (first-passage processes) remain largely unexplored in open quantum systems, despite being well studied classically. The authors aim to investigate how quantum measurement and energy quantization modify first-passage-time statistics compared to classical predictions, and to understand the quantum-classical crossover in monitored systems.
AI.method: The authors analyze a harmonic oscillator driven by classical additive noise using two complementary theoretical descriptions: (1) ensemble-averaged conditioned density-matrix dynamics and (2) trajectory-resolved stochastic pure-state dynamics (quantum trajectories). They compute the first-passage time to an energy threshold and compare the quantum results with classical first-passage statistics, examining the phase-space distributions of surviving states and Wigner functions along individual trajectories.
AI.result: Projective measurements and energy quantization produce substantial differences between quantum and classical first-passage-time distributions at low energy thresholds, which gradually vanish as the threshold energy increases. The ensemble-averaged and trajectory-resolved descriptions yield indistinguishable timing statistics. Quantum effects appear as quantized structures in the ensemble-level phase-space distributions of surviving states at low thresholds, and individual trajectories exhibit emergent quantum signatures—such as persistent Wigner negativity—induced by repeated measurements.
AI.conclusion: The work establishes a framework for using first-passage processes to both generate measurement-induced nonclassical resource states and study the quantum–classical crossover of monitored open quantum systems, connecting timing statistics with quantum resource creation.

title: On Demand magnetic-Doppler nuclear frequency comb memory for hard X-ray photons
summary: Nuclear quantum memories in the hard X-ray regime offer some key advantages over their optical counterparts, such as broader bandwidth and lower background noise. A Doppler frequency comb protocol has been theoretically proposed [X. Zhang \textit{et al.}, Phys. Rev. Lett. \textbf{123}, 250504 (2019)] and recently demonstrated experimentally [S. Velten \textit{et al.}, Sci. Adv. \textbf{10}, eadn9825 (2024)] for the storage and retrieval of X-ray photons. However, achieving on-demand retrieval remains challenging because of the requirement for precise and synchronous mechanical motion of multiple absorbers. We propose a hybrid, magnetic-Doppler nuclear frequency comb composed of Doppler-shifted resonant absorbers with lifted nuclear spin degeneracy, which expands the Doppler comb structure. By synchronously reversing the directions of both the magnetic fields and absorber velocities, the system achieves time-reversed phase evolution dynamics that allows for efficient on-demand photon retrieval with significantly reduced mechanical complexity.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes a hybrid magnetic-Doppler nuclear frequency comb for hard X-ray quantum memories, combining Doppler-shifted resonant absorbers with lifted nuclear spin degeneracy to enable on-demand photon retrieval with reduced mechanical complexity compared to purely Doppler-based approaches.
AI.motivation: Nuclear quantum memories in the hard X-ray regime offer advantages over optical counterparts (broader bandwidth, lower background noise). However, on-demand retrieval is challenging in existing Doppler frequency comb protocols because it requires precise and synchronous mechanical motion of multiple absorbers.
AI.method: The authors propose a hybrid magnetic-Doppler nuclear frequency comb that combines Doppler-shifted resonant absorbers with lifted nuclear spin degeneracy (via magnetic fields), expanding the Doppler comb structure. By synchronously reversing both the magnetic field directions and absorber velocities, the system achieves time-reversed phase evolution dynamics for efficient on-demand photon retrieval.
AI.result: The proposed scheme achieves efficient on-demand photon retrieval with significantly reduced mechanical complexity compared to purely Doppler-based frequency comb protocols.
AI.conclusion: The magnetic-Doppler hybrid approach offers a practical pathway to on-demand hard X-ray quantum memories, mitigating the mechanical synchronization challenges of previous Doppler comb protocols while preserving the advantages of the X-ray regime.

title: Toward Standardized Quantum Provenance: A Cross-Provider Analysis, Unified API, and Reference Prototype
summary: Quantum software development requires provenance describing programs, compilation, execution, hardware characterization, results, and software environments, but providers expose this information through heterogeneous software development kits, application programming interfaces, and resource models. We analyze publicly documented provenance access across 15 quantum platforms spanning five hardware technologies and find fragmented, incomplete coverage, with compilation provenance weakest. We propose an evidence-aware OpenAPI 3.1 provenance contract and provider-adapter architecture, evaluated through a fixture-backed reference prototype at QMill covering Amazon Braket, IBM Quantum, and IonQ. All records validate against one common contract while preserving provider-specific semantics, explicit evidence origins, and graceful handling of incomplete data.

AI.tldr: This paper analyzes provenance access across 15 quantum platforms and proposes an OpenAPI 3.1-based provenance contract with a provider-adapter architecture to unify heterogeneous quantum software provenance data.
AI.motivation: Quantum software development requires comprehensive provenance (programs, compilation, execution, hardware characterization, results, software environments), but providers expose this via heterogeneous SDKs, APIs, and resource models, making it fragmented and incomplete—especially compilation provenance.
AI.method: Analyzed publicly documented provenance access across 15 quantum platforms spanning five hardware technologies; proposed an evidence-aware OpenAPI 3.1 provenance contract and provider-adapter architecture; evaluated via a fixture-backed reference prototype at QMill covering Amazon Braket, IBM Quantum, and IonQ.
AI.result: Found fragmented, incomplete provenance coverage with compilation provenance being weakest. The prototype demonstrated that all records validate against one common contract while preserving provider-specific semantics, explicit evidence origins, and graceful handling of incomplete data.
AI.conclusion: A unified, evidence-aware provenance contract with provider adapters can standardize quantum software provenance across diverse platforms while maintaining provider-specific semantics and robustness to incomplete data.

title: Energetic Cost of Temporal Information Processing in Quantum Reservoirs
summary: Quantum reservoir computing offers a promising route toward energy-efficient machine learning by processing temporal information with minimal training overhead. Yet, the physical principles linking its energetic cost to computational performance remain largely unexplored. Here we show that, in an interacting spin reservoir, information encoding and information processing are governed by distinct physical mechanisms. In the weak interacting regime, we derive an analytical expression for the average (switching) work, showing that the energetic cost of encoding new inputs is determined by the local response of the reservoir units. In contrast, interactions primarily redistribute the encoded information, generating memory and nonlinear features while only weakly affecting the work. This separation produces opposite correlations between energetic cost and performance for representative linear and nonlinear benchmark tasks. Our results identify the switching work as the energetic signature of information encoding and clarify when energetic efficiency and computational performance are compatible.

AI.tldr: This paper shows that in interacting spin-based quantum reservoir computing, information encoding and processing are governed by different physical mechanisms. In the weak-interaction regime, the energetic cost of encoding (switching work) is determined by local reservoir responses, while interactions mainly redistribute encoded information to create memory and nonlinearity at low energy cost. This leads to opposite correlations between energy cost and performance for linear versus nonlinear tasks.
AI.motivation: The connection between energetic cost and computational performance in quantum reservoir computing remains largely unexplored, despite the promise of energy-efficient machine learning. Understanding the physical principles linking these two aspects is essential for designing energy-efficient quantum reservoirs.
AI.method: The authors analyze an interacting spin reservoir in the weak-interaction regime. They derive an analytical expression for the average switching work associated with encoding new inputs, showing it depends on the local response of reservoir units. They then study how interactions redistribute encoded information (creating memory and nonlinear features) while weakly affecting the work, and measure correlations between energetic cost and performance on linear and nonlinear benchmark tasks.
AI.result: The energetic cost of information encoding is governed by local reservoir responses, while interactions primarily redistribute information to generate memory and nonlinear features with minimal energetic impact. This mechanistic separation produces opposite correlations between energy cost and computational performance for linear versus nonlinear benchmarks.
AI.conclusion: The switching work serves as the energetic signature of information encoding in quantum reservoir computing. Energetic efficiency and computational performance can be compatible when tasks align with the physical mechanism of information processing, clarifying when energy-efficient quantum reservoirs can also be computationally effective.

title: Machine Learning for Specialized QKD Aspects: A Survey of Adaptive Protocols, Free-Space Links, 6G Integration, and Steerability-Aware Security
summary: Quantum Key Distribution (QKD) provides information-theoretic security grounded in the laws of quantum mechanics, yet practical deployment increasingly extends beyond conventional point-to-point fiber links. Several rapidly emerging QKD directions are often studied separately, including adaptive protocol and parameter support; free-space, satellite, UAV, and high-altitude platform (HAP) channels; integration with IoT and 6G networks; quantum-secured federated learning; Quantum Machine Learning (QML) assisted decision support; and steerability-aware estimation for one-sided device-independent QKD. This survey examines how Machine Learning (ML), Reinforcement Learning (RL), and QML address these specialized scenarios and organizes the literature into five thematic pillars: (I) adaptive protocol and parameter support; (II) free-space, satellite, UAV, and HAP-assisted QKD; (III) QKD for IoT, 6G, and quantum-secured federated learning; (IV) QML-assisted QKD functions; and (V) steerability-aware and one-sided device-independent QKD security estimation. For each theme, we follow a consistent problem, conventional solution, and ML/RL/QML solution structure and summarize reported gains using metrics such as accuracy, mean absolute percentage error, QBER reduction, and secret key rate improvement. We further provide thematic and cross-theme comparison tables and identify open challenges, including dataset scarcity, transferability across weather and mobility conditions, interpretability, trustworthy QML, and the boundary between ML-based decision support and security certification. This survey serves as a focused reference for adaptive, non-terrestrial, and application-integrated QKD systems.

AI.tldr: A comprehensive survey organizing ML/RL/QML approaches for Quantum Key Distribution (QKD) into five thematic pillars: adaptive protocol support, non-terrestrial channels (free-space/satellite/UAV/HAP), IoT/6G/federated learning integration, QML-assisted QKD functions, and steerability-aware one-sided device-independent security estimation, with cross-theme comparisons and identified open challenges.
AI.motivation: Practical QKD deployment has expanded beyond point-to-point fiber links into diverse emerging scenarios (free-space, satellite, UAV, HAP, IoT, 6G, federated learning, device-independent settings), but these directions are often studied in isolation. A unified survey is needed to systematically examine how ML, RL, and QML address these specialized scenarios.
AI.method: The survey organizes literature into five thematic pillars and, for each theme, follows a consistent structure of problem, conventional solution, and ML/RL/QML solution, while summarizing reported gains via metrics such as accuracy, mean absolute percentage error, QBER reduction, and secret key rate improvement. It includes thematic and cross-theme comparison tables.
AI.result: Provides structured comparisons across the five QKD themes, quantifies reported performance gains, and identifies open challenges including dataset scarcity, transferability across weather and mobility conditions, interpretability, trustworthy QML, and the boundary between ML-based decision support and security certification.
AI.conclusion: This survey serves as a focused reference for adaptive, non-terrestrial, and application-integrated QKD systems, highlighting both the promise of ML/RL/QML in advancing QKD and the unresolved challenges that remain.

title: Randomness Certification and Trade-offs in the Prepare-and-Broadcast Scenario
summary: We investigate the prepare-and-broadcast scenario, a multipartite extension of dimension-constrained prepare-and-measure experiments in which a quantum system is distributed to multiple receivers. We derive fundamental trade-offs between prepare-and-measure witnesses, Bell nonlocality, and quantum random access code performance. We further develop a semi-device-independent randomness certification framework based on prepare-and-broadcast witnesses, showing that the maximal quantum violation certifies two bits of joint randomness, exceeding the limit achievable from the CHSH inequality while remaining robust to noise. Finally, we show that the prepare-and-broadcast scenario naturally accommodates stronger adversarial models in which the eavesdropper retains a quantum system correlated with the measurement device, providing a natural framework for semi-device-independent randomness certification against quantum side information.

AI.tldr: The paper investigates the prepare-and-broadcast scenario, a multipartite extension of prepare-and-measure experiments, deriving trade-offs between prepare-and-measure witnesses, Bell nonlocality, and quantum random access codes. It develops a semi-device-independent randomness certification framework where maximal quantum violation certifies two bits of joint randomness, surpassing CHSH-based limits while remaining noise-robust, and shows the framework naturally accommodates stronger adversarial models with quantum side information.
AI.motivation: To extend dimension-constrained prepare-and-measure experiments to a multipartite setting (prepare-and-broadcast), and to develop a certification framework for joint randomness that exceeds what is achievable from the CHSH inequality while being robust to noise and capable of handling quantum side information from adversaries.
AI.method: The authors define the prepare-and-broadcast scenario where a quantum system is distributed to multiple receivers, derive trade-offs between prepare-and-measure witnesses, Bell nonlocality, and quantum random access code performance, and formulate a semi-device-independent randomness certification framework based on prepare-and-broadcast witnesses. They also extend the adversarial model to include eavesdroppers holding quantum systems correlated with the measurement device.
AI.result: The maximal quantum violation of prepare-and-broadcast witnesses certifies two bits of joint randomness, which exceeds the limit achievable from the CHSH inequality. The framework remains robust to noise and supports stronger adversarial models where the eavesdropper retains a quantum system correlated with the measurement device.
AI.conclusion: The prepare-and-broadcast scenario provides a natural and powerful framework for semi-device-independent randomness certification, offering advantages over standard Bell-based approaches (greater certified randomness and robustness) and naturally accommodating quantum side-information adversaries.

title: Entanglement and non-local magic in a non-unitarily deformed non-Hermitian bipartite system
summary: Non-Hermitian degeneracies are usually discussed through spectral coalescence, whereas entanglement is a property of eigenvectors and need not be fixed by the eigenvalues alone. We formulate a compact bipartite model that separates these two notions. A Hermitian operator with a degenerate eigenspace is transformed by an invertible non-unitary similarity map. The resulting Hamiltonian is non-Hermitian and retains a non-defective degeneracy at every finite value of the non-Hermiticity parameter. For an exactly solvable two-qubit realization, the right eigenstates evolve continuously from product states to maximally entangled states although the spectrum is unchanged. We distinguish the positive right-state reduced density matrix from the generally non-positive biorthogonal reduction, for which entropy may become complex. The same two-qubit solution gives a closed partial-transpose negativity and a Schmidt-gauged non-local magic. Entanglement grows monotonically with the non-Hermiticity parameter, whereas the non-local magic vanishes for both the product and maximally entangled limits and is largest at an intermediate coupling. In larger bipartite spaces, the Page entropy and Haar-averaged purity provide reference values for eigenstate typicality. These diagnostics separate non-defective degeneracy, exceptional-point sensitivity, Haar-typical entanglement, and non-stabilizer correlations without relying on a proliferation of basis-dependent spectral quantities.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces a compact bipartite model that separates non-Hermitian spectral degeneracy from eigenvector entanglement. Using an invertible non-unitary similarity transformation of a Hermitian operator, they construct non-Hermitian Hamiltonians with non-defective degeneracies at all coupling values. In a two-qubit realization, eigenstates continuously evolve from product to maximally entangled states while the spectrum remains unchanged. They distinguish positive right-state reduced density matrices from non-positive biorthogonal reductions, and analyze negativity and Schmidt-gauged non-local magic, showing entanglement grows monotonically while magic peaks at intermediate coupling.
AI.motivation: Non-Hermitian degeneracies are typically understood through spectral coalescence, but entanglement is a property of eigenvectors that need not be determined by eigenvalues alone. This work aims to decouple these two notions and clarify entanglement-related quantities in non-Hermitian systems.
AI.method: The authors construct a bipartite model where a Hermitian operator with a degenerate eigenspace is transformed by an invertible non-unitary similarity map, yielding a non-Hermitian Hamiltonian with a non-defective degeneracy. They solve exactly a two-qubit realization, computing right-state reduced density matrices, biorthogonal reductions, partial-transpose negativity, and Schmidt-gauged non-local magic. For larger bipartite spaces, they use Page entropy and Haar-averaged purity as typicality references.
AI.result: Right eigenstates evolve continuously from product to maximally entangled states despite unchanged spectrum. Entanglement grows monotonically with the non-Hermiticity parameter, while non-local magic vanishes at both the product and maximally entangled limits and peaks at intermediate coupling. The biorthogonal reduced density matrix can yield complex entropy, unlike the positive right-state reduction.
AI.conclusion: The model cleanly separates non-defective degeneracy, exceptional-point sensitivity, Haar-typical entanglement, and non-stabilizer correlations, providing diagnostics that distinguish these phenomena without relying on a proliferation of basis-dependent spectral quantities.

title: Deep Holes in the Clifford Hierarchy
summary: We determine the covering radius of the topological closure of the single-qubit Clifford hierarchy in $\SU(2)\cong S^3$. This closure is a union of $18$ great circles --- the Clifford--Pauli circles --- and we prove that its covering radius is $\arccos\sqrt{5/6}$. The extremal points, which we call \emph{deep holes}, form a single orbit of size $192$ under left and right multiplication by Clifford gates, and are described in closed form. Equivalently, the minimum over one-qubit unitaries of the all-level Clifford fidelity is $5/6$. The proof rests on two structures attached to the configuration of $18$ planes in $\R^4$: their centered rank-two projectors form an orthonormal basis of the irreducible $\SO(4)$-module $\Sym_0(4)$, and the projection profile of a unit quaternion is exactly its image under the double cover $\SU(2)\to\SO(3)$. These reduce the covering problem to a minimax statement for the $\ell^\infty$-norm on $\SO(3)$ which we solve exactly, classifying its equality cases.

AI.tldr: The paper determines the covering radius of the topological closure of the single-qubit Clifford hierarchy in SU(2), proving it equals arccos√(5/6). The extremal points (deep holes) form a single orbit of size 192 under Clifford gate multiplication and are given in closed form. This is equivalent to the minimum all-level Clifford fidelity over one-qubit unitaries being 5/6.
AI.motivation: To understand the geometric structure of the Clifford hierarchy closure in SU(2)≅S³, particularly its covering radius — a quantity relevant to quantum circuit synthesis and the distance from arbitrary unitaries to the Clifford hierarchy.
AI.method: The proof uses two key structures: (1) the centered rank-two projectors of the 18 Clifford–Pauli great circles form an orthonormal basis of the irreducible SO(4)-module Sym₀(4), and (2) the projection profile of a unit quaternion is exactly its image under the double cover SU(2)→SO(3). These reduce the covering problem to a minimax statement for the ℓ∞-norm on SO(3), which is solved exactly with a classification of equality cases.
AI.result: The covering radius of the Clifford–Pauli circle configuration in SU(2) is arccos√(5/6) ≈ 0.420 rad. The deep holes form a single orbit of 192 points under left/right Clifford multiplication, described in closed form, and the all-level Clifford fidelity is minimized at 5/6.
AI.conclusion: The covering problem for the Clifford hierarchy closure reduces to a solvable minimax problem for the ℓ∞-norm on SO(3), yielding an exact covering radius and a complete classification of the extremal (deep hole) configurations.

title: Optimal strategies for shadow tomography with limited resources
summary: Shadow tomography addresses the task of efficiently predicting many expectation values of an unknown quantum state from randomized measurements on comparatively few copies. Existing analyses promise large scaling advantages, but the optimal strategies realizing these guarantees are not always known, and the required measurements are potentially challenging to implement on current hardware. We address this gap for Pauli observables by computing optimal sample-complexity parameters and constructing optimal measurement strategies under realistic resource constraints. We focus on memoryless protocols, where each copy is measured only once, and on measurements with bounded interaction range. Our approach reduces the problem to the analysis of graph parameters of the frustration graph encoding the Pauli anticommutation relations. We provide efficient numerical methods for the general case and analytically prove that Clifford measurements are optimal in many situations. This includes all perfect graphs, all single-qubit, all two-qubit measurement scenarios, and more. Applied to Hamiltonian energy estimation, our framework yields constructive strategies and improved variance bounds for molecular benchmarks.

AI.tldr: This paper solves the shadow tomography problem for Pauli observables under realistic constraints (memoryless protocols and bounded interaction range) by reducing it to graph parameters of the frustration graph encoding Pauli anticommutation relations. It provides efficient numerical methods, proves Clifford measurements are optimal for perfect graphs, all single-qubit and two-qubit scenarios, and demonstrates improved variance bounds for molecular Hamiltonian energy estimation.
AI.motivation: Existing shadow tomography analyses promise large scaling advantages, but optimal strategies realizing these guarantees are not always known, and the required measurements are challenging to implement on current hardware. The paper addresses this gap by finding optimal sample-complexity parameters and constructing practical optimal measurement strategies for Pauli observables under realistic resource constraints.
AI.method: The approach reduces the shadow tomography problem for Pauli observables to analyzing graph parameters of the frustration graph encoding Pauli anticommutation relations. It focuses on memoryless protocols (each copy measured once) and measurements with bounded interaction range, providing efficient numerical methods for the general case and analytical proofs that Clifford measurements are optimal in many scenarios.
AI.result: Clifford measurements are shown to be optimal for all perfect graphs, all single-qubit, and all two-qubit measurement scenarios. Applied to Hamiltonian energy estimation, the framework yields constructive strategies with improved variance bounds for molecular benchmarks.
AI.conclusion: The paper bridges the gap between theoretical shadow tomography guarantees and practically implementable strategies, providing both optimal sample-complexity parameters and constructive measurement protocols that work on realistic hardware constraints, with demonstrated improvements for molecular energy estimation.

title: The Input Problem: A Permanent Bottleneck for Quantum Machine Learning
summary: Quantum algorithms are conventionally presented with their input state supplied for free. When the input is classical data, this convention conceals a cost that is frequently larger than the algorithm it precedes. We review what the three standard encodings, such as basis encoding, amplitude encoding, and Grover--Rudolph distribution loading, actually cost once transpiled to a hardware gate set, and argue that the resulting $Θ(N)$ bound is a counting theorem rather than an engineering limitation that improved hardware will remove. Measured gate counts for a representative loading task are reported: an optimal library implementation requires $247$ CNOT gates at $n=8$ qubits and doubles with each additional qubit, while the classical preprocessing that produces the rotation angles requires reading the entire input vector. We show how this cost eliminates the quadratic advantage of quantum amplitude estimation for Monte Carlo integration, and argue that the same accounting constrains quantum machine learning more broadly: the strong input models that make quantum algorithms fast on classical data also enable classical dequantization, and quantum kernel methods carry a $Θ(M^2)$ state-preparation cost for the Gram matrix that does not amortize. We explain that the efficiently preparable states, device-generated distributions, variationally learned loading, and amortized preparation are required to get advantage from quantum machine learning and close with a checklist for evaluating input-dependent advantage claims. Executable notebooks reproducing every construction and measurement discussed here are available.

AI.tldr: This paper analyzes the hidden costs of encoding classical data into quantum states via three standard encodings (basis, amplitude, Grover-Rudolph), showing that transpiling these encodings to hardware gate sets costs Θ(N) and this is a counting theorem not an engineering limitation. This cost eliminates quantum amplitude estimation's quadratic advantage for Monte Carlo integration and constrains quantum machine learning broadly. The paper argues that efficient state preparation, device-generated distributions, variational loading, and amortized preparation are necessary for QML advantage, and provides a checklist for evaluating input-dependent advantage claims.
AI.motivation: Quantum algorithms are conventionally presented assuming input states are supplied for free, which conceals costs that frequently exceed the algorithm itself when input is classical data. The paper aims to expose these hidden costs and demonstrate their fundamental nature and consequences for quantum advantage claims.
AI.method: The authors review the three standard encodings (basis, amplitude, Grover-Rudolph) and analyze their transpiled costs to hardware gate sets. They measure gate counts for a representative loading task using an optimal library implementation, and analyze the consequences for quantum amplitude estimation in Monte Carlo integration and for quantum machine learning including kernel methods and dequantization.
AI.result: The transpiled cost is Θ(N) and is argued to be a counting theorem rather than an engineering limitation. An optimal library implementation requires 247 CNOT gates at n=8 qubits, doubling with each additional qubit. Classical preprocessing for rotation angles requires reading the entire input vector. This cost eliminates quadratic quantum advantage for Monte Carlo amplitude estimation, enables classical dequantization, and quantum kernel methods carry Θ(M²) non-amortizing state-preparation cost for the Gram matrix.
AI.conclusion: Efficiently preparable states, device-generated distributions, variationally learned loading, and amortized preparation are required to obtain quantum advantage in machine learning. The paper provides a checklist for evaluating input-dependent advantage claims, along with executable notebooks reproducing all constructions and measurements.

title: Effect of Strong Field Space-time Features on Vacuum Pair
summary: The relativistic dynamics of bound states across inertial reference frames are investigated using the computational quantum field theory (CQFT). The results reveal that the spatiotemporal properties of bound states within a given potential well are strictly frame-dependent. Crucially, this spatiotemporal modulation of the external field enables a reduction in the laser intensity threshold required for vacuum electron-positron pair creation. Analytical and numerical calculations demonstrate that this threshold reduction originates from the Lorentz transformation of the four-momentum, which reshapes the vacuum excitation pathways in phase space. By developing CQFT, we establish a comprehensive framework in which relativistic effects intrinsically govern the quantum vacuum decay process

AI.tldr: This paper uses computational quantum field theory (CQFT) to investigate relativistic bound-state dynamics across inertial reference frames, demonstrating that spatiotemporal properties of bound states are frame-dependent. This frame-dependent modulation reduces the laser intensity threshold for vacuum electron-positron pair creation, with the Lorentz transformation of four-momentum reshaping vacuum excitation pathways in phase space.
AI.motivation: To understand how relativistic frame-dependent effects influence bound-state dynamics and quantum vacuum decay, specifically investigating whether frame transformations can lower the laser intensity threshold required for vacuum electron-positron pair production.
AI.method: The study employs computational quantum field theory (CQFT) to analyze bound-state dynamics across inertial frames. Both analytical and numerical calculations are performed to examine the Lorentz transformation of four-momentum and its effect on vacuum excitation pathways in phase space.
AI.result: The spatiotemporal properties of bound states within a potential well are strictly frame-dependent. This spatiotemporal modulation of the external field enables a reduction in the laser intensity threshold required for vacuum electron-positron pair creation, originating from Lorentz transformation effects on four-momentum that reshape vacuum excitation pathways in phase space.
AI.conclusion: The CQFT framework establishes that relativistic effects intrinsically govern quantum vacuum decay processes, providing a comprehensive theoretical framework connecting frame-dependent bound-state dynamics to vacuum instability and pair-production thresholds.

title: Levitated Milligram-scale Ferromagnetic Magnetometer at Room Temperature
summary: Levitated mechanical oscillators are emerging ultrasensitive sensors with tremendous potential in both applied and fundamental physics. Levitated ferromagnets, with internal spin noises rapidly averaged, promise ultrahigh magnetic sensitivity. Here, we demonstrate a milligram-scale diamagnetically levitated ferromagnet system operating at room temperature. Through optimized geometry and multi-channel dissipation control, we achieve a magnetic sensitivity of 23~fT$/\sqrt{\text{Hz}}$ at frequency of 100-Hz level. We anticipate that a ferromagnetic magnetometer with subfemtotesla sensitivity is within reach, after modest technical improvements. This platform establishes a high-performance magnetometer for biomagnetic field detection and beyond-standard-model force searches.

AI.tldr: The paper demonstrates a milligram-scale diamagnetically levitated ferromagnet magnetometer operating at room temperature, achieving a magnetic sensitivity of 23 fT/√Hz at 100 Hz, with subfemtotesla sensitivity projected after modest improvements.
AI.motivation: Levitated mechanical oscillators are emerging as ultrasensitive sensors with potential in both applied and fundamental physics, and levitated ferromagnets with averaged internal spin noises promise ultrahigh magnetic sensitivity.
AI.method: A milligram-scale diamagnetically levitated ferromagnet system operating at room temperature, utilizing optimized geometry and multi-channel dissipation control.
AI.result: Achieved magnetic sensitivity of 23 fT/√Hz at a frequency of 100 Hz, with subfemtotesla sensitivity anticipated after modest technical improvements.
AI.conclusion: This platform establishes a high-performance magnetometer for biomagnetic field detection and beyond-standard-model force searches.

title: Quantum discord of Ganssian states in an expanding universe
summary: We investigate the redistribution of continuous-variable quantum discord within the framework of an expanding universe. We find that quantum discord exhibits stronger sensitivity to the spacetime expansion rate than to the expansion volume. As both the expansion rate and expansion volume increase, the initial quantum discord shared by the two bosonic modes decays, while quantum discord is induced in additional mode pairs by the underlying spacetime expansion, signaling a global redistribution of quantum correlations across the system. Specifically, the induced discord is largest for cross-observer bosonic-antibosonic pairs, followed by same-observer bosonic-antibosonic pairs, and smallest for the pair of antibosonic modes. Furthermore, our quantum discord analysis demonstrates that particles with lower momentum and optimal mass serve as more favorable candidates for extracting information about the expanding universe. This work substantially enriches the theoretical framework of quantum discord in expanding spacetimes, and provides new perspectives as well as a solid theoretical foundation for further investigations.

AI.tldr: The paper investigates how continuous-variable quantum discord is redistributed among bosonic modes in an expanding universe, finding that discord is more sensitive to expansion rate than volume. As spacetime expands, initial discord decays while new discord is induced across additional mode pairs, with cross-observer bosonic-antibosonic pairs showing the largest induced discord. Lower-momentum particles with optimal mass are identified as better candidates for probing the expanding universe.
AI.motivation: To understand how quantum correlations evolve in curved spacetime, specifically how quantum discord is redistributed across a multimode bosonic system under the influence of an expanding universe, and to identify which physical parameters (momentum, mass) optimize information extraction from spacetime expansion.
AI.method: The study models continuous-variable quantum discord between bosonic modes in an expanding-universe framework, analyzing how both the expansion rate and expansion volume affect the redistribution of discord across different mode pairs—including cross-observer bosonic-antibosonic pairs, same-observer bosonic-antibosonic pairs, and antibosonic mode pairs.
AI.result: Quantum discord shows stronger sensitivity to expansion rate than expansion volume. Increasing expansion rate and volume degrades initial discord while inducing discord in additional mode pairs, indicating global redistribution. Induced discord is largest for cross-observer bosonic-antibosonic pairs, intermediate for same-observer pairs, and smallest for antibosonic pairs. Lower-momentum particles with optimal mass are most favorable for extracting information about the expanding universe.
AI.conclusion: The work significantly extends the theoretical framework of quantum discord in expanding spacetimes, offering new perspectives and a solid theoretical foundation for future research on quantum correlations and information extraction in cosmological settings.

title: Dissipation-engineered dual-charger quantum batteries
summary: Suppressing coherent energy backflow while maintaining extractable energy in a stable nonequilibrium state remains a central challenge for quantum energy storage. Here, we introduce a reservoir-engineered dual-charger quantum battery architecture, in which nonequilibrium dissipation is exploited as a control resource to stabilize useful stored energy. A hot-reservoir-coupled driver supplies excitations, while a cold-reservoir-coupled cache biases the resonant three-body transition toward charging and suppresses the dressed-state coherences responsible for energy backflow. This mechanism establishes a population-inverted steady state with finite ergotropy and converts reversible charger--battery exchange into persistent energy storage. For uniformly spaced multilevel batteries, we show that the stored energy and ergotropy scale approximately linearly with the number of accessible levels, while the stored-energy utilization approaches unity. The accompanying stationary heat current provides a thermodynamic signature of the charging regime. Our results demonstrate dissipation engineering as a strategy for achieving stable and scalable quantum energy storage beyond transient coherent charging protocols.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces a reservoir-engineered dual-charger quantum battery that uses nonequilibrium dissipation to suppress coherent energy backflow, stabilize a population-inverted steady state with finite ergotropy, and achieve scalable energy storage that scales linearly with the number of accessible battery levels.
AI.motivation: A central challenge in quantum energy storage is maintaining stable stored energy in nonequilibrium states while suppressing coherent energy backflow that degrades or reverses the charging process. Existing transient coherent charging protocols cannot sustain useful stored energy indefinitely.
AI.method: The authors introduce a dual-charger architecture: a hot-reservoir-coupled driver supplies excitations, while a cold-reservoir-coupled cache biases the resonant three-body transition toward charging and suppresses dressed-state coherences responsible for energy backflow. This creates a population-inverted steady state with finite ergotropy and converts reversible charger-battery exchange into persistent energy storage.
AI.result: For uniformly spaced multilevel batteries, stored energy and ergotropy scale approximately linearly with the number of accessible levels, while stored-energy utilization approaches unity. The stationary heat current provides a thermodynamic signature of the charging regime.
AI.conclusion: The work demonstrates dissipation engineering as a viable strategy for stable, scalable quantum energy storage beyond transient coherent charging protocols, establishing a robust framework for steady-state quantum batteries.

title: Born-Oppenheimer, Born-Huang, and exact factorization: quantum geometry and error in analytically transparent benchmark models
summary: The phrase "potential energy surface" refers to several distinct objects. The Born-Oppenheimer construction gives a clamped-nucleus electronic eigenvalue, the single-surface Born-Huang construction adds the diagonal correction, and exact factorization gives a state-dependent exact scalar potential. These constructions answer different questions and should not be regarded as competing definitions of one universal surface. We compare them in two analytically transparent benchmark models. For Fernández's bilinearly coupled oscillators, the exact molecular spectrum, the Born-Oppenheimer and Born-Huang spectra, and the ground-state exact-factorization surface are obtained in closed form. We prove the ground-state ordering of these energies for every admissible mass ratio and coupling and show why it does not extend uniformly to excited states. The diagonal Born-Huang correction is identified with the mass-weighted quantum metric, and Fernández's sixth-order result is recast as a leading geometric error budget involving the metric and a gap-weighted spectral moment of the same derivative couplings. In a linear vibronic-coupling model the metric localizes at an avoided crossing while the total Fubini-Study length remains $π/2$, separating the localization of electronic-state change from its total magnitude. Exact factorization is smooth for the nodeless ground state but becomes increasingly ill-conditioned, while remaining finite, when an excited-state nuclear marginal becomes small. These models separate approximation error, geometric correction, and conditioning in a form that can be checked directly.

AI.tldr: This paper clarifies that "potential energy surface" refers to distinct objects under different constructions (Born-Oppenheimer, Born-Huang, and exact factorization), analyzes them in two analytically solvable benchmark models, and demonstrates key physical and mathematical differences including energy ordering, geometric corrections via the quantum metric, and conditioning behavior near avoided crossings.
AI.motivation: The term "potential energy surface" is used ambiguously across different theoretical constructions (Born-Oppenheimer clamped-nucleus eigenvalues, Born-Huang diagonal corrections, and exact-factorization scalar potentials). These constructions answer fundamentally different questions and should not be conflated as competing definitions of a single universal surface. The authors aim to clarify these distinctions using analytically transparent models where exact results are obtainable.
AI.method: The authors employ two exactly solvable benchmark models: (1) Fernández's bilinearly coupled harmonic oscillators, where the molecular spectrum, Born-Oppenheimer and Born-Huang spectra, and the ground-state exact-factorization surface are derived in closed form; and (2) a linear vibronic-coupling model where the quantum metric localizes at an avoided crossing. They prove ground-state energy ordering for all admissible mass ratios and couplings, identify the diagonal Born-Huang correction with the mass-weighted quantum metric, and recast Fernández's sixth-order result as a geometric error budget involving the metric and gap-weighted spectral moments of derivative couplings.
AI.result: The ground-state energy ordering is proven for all mass ratios and coupling strengths, but it is shown not to extend uniformly to excited states. The diagonal Born-Huang correction equals the mass-weighted quantum metric. In the linear vibronic-coupling model, the metric localizes at an avoided crossing while the total Fubini-Study length remains π/2, separating localization of electronic-state change from its total magnitude. Exact factorization is smooth for the nodeless ground state but becomes increasingly ill-conditioned (while remaining finite) when an excited-state nuclear marginal becomes small.
AI.conclusion: The three distinct "potential energy surface" constructions answer different physical questions and cannot be regarded interchangeably. The analytic benchmark models cleanly separate approximation error, geometric correction, and conditioning issues, enabling direct verification of the relationships among the Born-Oppenheimer surface, Born-Huang corrected surface, and the exact-factorization potential.

title: Point-gap topology in amorphous non-Hermitian quantum systems
summary: Recent studies have revealed that not only does the correspondence between spectral winding numbers and skin modes break down in non-Hermitian systems, but the energy spectrum itself is highly sensitive to generic perturbations, system size, and boundary conditions. In amorphous non-Hermitian systems, where the positions of lattice sites are uncertain, the spectral instability becomes even more severe, making it difficult to identify stable topological edge states from the eigenvalue spectrum alone. To overcome this challenge, we introduce a correspondence between stable zero-mode singular states and mid-gap states of the energy spectrum in the thermodynamic limit. Because the singular value spectrum is highly robust against small perturbations and variation in size, topological edge states can be reliably probed via singular values even in finite-sized systems. Based on the singular-value decomposition of the Hamiltonian, we construct a topological invariant in real space to characterize the associated topologically protected edge states. Our approach provides a general strategy for exploring point-gap topology in real space and redefine the non-Hermitian skin effect from a new perspective.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces a singular-value-based correspondence between stable zero-mode singular states and mid-gap states in amorphous non-Hermitian systems, enabling reliable detection of topological edge states despite spectral instability. A real-space topological invariant is constructed via singular value decomposition to characterize topologically protected edge states and redefine the non-Hermitian skin effect.
AI.motivation: In non-Hermitian systems, the correspondence between spectral winding numbers and skin modes breaks down, and the energy spectrum is highly sensitive to perturbations, system size, and boundary conditions. In amorphous systems with uncertain lattice site positions, spectral instability is even more severe, making it difficult to identify stable topological edge states from eigenvalues alone.
AI.method: The authors introduce a correspondence between stable zero-mode singular states and mid-gap states of the energy spectrum in the thermodynamic limit. They use singular value decomposition of the Hamiltonian to construct a real-space topological invariant characterizing topologically protected edge states.
AI.result: The singular value spectrum is highly robust against small perturbations and size variations, allowing reliable probing of topological edge states even in finite-sized and amorphous non-Hermitian systems where eigenvalue spectra are unstable.
AI.conclusion: The approach provides a general strategy for exploring point-gap topology in real space and offers a new perspective on redefining the non-Hermitian skin effect.

title: A Resource-Efficient Quantum Framework for Graph Coloring and Chromatic Number Estimation
summary: Many industrial optimization tasks can be modeled as graph coloring, where adjacent vertices must have different colors. This NP-hard problem is challenging for large graphs. We present a quantum encoding requiring qubits that scale logarithmically with the number of colors and linearly with vertices. Using adiabatic evolution with a novel mixer Hamiltonian and vertex terms, we compute the chromatic number and demonstrate robustness by solving constrained truck loading problems.

AI.tldr: A quantum encoding for graph coloring is proposed where qubits scale logarithmically with colors and linearly with vertices, using adiabatic evolution with a novel mixer Hamiltonian to compute chromatic numbers and solve constrained industrial problems like truck loading.
AI.motivation: Graph coloring is an NP-hard problem that is difficult to solve for large graphs, and many industrial optimization tasks can be formulated as such. Efficient quantum approaches that reduce qubit requirements are needed to make these problems tractable.
AI.method: A quantum encoding requiring qubits that scale logarithmically with the number of colors and linearly with the number of vertices. The approach uses adiabatic evolution with a novel mixer Hamiltonian and vertex terms to solve the graph coloring problem.
AI.result: The method computes the chromatic number of graphs and demonstrates robustness by successfully solving constrained truck loading problems.
AI.conclusion: The proposed quantum encoding with logarithmic color scaling and adiabatic evolution offers an efficient and robust approach to graph coloring and related industrial optimization tasks such as truck loading.

title: DA-CASE: reusable measurements for adaptive quantum subspaces
summary: Quantum subspace methods are often compared by basis dimension or energyerror, although their dominant experimental costs arise from different statepreparations, measurement settings, and shot allocations. We present theDyadic Adaptive Clifford-Algebra Subspace Eigensolver (DA-CASE), whose basisstates are virtual directions $A_i|ψ\rangle$ generated from one reference.Overlap, Hamiltonian, and observable matrices are reconstructed from onecached set of Pauli expectations on that reference. The method thereforetrades multiple prepared basis states for a potentially wide measurement bank.We make that trade explicit on a frozen eight-qubit H$_4$ Hamiltonian. Twogenerator resolutions reach the same nine-dimensional subspace and the sameenergy to machine precision, while the retained bank changes from 7371 to 2240Pauli words. A reference-conditioned symmetry test certifies the narrower spanwithout asserting that its individual Pauli words conserve the sector asabstract operators. Independently, a dyadic commuting hierarchy reduces thedeterminant bank from 913 qubit-wise-commuting settings to 64 fully commutingsettings, while exposing the added logical-CX cost. In a separate four-qubitfinite-shot diagnostic, covariance-aware allocation reduces theprojected-matrix variance target by 68.9%. Mode-wise overlap regularizationremoves the observed catastrophic energy estimates and lowers RMSE, butdoubles the median error relative to a fixed cutoff. These are small-instanceexact and Monte Carlo results, not a hardware demonstration, scaling result,or quantum advantage claim. The contribution is a single-referencemeasurement architecture and a resource ledger that keeps contexts, settings,shots, circuit depth, and post-selection retries in their proper units.

AI.tldr: DA-CASE is a quantum subspace eigensolver that uses a single reference state and cached Pauli expectations to build basis states virtually (Ai|ψ⟩), trading multiple prepared states for a wider measurement bank. On an 8-qubit frozen H4 Hamiltonian, it matches energies to machine precision while shrinking the measurement bank from 7371 to 2240 Pauli words, reduces commuting measurement settings from 913 to 64 via a dyadic commuting hierarchy, cuts projected-matrix variance by 68.9% with covariance-aware shot allocation, and uses mode-wise overlap regularization to remove catastrophic energy estimates.
AI.motivation: Existing quantum subspace method comparisons focus on basis dimension or energy error, but the dominant experimental costs stem from different state preparations, measurement settings, and shot allocations. The authors seek to make the trade-off between prepared basis states and measurement resources explicit, and to provide a resource ledger that accounts for contexts, settings, shots, circuit depth, and post-selection retries in proper units.
AI.method: DA-CASE constructs basis states as virtual directions Ai|ψ⟩ from one reference. Overlap, Hamiltonian, and observable matrices are reconstructed from a single cached set of Pauli expectations on that reference, eliminating the need for multiple prepared states. A reference-conditioned symmetry test certifies the narrower span without requiring individual Pauli operators to conserve the sector abstractly. A dyadic commuting hierarchy reduces the determinant bank from 913 qubit-wise-commuting settings to 64 fully commuting settings. Covariance-aware shot allocation is used to reduce projected-matrix variance, and mode-wise overlap regularization mitigates catastrophic energy estimates.
AI.result: On a frozen eight-qubit H4 Hamiltonian, two generator resolutions reach the same nine-dimensional subspace and the same energy to machine precision, while the Pauli measurement bank shrinks from 7371 to 2240 words. The dyadic commuting hierarchy reduces measurement settings from 913 qubit-wise-commuting to 64 fully commuting settings (with exposed logical-CX cost). In a four-qubit finite-shot diagnostic, covariance-aware allocation reduces projected-matrix variance by 68.9%. Mode-wise overlap regularization removes catastrophic energy estimates and lowers RMSE but doubles median error relative to a fixed cutoff.
AI.conclusion: The contribution is a single-reference measurement architecture that eliminates the need for multiple prepared basis states, plus a comprehensive resource ledger that properly distinguishes and accounts for contexts, settings, shots, circuit depth, and post-selection retries. These are small-instance exact and Monte Carlo results—not hardware demonstrations, scaling results, or quantum advantage claims.

title: Promise and Challenges of Distimation
summary: Estimating the quality of raw entangled states and distilling high-fidelity entanglement traditionally require two separate link-layer protocols in a quantum network stack, each consuming its own share of fragile entangled pairs. The recently introduced distimation concept merges these two protocols by directly extracting state estimation data from the classical syndromes generated during entanglement distillation. By removing the dedicated "test-then-distill'' stage, distimation lowers the number of raw entangled pairs required to operate the network, reduces latency, and streamlines the network control plane. The paradigm is especially attractive for near-term hardware platforms, where entanglement generation remains a severe bottleneck. Alongside these promises, distimation introduces new engineering challenges, ranging from accurate local-device modeling to protocols for tracking time-varying sources. This article surveys the core principles of distimation, quantifies expected gains for realistic architectures, and outlines a research roadmap toward making distimation a standard building block in future quantum networks.

AI.tldr: This article surveys "distimation," a paradigm that merges entanglement distillation and state estimation in quantum networks by extracting estimation data from classical syndromes generated during distillation, eliminating the separate "test-then-distill" stage. It quantifies gains in resource efficiency, latency, and control-plane simplification for near-term hardware, while also outlining engineering challenges and a research roadmap.
AI.motivation: In quantum network stacks, estimating raw entangled state quality and distilling high-fidelity entanglement are traditionally performed as two separate link-layer protocols, each consuming fragile entangled pairs. Given that entanglement generation is a severe bottleneck in near-term platforms, reducing the number of raw pairs consumed by these processes is highly desirable.
AI.method: The paradigm of "distimation" directly extracts state estimation data from the classical syndromes generated during entanglement distillation, thereby merging the estimation and distillation protocols into one and removing the dedicated "test-then-distill" stage. The article surveys the core principles of distimation, quantifies expected gains for realistic architectures, and addresses engineering challenges such as accurate local-device modeling and protocols for tracking time-varying entanglement sources.
AI.result: Distimation lowers the number of raw entangled pairs required, reduces latency, and streamlines the network control plane. Quantitative gains are presented for realistic architectures, establishing the paradigm's attractiveness for near-term quantum hardware while identifying remaining engineering challenges.
AI.conclusion: Distimation offers a promising path toward more resource-efficient quantum network operation by unifying two traditionally separate link-layer functions. A research roadmap is outlined to address engineering challenges and establish distimation as a standard building block in future quantum networks.

title: How to Test Bell Nonlocality for Gravity?
summary: We propose an experiment to test Bell nonlocality, a genuine nonclassicality, for the gravitational field. Two masses with embedded entangled spins (e.g., two diamonds with their NV-centre spins entangled) are placed well outside each other's light cones, ensuring a locality-loophole-free scenario. The spins are then coupled to the motion of their respective masses to generate spatial superpositions. Finally, local measurements are performed only on the gravitational fields of the two masses. If gravity is quantum, then the two entangled masses would entangle their gravitational fields, leading to correlations certifying Bell nonlocality of gravity. Trapped and ground-state cooled nano-objects with micron-sized spatial superposition are sufficient for this test. This goes beyond the recent proposals to test nonclassicality of gravity by providing, for the first time in the literature, a minimal tool to (i) create Einstein-Podolsky-Rosen (EPR) state of gravitational curvatures, (ii) witness entangled gravitational curvatures, (iii) rule out any local-realist description of gravity, and (iv) achieve a loophole-free test of gravity's nonclassicality in a fully device-independent way.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes an experiment to test Bell nonlocality of the gravitational field using two masses with embedded entangled spins.
