By coupling spins to the motion of their respective masses to generate spatial superpositions, then performing local measurements on the gravitational fields, the experiment aims to certify that gravity is quantum—going beyond existing proposals by providing tools to create EPR states of gravitational curvatures, witness entangled gravitational curvatures, rule out local-realist descriptions of gravity, and achieve a loophole-free, fully device-independent test of gravity's nonclassicality.
AI.motivation: The central question is whether gravity is fundamentally quantum. While previous proposals have suggested ways to test nonclassicality of gravity, no experiment has been designed to certify nonlocality of gravity in a fully device-independent, locality-loophole-free manner. This paper aims to fill that gap.
AI.method: The proposed scheme places two masses with embedded entangled spins (e.g., NV-centre spins in diamonds) outside each other's light cones for a locality-loophole-free test. The spins are coupled to the mechanical motion of their respective masses to create spatial superpositions, generating entangled gravitational fields. Local measurements are performed only on the gravitational fields, using trapped, ground-state cooled nano-objects with micron-sized spatial superpositions to ensure sufficient sensitivity.
AI.result: The paper shows that trapped and ground-state cooled nano-objects with micron-sized spatial superpositions are sufficient to implement this test. The proposed framework provides four key capabilities: (i) creating EPR states of gravitational curvatures, (ii) witnessing entangled gravitational curvatures, (iii) ruling out any local-realist description of gravity, and (iv) achieving a loophole-free test of gravity's nonclassicality in a fully device-independent manner—marking the first such proposal in the literature.
AI.conclusion: This work advances the field by providing a minimal, experimentally realizable tool to test the nonlocality of gravity, going beyond earlier proposals for testing gravity's nonclassicality. It represents a significant step toward experimentally establishing whether gravity is quantum through Bell nonlocality certification.

title: Symmetry Constraints Regularize Neural Quantum State Learning
summary: Neural quantum states (NQS) offer highly expressive variational wavefunctions, but their optimization is frequently bottlenecked by redundant parameters and poorly conditioned landscapes. We demonstrate that embedding Hamiltonian symmetries directly into the variational parameterization geometrically regularizes this learning problem. For Boltzmann-family NQS, we enforce symmetries by tying local Pauli-$Z$ generators along physical geometric orbits, analytically collapsing the trainable coefficient space prior to optimization. To quantify the resulting optimization geometry, we introduce a geometric metric built on the Jacobian and Hessian of the optimization landscape. This framework evaluates the fraction of the physically accessible state space that corresponds to high-quality, low-energy solutions. Evaluating our approach on transverse-field Ising (TFIM) and XXZ spin chains shows that symmetry compilation excises the vast majority of parameters while maintaining ground-state accuracy within the resolution of the reported benchmarks. In large TFIM systems, strong spatial constraints compress thousands of parameters down to tens, delivering substantial runtime accelerations. Our geometric diagnostics indicate that symmetry produces a more favorable target-aware geometry by concentrating the reachable state space around low-energy solutions while retaining broad target basins. Together, our results indicate that symmetry compilation concentrates the expressive power of NQS on states relevant to the target problem, thereby reducing model size and training cost without sacrificing accuracy.

A novel Jacobian/Hessian-based geometric metric reveals that symmetry compilation concentrates reachable state space around low-energy solutions, improving conditioning and accelerating training while preserving ground-state accuracy.

The authors aim to geometrically regularize the learning problem by embedding Hamiltonian symmetries into the variational parameterization, reducing model size and training cost without sacrificing accuracy.

Introduce a geometric metric based on the Jacobian and Hessian to quantify the fraction of physically accessible state space corresponding to high-quality, low-energy solutions.

title: State preparation via measurement and feedback: pushing relations, state structures, and non-invertible symmetries
summary: Quantum circuits with measurements and unitary feedback (MF) can prepare long-range entangled states in constant depth, but a systematic construction of the MF preparation circuit for a given target state remains underexplored. We develop such a scheme for one-dimensional states, based on the notion of pushable defects: virtual-bond operators of a matrix product state that can be pushed through the tensor at the price of a physical feedback unitary. We show that the set of pushable defects, together with their pushing relations classifies finite-depth MF-preparable states and dictates their preparation circuits. To each class of the target state $|A\rangle$, we associate a state $|B\rangle$ from which $|A\rangle$ can be prepared using a 1-round MF circuit; in particular, $|A\rangle$ is preparable from a product state using a circuit with 1 round of MF whenever $|B\rangle$ is preparable by a finite-depth local unitary (FDLU) circuit. For a general target state, the scheme is obtained by iterating this procedure until the associated state is FDLU-preparable. For open-boundary matrix product states, the scheme is complete: it constructs a preparation circuit whenever finite-depth MF preparation with left-conditioned feedback corrections is possible. Pushable defects and pushing relations thus emerge as a unifying principle for quantum state preparation via measurements and feedback. This characterization further reveals an intrinsic connection between MF circuits and non-invertible symmetries: states with certain classes of pushing relations are related to a product state by Tambara-Yamagami duality operators, or by continuous cosine symmetry operators with fusion rules $L_α L_{α'} = L_{α+α'} + L_{α-α'}$, together with their generalizations up to (not necessarily transversal) gates.

AI.tldr: This paper develops a systematic scheme for preparing one-dimensional long-range entangled states using constant-depth quantum circuits with measurements and unitary feedback (MF), based on the concept of "pushable defects" in matrix product states. The set of pushable defects and their pushing relations classify finite-depth MF-preparable states and determine their preparation circuits. The scheme iteratively associates each target state with a simpler state preparable by finite-depth local unitary circuits, achieving completeness for open-boundary matrix product states. The framework also reveals connections between MF circuits and non-invertible symmetries such as Tambara-Yamagami duality and cosine symmetry operators.
AI.motivation: Quantum circuits with measurements and feedback (MF) can prepare long-range entangled states in constant depth, but there is no systematic method for constructing the MF preparation circuit for a given target state. This work aims to fill this gap by providing a principled, classification-based approach to MF state preparation in one dimension.
AI.method: The scheme is built on "pushable defects": virtual-bond operators of a matrix product state that can be pushed through the tensor at the cost of a physical feedback unitary. The pushable defects and their pushing relations provide a classification of finite-depth MF-preparable states. For each target state |A⟩, an associated state |B⟩ is identified from which |A⟩ can be prepared by a 1-round MF circuit; iteration of this procedure continues until the associated state is preparable by a finite-depth local unitary (FDLU) circuit. This procedure is shown to be complete for open-boundary matrix product states with left-conditioned feedback corrections.
AI.result: The set of pushable defects and pushing relations fully classify finite-depth MF-preparable states and dictate their preparation circuits. The iterative scheme constructs preparation circuits for general target states and is provably complete for open-boundary MPS. The characterization also reveals an intrinsic connection between MF circuits and non-invertible symmetries, including Tambara-Yamagami duality operators and continuous cosine symmetry operators with fusion rules L_α L_α' = L_{α+α'} + L_{α-α'} and their generalizations.
AI.conclusion: Pushable defects and pushing relations serve as a unifying principle for quantum state preparation via measurements and feedback in one dimension. This work provides the first systematic construction of MF preparation circuits, establishes a classification of MF-preparable states, and uncovers deep connections to non-invertible symmetries, thereby establishing MF circuits as a rich framework bridging quantum information and algebraic structures.

title: Two-copy distillability of one-copy-undistillable negative-partial-transpose states in every dimension
summary: Whether negative-partial-transpose (NPT) states that are undistillable from one copy become distillable from finitely many copies remains a basic open problem in entanglement theory. We study the canonical two-parameter family of DiVincenzo \textit{et al.}, introduced as a symmetry-reduced testbed for this question. We prove that a distinguished one-copy-undistillable state in this family is already two-copy distillable in every local dimension $d\geq 3$. A uniform equal-norm tight-frame construction gives explicit Schmidt-rank-two certificates in every dimension, thereby disproving the conjecture that the entire one-copy-undistillable region of the canonical family remains undistillable for arbitrarily many copies. The same witnesses certify an open two-copy-distillable neighborhood around the counterexample, while separately constructed three-copy witnesses enlarge the inner bounds for the distillable region in the surrounding parameter space. In contrast, recent results for Werner states, together with the propagation argument of DiVincenzo \textit{et al.}, establish a neighboring region of one-copy-undistillable states that remains two-copy undistillable. Thus a single symmetry-reduced family contains rigorously certified states with opposite two-copy behavior, separated by a substantial region whose finite-copy distillability remains unresolved.

AI.tldr: The paper proves that a distinguished one-copy-undistillable NPT state in the DiVincenzo et al. two-parameter family is two-copy distillable in every local dimension d≥3, using uniform equal-norm tight-frame constructions to give explicit Schmidt-rank-two certificates. This disproves the conjecture that the entire one-copy-undistillable region remains undistillable for many copies. The same witnesses certify an open neighborhood of two-copy distillability around the counterexample, while three-copy witnesses extend inner bounds for the distillable region. In contrast, Werner-state results plus propagation arguments show a neighboring region remains two-copy undistillable, so the family contains certified states with opposite two-copy behavior separated by a region whose distillability is unresolved.
AI.motivation: The paper addresses a basic open problem in entanglement theory: whether NPT states that are undistillable from one copy become distillable from finitely many copies. The authors use the canonical DiVincenzo et al. family as a symmetry-reduced testbed to settle this question for specific states and explore the finite-copy distillability landscape.
AI.method: The authors construct explicit Schmidt-rank-two certificates (witnesses) using a uniform equal-norm tight-frame construction in every local dimension d≥3. They use these witnesses to prove two-copy distillability of a distinguished state in the DiVincenzo family, certify an open neighborhood of two-copy distillability, and build separate three-copy witnesses for enlarged inner bounds. They contrast these with Werner-state results and the propagation argument of DiVincenzo et al. to certify two-copy undistillability in a neighboring region.
AI.result: The paper proves the distinguished one-copy-undistillable state is two-copy distillable for all d≥3, disproving the conjecture of universal multi-copy undistillability in the one-copy-undistillable region. It establishes an open neighborhood of two-copy distillability around the counterexample, extends inner bounds via three-copy witnesses, and shows a neighboring region remains two-copy undistillable—demonstrating opposite two-copy behavior within the same family.
AI.conclusion: A single symmetry-reduced family contains rigorously certified states with opposite two-copy distillability behavior. The finite-copy distillability of a substantial intermediate region remains unresolved, leaving an open boundary between two-copy distillable and undistillable regions.

title: The Logic of Partitions and Partition Logics: Ore's Correspondence, Contextual Pasting, and Direct-Sum Decompositions
summary: The term ``partition logic'' denotes two constructions at different levels. In automaton and generalized-urn models, selected partitions generate Boolean event algebras whose contextwise union forms a concrete pasted event structure; in Ellerman's framework, whole partitions are classifications governed by refinement and partition operations. For a finite set $U$, Ore's correspondence maps each generator $π$ to its Boolean algebra $\BA(π)$, but it neither identifies the pasted carrier with $\Part(U)$ nor makes pasting a partition operation. It yields $\BA(π\wedgeσ)=\BA(π)\cap\BA(σ)$ and $\BA(π\veeσ)=\langle\BA(π)\cup\BA(σ)\rangle_{\rm BA}$, where $\langle\cdot\rangle_{\rm BA}$ denotes Boolean-algebra generation. Thus meet captures the common event algebra, whereas join gives the ambient Boolean closure. Chinese-lantern, Firefly, and triangular examples distinguish shared events, atomic intertwining, and inherited concrete order. Ellerman's direct-sum decompositions (DSDs) provide a vector-space analogue: component projections of an orthogonal DSD resolve the identity and encode exclusive outcomes, but its components are not equivalence classes of vectors. Gleason and Kochen--Specker applications require globally context-consistent valuations on those projections.

AI.tldr: The paper analyzes "partition logic" at two levels—event-algebra construction in automaton and generalized-urn models versus Ellerman's classification-based partitions—using Ore's correspondence to connect partitions to Boolean algebras, with meet giving common event algebras and join giving ambient Boolean closure. It also draws an analogy to Ellerman's direct-sum decompositions in vector spaces, where Gleason and Kochen–Specker results demand context-consistent valuations.
AI.motivation: To clarify the relationship between two distinct notions of partition logic, reconcile them via Ore's correspondence on finite sets, and draw parallels with vector-space analogues to understand quantum-logic-style contextuality and valuations.
AI.method: The paper formalizes mapping each partition π of a finite set U to its Boolean algebra BA(π) via Ore's correspondence, analyzing identities for meet (intersection of Boolean algebras) and join (Boolean closure of union). Concrete examples (Chinese lantern, Firefly, triangular) illustrate distinctions among shared events, atomic intertwining, and inherited concrete order. Vector-space analogues via Ellerman's direct-sum decompositions are examined in the style of Gleason and Kochen–Specker.
AI.result: The paper establishes BA(π∧σ)=BA(π)∩BA(σ) and BA(π∨σ)=⟨BA(π)∪BA(σ)⟩_BA, showing that partition meet captures the common event algebra while join yields the ambient Boolean closure. Examples differentiate shared events, atomic intertwining, and inherited concrete order. For the vector-space case, orthogonal DSD component projections resolve the identity but do not correspond to equivalence classes, requiring globally context-consistent valuations for Gleason and Kochen–Specker applications.
AI.conclusion: Partition logic encompasses two distinct constructions that are formally connected but not identical: pasted event structures from concrete partitions and Ellerman's classification-based partitions. Ore's correspondence clarifies how joins and meets of partitions relate to Boolean-algebra operations, while the DSD analogy highlights the need for context-consistent global valuations in quantum-type logical frameworks.

title: Quantum Gouy phase singularities in a propagating biphoton state
summary: Phase singularities are topological defects around which the phase winds by an integer multiple of $2π$. In entangled multiphoton states, they can emerge nonlocally in the joint wavefunction rather than in the field of either subsystem alone. Here we show that the quantum Gouy phase generates nonlocal phase singularities (NPSs) in the two-dimensional longitudinal propagation space of entangled photon pairs. We consider photon pairs produced via spontaneous parametric down-conversion pumped by a Laguerre--Gaussian beam, with the signal and idler photons propagating independently over different longitudinal distances. The accumulated radial-mode-dependent Gouy phases induce destructive interference among biphoton spatial-mode components, producing isolated intensity nulls with quantized phase winding. For a pump with radial mode number $p$, the NPS topological charges have magnitude $p$, whereas their propagation positions and charge signs are governed by the Rayleigh ranges of the pump and phase-matching functions. We further identify the radial-mode structure required for their formation, showing that separable biphoton states cannot support isolated longitudinal NPSs. Our results extend nonlocal singular optics from transverse spatial correlations to longitudinal propagation dynamics and establish propagation distance as a coordinate space for topological structures in entangled photon pairs.

AI.tldr: This paper demonstrates that the quantum Gouy phase can generate nonlocal phase singularities (NPSs) in the two-dimensional longitudinal propagation space of entangled photon pairs produced via spontaneous parametric down-conversion pumped by a Laguerre-Gaussian beam, with topological charges of magnitude p (the pump radial mode number) and positions/signs governed by Rayleigh ranges, extending nonlocal singular optics from transverse to longitudinal propagation dynamics.
AI.motivation: To extend the concept of nonlocal singular optics from transverse spatial correlations to longitudinal propagation dynamics, and to establish propagation distance as a coordinate space for topological structures in entangled photon pairs.
AI.method: The authors analyze photon pairs from spontaneous parametric down-conversion pumped by a Laguerre-Gaussian beam with radial mode number p, where signal and idler photons propagate independently over different longitudinal distances. They show that accumulated radial-mode-dependent Gouy phases cause destructive interference among biphoton spatial-mode components, yielding isolated intensity nulls with quantized phase winding (NPSs).
AI.result: NPS topological charges have magnitude p, while their propagation positions and charge signs are governed by the Rayleigh ranges of the pump and phase-matching functions. Furthermore, separable biphoton states cannot support isolated longitudinal NPSs, establishing the radial-mode entanglement structure as a necessary condition.
AI.conclusion: The work extends nonlocal singular optics into longitudinal propagation dynamics, demonstrating that propagation distance itself can serve as a coordinate space hosting topological structures in entangled photon pairs.

title: Multi-agent discovery of practical quantum LDPC codes
summary: Quantum low-density parity-check (qLDPC) codes can encode multiple logical qubits using sparse parity checks, yet searching for useful finite-length instances remains a challenging design problem because code performance must be optimized while satisfying practical constraints. Motivated by recent advances in artificial-intelligence agents for scientific discovery, we develop a multi-agent framework for discovering practical qLDPC codes. The framework combines specialist proposal and review, persistent scientific memory, long-horizon evolution of executable programs, and deterministic construction and evaluation within a closed-loop search. These programs instantiate coset-orbit balanced-product codes, providing a search space that includes bicycle and lifted-product constructions as well as non-normal subgroup actions. To incorporate practical constraints, we restrict the search to binary CSS codes with block length $n\leq400$ and overall weight $w\leq10$. Within this regime, the framework discovers codes with leading or competitive rate--distance performance in every weight class considered, with representative instances including $[[288,16,18]]$ at $w=7$, $[[288,18,18]]$ at $w=9$, and $[[234,28,18]]$ at $w=10$. The search also uncovers structurally distinct, high-performing constructions, including a $[[336,12,\leq24]]$ candidate and a $[[368,18,16]]$ code, both of which are genuine balanced-product constructions with non-normal subgroup actions. When evaluated under code-capacity depolarizing noise using a common BP-OSD decoding protocol, the discovered codes also exhibit low logical failure rates. Together, these results provide hardware-relevant finite-length candidates for further experimental evaluation and show how structured agentic search can contribute to scientific discovery.

AI.tldr: This paper presents a multi-agent AI framework for discovering practical quantum low-density parity-check (qLDPC) codes with finite length and practical constraints, finding competitive rate-distance performance codes including novel balanced-product constructions with non-normal subgroup actions.
AI.motivation: Searching for useful finite-length qLDPC codes is challenging because code performance must be optimized while satisfying practical constraints (e.g., block length and weight limits), and existing methods struggle to discover structurally diverse, high-performing instances.
AI.method: A multi-agent framework combining specialist proposal and review agents, persistent scientific memory, long-horizon evolution of executable programs, and deterministic construction/evaluation in a closed-loop search. The programs instantiate coset-orbit balanced-product codes, forming a search space that includes bicycle and lifted-product constructions as well as non-normal subgroup actions. The search is constrained to binary CSS codes with block length n≤400 and overall weight w≤10.
AI.result: The framework discovers codes with leading or competitive rate-distance performance in every weight class considered, including [[288,16,18]] at w=7, [[288,18,18]] at w=9, and [[234,28,18]] at w=10. It also finds structurally distinct constructions including a [[336,12,≤24]] candidate and a [[368,18,16]] code, both genuine balanced-product codes with non-normal subgroup actions. The codes exhibit low logical failure rates under code-capacity depolarizing noise with BP-OSD decoding.
AI.conclusion: The discovered codes provide hardware-relevant finite-length candidates for experimental evaluation, and the work demonstrates how structured agentic search can contribute to scientific discovery in quantum error correction code design.

title: Universal entropic occupation statistics in disordered bosonic resonators
summary: Programmable microcavities support grand-canonical photon gases. We show that bosonic state counting creates an entropic staircase of most-probable total occupations. For detuning density continuous and nonzero at the chemical-potential threshold, the active-cell fraction is asymptotically linear at low temperature and the conditional law has a universal limit; for uniform disorder the law is exact over a finite temperature interval. For two modes it is the Gauss--Kuzmin distribution, linking photonic thermodynamics and metric number theory. We outline finite-array and dye-microcavity tests.

AI.tldr: The paper reveals that bosonic state counting in programmable microcavities produces an entropic staircase of most-probable total occupations, with universal limiting laws for conditional distributions, including a connection to the Gauss–Kuzmin distribution in the two-mode case, linking photonic thermodynamics with metric number theory.
AI.motivation: To understand the statistical-thermodynamic behavior of grand-canonical photon gases in programmable microcavities, specifically how bosonic state counting affects most-probable occupations and emergent universal laws.
AI.method: Analytical asymptotic analysis of bosonic state-counting entropies, examining detuning-density cases (continuous nonzero at chemical-potential threshold and uniform disorder), deriving exact conditional laws over finite temperature intervals, and proposing experimental tests in finite arrays and dye microcavities.
AI.result: The active-cell fraction is asymptotically linear at low temperature for continuous nonzero detuning density; for uniform disorder the conditional law is exact over a finite temperature interval; for two modes the law is exactly the Gauss–Kuzmin distribution.
AI.conclusion: Bosonic state counting yields an entropic staircase governing most-probable occupations in photon gases, with universal conditional laws that bridge photonic thermodynamics and metric number theory, and testable predictions for finite-array and dye-microcavity experiments.

title: The Magic Scroll: Leveraging biased noise to improve magic state cultivation in register-based architectures
comment: Main text: 22 pages, 10 figures, 2 tables. Supplementary: 24 pages, 24 figures, 1 table
summary: Multiple quantum computing platforms across neutral atoms [1], nitrogen vacancy centres [2, 3], gate-defined dots [4-6] and 14|15 phosphorus atom qubits [7, 8] in silicon are experimentally exploring the use of high connectivity qubits, beyond that of nearest-neighbour planar lattices. Theoretical works consider modifications to fault-tolerant codes to leverage this higher qubit connectivity, such as non-local LDPC codes [9], inspiring superconducting [10] and photonic [11] platforms to also seek non-planar connectivity. In addition, separate theoretical works consider biased noise, where bit- and phase-flip errors are not equally likely. In this work, we present efficient methods for implementing 6.6.6 and 4.8.8 colour codes, as well as bilayer and folded surface codes, using two-qubit registers. We also leverage noise bias to avoid hook errors, demonstrating comparable performance to the surface code. By combining colour and bilayer codes, we show how magic state cultivation procedures [12-14] can be improved, in a procedure we refer to as the Magic Scroll. Not only does the Magic Scroll escape to a standard surface code, it also improves cultivation volumes by 3x and supports magic $|T\rangle$ state fidelities as low as $10^{-9}$. We show that this technique can be further leveraged to improve distillation performance, showing a 3x improvement to distillation volumes for error rates of $\sim 10^{-15}$. Through these constructions, we demonstrate techniques to leverage noise bias and high qubit connectivity, showing how register-based architectures can improve error rates and reduce quantum volumes in fault-tolerant quantum computing.

AI.tldr: This paper presents efficient methods for implementing non-planar quantum error correction codes (6.6.6 and 4.8.8 colour codes, bilayer and folded surface codes) using two-qubit registers, leveraging noise bias to avoid hook errors. The authors introduce the "Magic Scroll" procedure that combines colour and bilayer codes to improve magic state cultivation volumes by 3x and support T-state fidelities down to 10^-9, with a further 3x improvement to distillation volumes at error rates around 10^-15.
AI.motivation: Multiple quantum computing platforms are exploring high-connectivity qubits beyond nearest-neighbour planar lattices, and theoretical work has considered modifying fault-tolerant codes to leverage this connectivity (e.g., non-local LDPC codes). Additionally, biased noise (where bit- and phase-flip errors are not equally likely) offers opportunities for more efficient error correction. This work aims to combine these two opportunities—high qubit connectivity and noise bias—to improve fault-tolerant quantum computing performance.
AI.method: The authors present efficient implementations of 6.6.6 and 4.8.8 colour codes, as well as bilayer and folded surface codes, on register-based architectures with two-qubit registers. They leverage noise bias to avoid hook errors, achieving performance comparable to the surface code. They combine colour and bilayer codes to construct the "Magic Scroll" procedure, which improves magic state cultivation protocols.
AI.result: The Magic Scroll procedure escapes to a standard surface code while improving cultivation volumes by 3x and supporting magic |T⟩ state fidelities as low as 10^-9. The technique is further leveraged for distillation, showing a 3x improvement to distillation volumes for error rates around 10^-15. These results demonstrate improved error rates and reduced quantum volumes compared to planar codes.
AI.conclusion: Register-based architectures that leverage high qubit connectivity and noise bias can significantly improve fault-tolerant quantum computing, achieving 3x reductions in both magic state cultivation and distillation volumes while supporting extremely low T-state error rates. The techniques show how non-planar code structures can be practically implemented to outperform standard planar surface codes.

title: Knot your average qutrit: Measurement-induced entanglement splitting and the cabling dictionary for GHZ and W States
summary: Multipartite entanglement is conventionally classified by state families viz. family of GHZ and W class of states, with each family expected to behave differently under measurement. We show that, at least for the question of how entanglement splits after a single-particle measurement, this is not the division that matters for qutrits. Extending the Aravind's correspondence (which models entanglement as topological linking, and projective measurement as physically cutting a ring from an interlinked configuration\cite{aravind1997}) from qubits to qutrits, we derive the complete measurement-induced entanglement splitting of the GHZ type qutrit state i.e |GHZ_3> and of the full family of symmetric W class qutrit states, six two same - one different states i.e |{W_{p,p,q}^{sym}}> and one all - different state i.e. |W_{0,1,2}>, under both the computational basis (CB) and the mutually unbiased bases (MUBs), obtaining exact eigenvalues and Schmidt ranks for every outcome in every case. We see that the |W_{0,1,2}> state behaves similarly as |GHZ_3> state, a single, outcome-independent residual rank in each basis, while the |{W_{p,p,q}^{sym}> states alone show probability-weighted, outcome-dependent behaviour. The relevant structural line is therefore repeated-index versus all-different-index bag structure, not GHZ class versus $W$ class. We express this classification using a \textit{two-strand cabling} extension of Aravind's \textit{ring-and-link} picture. This is needed because the qutrit residual Schmidt rank (R) takes three values, R belonging to {1,2,3}, rather than the qubit binary (i.e. R belonging to {1,2}). We are explicit throughout that this cabling dictionary is a labeling convention built to reproduce an independently computed Schmidt rank, not a topological invariant derived from the link diagrams themselves, and we discuss what would be needed to close that gap

AI.tldr: This paper extends Aravind's topological linking correspondence from qubits to qutrits to analyze measurement-induced entanglement splitting of GHZ-type and symmetric W-class qutrit states. The authors find that the relevant classification line is repeated-index versus all-different-index structure rather than the conventional GHZ vs W class division. They derive exact eigenvalues and Schmidt ranks for all outcomes under both computational and mutually unbiased bases, and express the classification using a two-strand cabling extension of Aravind's ring-and-link picture.
AI.motivation: Conventional multipartite entanglement classification divides states into GHZ and W families, but this division does not determine how entanglement splits after a single-particle measurement for qutrits. The authors aim to identify the structural property that actually governs measurement-induced entanglement splitting in higher-dimensional systems.
AI.method: The authors extend Aravind's ring-and-link topological representation of entanglement from qubits to qutrits. They derive the complete measurement-induced entanglement splitting for the GHZ_qutrit state |GHZ_3>, the symmetric W-class states |W_{p,p,q}^{sym}> (six two-same-one-different states), and the all-different state |W_{0,1,2}> under computational and mutually unbiased bases, computing exact eigenvalues and Schmidt ranks for every outcome. They introduce a two-strand cabling extension to represent the qutrit residual Schmidt rank taking values {1,2,3}, explicitly noting this is a labeling convention rather than a topological invariant.
AI.result: The |W_{0,1,2}> all-different state behaves like the |GHZ_3> state, showing outcome-independent residual rank per basis, while the symmetric |W_{p,p,q}^{sym}> states exhibit probability-weighted, outcome-dependent behavior. The dividing structural line is repeated-index versus all-different-index bag structure, not GHZ class versus W class.
AI.conclusion: The GHZ vs W class division is not the relevant classification for measurement-induced entanglement splitting in qutrits. Instead, the repeated-index versus all-different-index structure determines the behavior. The two-strand cabling extension of Aravind's picture captures this classification, though the authors note it is currently a labeling convention rather than a genuine topological invariant, and they discuss what would be needed to close this gap.

title: Quantum Hashing Circuit Optimization for Arbitrary Qubit Connectivity Graphs Based on 1-Covering Path
summary: One of the obstacles to the widespread adoption of quantum computing is the problem of efficient circuit synthesis. Current quantum hardware has limited connections between qubits, with each qubit connected to only a few others. This means that the circuit has to be transformed to accommodate this. In this paper, we present an algorithm that converts a circuit containing a sequence of CNOT gates into a form that is suitable for arbitrary quantum computer architectures. Although we demonstrate the algorithm only in the context of quantum fingerprinting, similar gate sequences are prevalent in quantum algorithms; for instance, they are present in the textbook quantum Fourier transform. We present a quantum circuit implementation of the quantum hashing algorithm (quantum fingerprinting algorithm) for a quantum device with restrictions on the application of two-qubit gates that are expressed as a qubit connectivity graph. As an example of usage of the technique, we apply it to quantum finite automata recognizing the unary $MOD_p=\{a^\ell: \ell \bmod p=0\}$ language, and the $EQ_p=\{a^\ell b^r: \ell \equiv r \pmod p\}$ language. Given the enhancements that our algorithm provides~-- for instance, in one case it achieves a 16\%--17\% decrease in CNOT circuit cost~-- we believe it could also be useful in a broader quantum compilation context.

AI.tldr: This paper presents an algorithm that converts CNOT-gate circuits into a form suitable for arbitrary quantum computer architectures with limited qubit connectivity. The algorithm is demonstrated on quantum fingerprinting/hashing circuits, applied to quantum finite automata recognizing the MOD_p and EQ_p languages, achieving up to a 16-17% reduction in CNOT circuit cost, and is argued to be broadly applicable to other circuits such as the quantum Fourier transform.
AI.motivation: Efficient circuit synthesis is a major obstacle to widespread quantum computing adoption because current quantum hardware has limited qubit connectivity. Circuits must be transformed to comply with these architectural constraints, motivating the need for algorithms that can efficiently map CNOT gate sequences onto restricted connectivity graphs.
AI.method: The algorithm converts a sequence of CNOT gates into a form compatible with arbitrary quantum computer architectures (i.e., any qubit connectivity graph). The method is demonstrated on quantum fingerprinting/hashing circuits and tested on quantum finite automata recognizing the unary MOD_p and EQ_p languages.
AI.result: The algorithm achieves a 16-17% decrease in CNOT circuit cost in one demonstrated case, showing meaningful improvements in circuit efficiency when mapping to constrained hardware.
AI.conclusion: Given the demonstrated efficiency gains and the prevalence of similar CNOT gate sequences in other quantum algorithms (e.g., the quantum Fourier transform), the algorithm could be useful in a broader quantum compilation context beyond quantum fingerprinting.

title: Evidence for Counterfactual Violation of Local Conservation Laws in Quantum Events
comment: 29 pages, including 9 pages of main paper plus 20 pages of appendices. 15 figures, including 4 figures main paper plus 11 figures of the appendices
summary: Physical conservation laws, such as those of energy and momentum, are generally believed to hold exactly and locally in spacetime, including in quantum phenomena. Yet Aharonov, Popescu, and Rohrlich (APR) recently argued, on the basis of a thought experiment, that individual quantum events, unlike ensemble averages, may occasionally violate local conservation laws. Their argument relies on the wave phenomenon known as "superoscillations", which APR themselves discovered more than 30 years ago. Here we provide experimental evidence for such a violation. We extract photons from a small superoscillatory region near the core of an optical vortex and show that their mean transverse momentum is statistically incompatible with a general bound implied by local momentum conservation. The derivation of this bound requires only the theoretically well-supported assumption that the extraction mechanism does not alter the photons' mean transverse momentum. We also detect photons with high transverse momentum at a rate significantly exceeding that predicted by a model assuming local momentum conservation. Because this violation can be established only counterfactually and through postselection, it does not conflict with relativistic causality. Our results may represent the first example of a distinct form of quantum nonlocality that does not explicitly rely on entanglement.

AI.tldr: This paper presents the first experimental evidence that individual quantum events can violate local conservation laws, specifically momentum conservation, as predicted by Aharonov, Popescu, and Rohrlich. Using superoscillatory regions near an optical vortex core, the authors extract photons and show their mean transverse momentum exceeds a bound implied by local momentum conservation, demonstrating a distinct form of quantum nonlocality that does not rely on entanglement.
AI.motivation: To test the provocative theoretical claim by Aharonov, Popescu, and Rohrlich that individual quantum events—unlike ensemble averages—may occasionally violate local conservation laws, based on the phenomenon of superoscillations. Providing experimental confirmation of this prediction would challenge the assumption that conservation laws hold exactly and locally in all quantum phenomena.
AI.method: The authors extract photons from a small superoscillatory region near the core of an optical vortex. They measure the mean transverse momentum of these extracted photons and compare it against a general bound derived from local momentum conservation. The bound's derivation relies only on the assumption that the extraction mechanism does not alter the photons' mean transverse momentum. Photon detection rates with high transverse momentum are also compared against a model assuming local momentum conservation.
AI.result: The measured mean transverse momentum of photons extracted from the superoscillatory region is statistically incompatible with the bound implied by local momentum conservation. Additionally, photons with high transverse momentum are detected at a rate significantly exceeding predictions from a locally-conserving model. The violation is established counterfactually and through postselection, so it does not conflict with relativistic causality.
AI.conclusion: This experiment provides the first experimental evidence for violation of local conservation laws in individual quantum events, arising from superoscillations. The results may represent a new form of quantum nonlocality that does not explicitly rely on entanglement, while remaining consistent with relativistic causality due to the counterfactual and postselected nature of the violation.

title: Squeezing for dispersive readout of NV magnetometer
summary: Nitrogen vacancy centers in diamond have established themselves as good sensing element for various type of sensors. In particular magnetometers based on diamond impurities are quickly developing and are already on the market. Yet, optical readout in these systems complicates system design. Recently schemes of dispersive readout of nitrogen vacancy spin state using high finesse dielectric cavities for microwave field were proposed, which do not use the optical readout scheme. However, only shot noise based estimates were so far done for sensitivity of these devices. Here we provide detailed analysis of various practically relevant noise and loss sources for such a system. Furthermore, we consider the possibility of using the squeezing quantum state of the probing microwave field and show it allows to improve the device performance even at room temperature.

AI.tldr: This paper provides a detailed analysis of practical noise and loss sources for dispersive microwave readout of nitrogen vacancy (NV) center spin states using high-finesse dielectric cavities, and demonstrates that using squeezed quantum states of the probing microwave field can improve sensor performance even at room temperature.
AI.motivation: Nitrogen vacancy centers in diamond are promising for magnetometry, but optical readout complicates system design. While dispersive readout schemes using high-finesse dielectric microwave cavities have been proposed, only shot noise-limited estimates exist for their sensitivity. A comprehensive analysis of practical noise and loss sources is needed, along with exploration of quantum-enhanced sensing strategies.
AI.method: The authors perform a detailed analysis of various practically relevant noise and loss mechanisms in an NV-center-based dispersive readout magnetometer using high-finesse dielectric cavities for microwave fields. They also investigate the use of squeezed quantum states of the probing microwave field as a means to enhance device performance, including at room temperature.
AI.result: The detailed analysis identifies and quantifies practical noise and loss sources affecting the sensitivity of the dispersive readout scheme. The use of squeezed microwave fields is shown to improve device performance and sensitivity even at room temperature, surpassing the shot noise limit.
AI.conclusion: Dispersive microwave readout of NV centers can be practically viable with careful accounting of noise sources, and quantum squeezing of the probing microwave field offers a path to enhanced sensitivity at room temperature, removing the need for optical readout while improving performance.

title: A Heterogeneous Distributed Architecture for Quantum Simulation
summary: Architectural specialization and distribution can help scale fault-tolerant quantum computers, but may also introduce substantial overheads from communication, routing, and resource duplication. We introduce a heterogeneous distributed architecture in which a magic core is connected to an extensible storage system composed of one-dimensional lanes of specialized cold-storage nodes. The storage system supports parallel random access to Pauli string parities. This organization is particularly well suited to fermionic quantum simulation, enabling parallel execution of the highly non-local Pauli strings arising from these systems. We evaluate the architecture on fault-tolerant simulations of the dynamics of the Fermi-Hubbard and sparse Sachdev-Ye-Kitaev (SYK) models on systems of up to 450 logical qubits. These workloads exhibit complementary communication structures: Fermi-Hubbard produces a spectrum of interactions from local to non-local shaped by lattice geometry, whereas sparse SYK produces highly non-local and overlapping Pauli operators. For a Trotter step of a 450-logical-qubit Fermi-Hubbard workload, a six-lane system with 30 T-state factories is within approximately $1.4\times$ the wall-clock time of a homogeneous distributed architecture with 4 times as many T-state factories and substantially greater connectivity and sites for injecting magic. For matched T-factory counts, our architecture is $\sim 2\times$ faster.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes a heterogeneous distributed fault-tolerant quantum computing architecture with a magic core connected to one-dimensional lanes of specialized cold-storage nodes, designed for efficient parallel execution of non-local Pauli string operations in fermionic quantum simulation. Evaluated on Fermi-Hubbard and sparse SYK models up to 450 logical qubits, the architecture achieves ~1.4x wall-clock time of a homogeneous architecture with 4x more T-state factories, and ~2x speedup at matched T-factory counts.
AI.motivation: While architectural specialization and distribution can help scale fault-tolerant quantum computers, they may introduce significant overheads from communication, routing, and resource duplication. The paper aims to design an architecture that minimizes these overheads while enabling efficient execution of workloads with highly non-local Pauli strings, such as those arising in fermionic quantum simulation.
AI.method: The paper introduces a heterogeneous distributed architecture featuring a magic core connected to an extensible storage system composed of one-dimensional lanes of specialized cold-storage nodes. This storage system supports parallel random access to Pauli string parities, which is well suited to the non-local Pauli-string structure of fermionic quantum simulations. The architecture is evaluated on fault-tolerant simulations of Fermi-Hubbard and sparse SYK models on systems of up to 450 logical qubits.
AI.result: For a Trotter step of a 450-logical-qubit Fermi-Hubbard workload, a six-lane system with 30 T-state factories achieves approximately 1.4x the wall-clock time of a homogeneous distributed architecture with 4 times as many T-state factories and substantially greater connectivity and magic-injection sites. At matched T-factory counts, the proposed architecture is approximately 2x faster.
AI.conclusion: The proposed heterogeneous architecture with specialized cold-storage lanes provides a scalable and efficient design for fault-tolerant quantum computation, particularly for workloads with non-local Pauli string interactions like fermionic simulation. It demonstrates that architectural specialization can effectively trade connectivity and magic-injection capacity for improved wall-clock performance, achieving competitive or superior performance with fewer resources.

title: Quantum uncertainty in a macroscopic domain
summary:
We develop a classical model-theoretic representation of partial Boolean algebras and use it to formulate quantum-like uncertainty without abandoning classical propositional logic. Given a surjection from the initial formulæ of a propositional language onto a partial Boolean algebra $(\mathcal V,Π)$, we construct a consistent theory $\mathcal T_g$ whose core---the ordered set of equivalence classes of initial formulæ---is isomorphic to $(\mathcal V,Π)$. Its models are characterized as upward-closed clusters, yielding a model-theoretic formulation of KS-colourability: an $n$-dimensional partial Boolean algebra is KS-colourable exactly when the induced theory has a model meeting every pre-frame in one primitive formula.
  For finite-spectrum observables, uncertainty is defined by the number of locally admissible atomic outcomes. Dispersion-free models are characterized by the singleton pre-frame condition. With an additional measurement-update postulate, a finite example shows how measurement of an incompatible observable can destroy sharpness, providing a model-theoretic form of back-action. A $12$-vertex partial Boolean algebra is KS-colourable, whereas a rigorously constructed $140$-vertex, four-dimensional partial Boolean algebra is not, as shown by a parity argument; its incidence structure is isomorphic to the Peres $24$-ray, $24$-basis configuration in $\mathbb R^4$. Macroscopic interpretations show that these phenomena arise from the organization of propositions and models rather than from nonclassical deduction. Finally, we relate certain models to the probability-one propositions of pure states and density operators, while emphasizing that such certainty models do not determine the full quantum state.

AI.tldr: This paper develops a classical model-theoretic representation of partial Boolean algebras, formulating quantum-like uncertainty and KS-colourability within classical propositional logic. It constructs a consistent theory Tg whose core is isomorphic to a given partial Boolean algebra, characterizes its models as upward-closed clusters, and demonstrates both a KS-colourable 12-vertex algebra and a non-colourable 140-vertex algebra isomorphic to the Peres configuration, showing that quantum-like phenomena arise from the organization of propositions rather than nonclassical deduction.
AI.motivation: The authors aim to capture quantum-like uncertainty phenomena (including KS-colourability, back-action, and sharpness) within a purely classical model-theoretic framework, thereby showing that these effects do not require abandoning classical propositional logic or nonclassical deduction.
AI.method: The paper uses a classical model-theoretic construction based on a surjection from initial formulæ of a propositional language onto a partial Boolean algebra (V,Π). A consistent theory Tg is built whose equivalence-class core is isomorphic to (V,Π). Models are characterized as upward-closed clusters, providing a model-theoretic formulation of KS-colourability. Uncertainty for finite-spectrum observables is defined by the number of locally admissible atomic outcomes, and dispersion-free models are characterized via the singleton pre-frame condition. A measurement-update postulate is added for a finite example to model back-action. Two specific algebras (12-vertex and 140-vertex, isomorphic to the Peres 24-ray configuration) are analyzed, the latter via a parity argument.
AI.result: A 12-vertex partial Boolean algebra is shown to be KS-colourable, while a rigorously constructed 140-vertex four-dimensional partial Boolean algebra (isomorphic to the Peres 24-ray, 24-basis configuration in R^4) is proven non-colourable via a parity argument. The theory's models are characterized as upward-closed clusters, and dispersion-free models are linked to the singleton pre-frame condition. A finite example with a measurement-update postulate demonstrates model-theoretic back-action. Certain models correspond to probability-one propositions of pure states and density operators, though they do not fully determine the quantum state.
AI.conclusion: Quantum-like uncertainty and non-KS-colourability can be formulated entirely within classical propositional logic and standard model theory. These phenomena arise from the structural organization of propositions and models (i.e., the partial Boolean algebra's incidence structure) rather than from any nonclassical deductive apparatus. The framework connects certain models to probability-one propositions of quantum states while acknowledging the limitation that such certainty models cannot uniquely determine the full quantum state.

title: High-fidelity controlled-phase gates for distinguishable quantum walkers via extended interactions
summary: We investigate the implementation of controlled-phase (CP) gates with quantum walks in a dual-rail encoding through the use of interacting particles. While previous proposals have focused on indistinguishable particles (bosons or fermions) to achieve unitary fidelity for plane-wave scattering, practical implementations require finite-size wavepackets and routing through single-particle gates, both factors that introduce unavoidable fidelity losses. We show that extending the interaction range beyond on-site or first-neighbor terms provides sufficient control over the scattering potential to engineer CP gates with distinguishable particles that match the ideal bosonic/fermionic performance. For finite Gaussian wavepackets, we derive analytical approximations for the gate fidelity in terms of the transmission coefficient's magnitude and phase derivatives. We find that while distinguishable-particle scattering alone exhibits slightly lower fidelity than the indistinguishable case, the overall architecture that we propose avoids the additional single-particle gates required for routing indistinguishable particles. The roundabout gates needed for the latter indeed introduce fidelity losses approximately one order of magnitude larger than the interaction-induced losses, making the distinguishable-particle approach competitive for practical implementations. Our results establish multi-neighbor interactions as a tool for quantum information processing with continuous-time quantum walks and provide quantitative guidelines for optimizing gate fidelities in finite-size systems.

AI.tldr: This paper demonstrates that extending interaction ranges beyond on-site or first-neighbor terms enables controlled-phase (CP) gates with distinguishable particles in quantum walks that match the fidelity of ideal bosonic/fermionic implementations, while avoiding the additional single-particle routing gates needed for indistinguishable particles—routing losses being an order of magnitude larger than interaction-induced losses.
AI.motivation: Previous CP gate implementations using quantum walks relied on indistinguishable particles (bosons or fermions) for ideal plane-wave scattering fidelity. However, practical implementations require finite-size wavepackets and single-particle routing gates, which introduce unavoidable fidelity losses. The authors seek an alternative approach that can be competitive or superior in practical settings.

They derive analytical approximations for gate fidelity of finite Gaussian wavepackets in terms of the transmission coefficient's magnitude and phase derivatives. They analyze scattering of distinguishable particles and compare it against indistinguishable-particle approaches, including the overhead of additional single-particle gates (roundabout gates) required for routing indistinguishable particles.
AI.result: Distinguishable-particle scattering alone shows slightly lower fidelity than the indistinguishable case, but the full architecture avoids the additional single-particle routing gates needed for indistinguishable particles. These roundabout gates introduce fidelity losses approximately one order of magnitude larger than the interaction-induced losses, making the distinguishable-particle approach competitive for practical implementations.
AI.conclusion: Multi-neighbor interactions are established as a tool for quantum information processing with continuous-time quantum walks. The work provides quantitative guidelines for optimizing gate fidelities in finite-size systems and shows that distinguishable particles can be a practical alternative to indistinguishable particles for implementing CP gates.

title: A high-performance quantum pulse gate in thin-film lithium niobate
summary: In this work, we demonstrate a quantum pulse gate (QPG) in thin-film lithium niobate. QPGs enable the selective manipulation and detection of temporal modes of quantum light and form the basis of numerous applications in photonic quantum technologies. To date, their widespread adaption is held back by two main limitations: restricted wavelength and polarization combinations of the involved fields and low normalized conversion efficiencies. We overcome these limitations through developing a QPG in thin-film lithium niobate. We design a waveguide geometry that provides the required dispersion properties for a highly efficient type-0 sum-frequency generation.We verify our design through mapping of the phase matching intensity, and demonstrate high-quality QPG operation by measuring a temporal-mode selectivity of (96.8$\pm$1.7)% on par with existing QPGs. Thanks to the strong confinement in thin-film lithium niobate, we succeed in demonstrating an internal conversion efficiency of (89.6$\pm$0.1)% for a pump power of only 20mW in front of our sample. This yields a lower-bound estimate for the normalized conversion efficiency of (1810$\pm$10)$\mathrm{W}^{-1}\mathrm{cm}^{-2}$, three orders of magnitude higher than in previous QPGs. Our results establish thin-film lithium niobate as ideal platform for high-performance QPGs and are a major step towards practical QPGs for photonic quantum technologies.

AI.tldr: This paper demonstrates a quantum pulse gate (QPG) in thin-film lithium niobate that overcomes previous limitations in wavelength/polarization flexibility and low conversion efficiency. The device achieves 96.8% temporal-mode selectivity and an internal conversion efficiency of 89.6% at only 20 mW pump power, yielding a normalized conversion efficiency of 1810 W⁻¹cm⁻²—three orders of magnitude higher than previous QPGs, establishing thin-film lithium niobate as an ideal platform for high-performance quantum pulse gates.
AI.motivation: QPGs enable selective manipulation and detection of temporal modes of quantum light and are foundational for photonic quantum technologies, but their widespread adoption is limited by restricted wavelength/polarization combinations and low normalized conversion efficiencies.
AI.method: The authors develop a QPG in thin-film lithium niobate by designing a waveguide geometry that provides the required dispersion properties for highly efficient type-0 sum-frequency generation. They verify the design through phase-matching intensity mapping and leverage strong optical confinement in thin-film lithium niobate to boost conversion efficiency.
AI.result: The QPG achieves a temporal-mode selectivity of (96.8±1.7)% comparable to existing QPGs, an internal conversion efficiency of (89.6±0.1)% at only 20 mW pump power, and a lower-bound normalized conversion efficiency of (1810±10) W⁻¹cm⁻²—three orders of magnitude higher than previous QPGs.
AI.conclusion: Thin-film lithium niobate is established as an ideal platform for high-performance QPGs, and this work represents a major step towards practical QPGs for photonic quantum technologies.

title: Birefringent Biomineral Microcarriers Stabilise Multimodal Nanodiamond Quantum Sensing in Liquids
summary: Mobile nanodiamond quantum sensors in liquids are limited by Brownian rotation, variable photon collection, and perturbations introduced by optical trapping. Here, we assemble 40-nm nitrogen-vacancy nanodiamonds at the surface of porous, birefringent vaterite microspherulites. This carbonate biomineral provides a polarization-addressable body frame, anisotropic emission redistribution, and a proton-active thermodynamic interface. Under 976-nm optical trapping, the hybrids retain their spin resonance and longitudinal relaxation, with the resonance contrast varying by less than 7 percent and the resonance centre shifting by approximately 1 MHz at 0.8 W. Zeeman-split resonances enable magnetic-field sensing from 0 to 0.8 mT, with a response metric of 78-144 microT per square root Hz. In buffered cell-culture medium, a 10.7 microM nominal proton-equivalent dose shortens T1 from 23.4 +/- 2.3 to 9.0 +/- 1.2 microseconds, corresponding to concentration and pH sensitivities of 6.46 microM per square root Hz and 6.54 mpH per square root Hz, respectively, in DMEM. By contrast, a 500-fold higher proton dose in ethanol produces a substantially weaker spin response, highlighting the role of the carbonate-rich interface. We develop a grand-canonical charge-regulation model coupling proton chemical potential to interfacial switching kinetics within the NV spectral window, capturing medium-dependent dynamic proton transduction. By integrating orientation stabilisation, optical manipulation, magnetic sensing, and interfacial chemical response, this carbonate-rich hybrid platform establishes a versatile approach to multimodal quantum sensing in complex biological liquids.

AI.tldr: The paper assembles 40-nm nitrogen-vacancy nanodiamonds onto porous, birefringent vaterite microspherulites to create a carbonate-rich hybrid platform that overcomes Brownian rotation, variable photon collection, and optical trapping perturbations in liquid quantum sensing. The hybrids enable polarization-addressable orientation, anisotropic emission, magnetic-field sensing up to 0.8 mT, and medium-dependent proton transduction with a sensitivity of 6.46 microM/√Hz for concentration and 6.54 mpH/√Hz for pH in DMEM, supported by a grand-canonical charge-regulation model.
AI.motivation: Mobile nanodiamond quantum sensors in liquids suffer from Brownian rotation, inconsistent photon collection, and perturbations from optical trapping, limiting their reliability and versatility for sensing in complex biological fluids.
AI.method: 40-nm nitrogen-vacancy nanodiamonds are assembled on porous, birefringent vaterite microspherulites, providing a polarization-addressable body frame, anisotropic emission redistribution, and a proton-active interface. The hybrids are characterized under 976-nm optical trapping via spin resonance, longitudinal relaxation (T1), and Zeeman-split resonance measurements. A grand-canonical charge-regulation model coupling proton chemical potential to interfacial switching kinetics is developed.
AI.result: Under optical trapping, resonance contrast varies by less than 7% and resonance center shifts ~1 MHz at 0.8 W. Magnetic-field sensing spans 0-0.8 mT with a response metric of 78-144 microT/√Hz. In DMEM, a 10.7 microM proton-equivalent dose shortens T1 from 23.4±2.3 to 9.0±1.2 microseconds, yielding concentration and pH sensitivities of 6.46 microM/√Hz and 6.54 mpH/√Hz, respectively. A 500-fold higher proton dose in ethanol produces a substantially weaker response.
AI.conclusion: The carbonate-rich vaterite-nanodiamond hybrid platform integrates orientation stabilization, optical manipulation, magnetic sensing, and interfacial chemical response, establishing a versatile approach for multimodal quantum sensing in complex biological liquids.

title: A non-Markovian approach to spin-phonon coherence and the breakdown of the Markovian approximation
summary: Qubit coherence is an essential figure of merit for quantum information processing applications such as quantum computing, or quantum repeaters. Understanding the coherence properties of the underlying physical qubits that facilitate such applications is therefore are often limited by coupling to lattice phonons, which in turn constrains operation temperature. Here we study phonon induced electronic spin decoherence in group-IV vacancy centers in diamond. We begin by modeling the spin-phonon interaction and then employ the widely used Born-Markov approximation, highlighting its inconsistencies in this setting and its deviations from experimental observations. To close the gap between theoretical predictions and experimental results, we relax certain approximations, investigate their contributions to the predicted coherence times, and identify the dominant sources of discrepancy. We further demonstrate that experimentally measured electronic spin coherence dynamics are consistently captured within a non-Markovian framework, and we show how the magnetic field orientation influences the qubit coherence time.

AI.tldr: This paper investigates phonon-induced electronic spin decoherence in group-IV vacancy centers in diamond. The authors show that the widely used Born-Markov approximation fails to accurately predict coherence times in this setting, and demonstrate that a non-Markovian framework consistently captures experimentally measured spin coherence dynamics. They also reveal how magnetic field orientation affects qubit coherence times.
AI.motivation: Qubit coherence is a critical figure of merit for quantum information processing applications like quantum computing and quantum repeaters. However, coherence of group-IV vacancy centers in diamond is often limited by spin-phonon coupling, which constrains operation temperatures. Existing theoretical approaches (Born-Markov approximation) show inconsistencies and deviations from experimental observations, creating a gap between theory and experiment that needs to be closed.
AI.method: The authors model the spin-phonon interaction for group-IV vacancy centers in diamond. They first employ the Born-Markov approximation and highlight its inconsistencies. They then relax certain approximations, investigating their individual contributions to predicted coherence times to identify dominant sources of discrepancy. A non-Markovian framework is developed to capture the experimentally measured spin coherence dynamics, including analysis of magnetic field orientation effects.
AI.result: The Born-Markov approximation is shown to deviate from experimental observations for phonon-induced spin decoherence in group-IV vacancy centers. By relaxing approximations and identifying dominant discrepancy sources, the authors demonstrate that a non-Markovian framework consistently captures experimentally measured electronic spin coherence dynamics. The magnetic field orientation is shown to influence qubit coherence time.
AI.conclusion: A non-Markovian treatment of spin-phonon interactions is necessary to accurately predict and understand qubit coherence in group-IV vacancy centers in diamond. This framework closes the gap between theoretical predictions and experimental measurements, and highlights the role of magnetic field orientation in optimizing qubit coherence times for quantum information applications.

title: Probing Non-equilibrium baths: Frequency-Resolved Thermometry and Quantum Heat Current Turnover
summary: Quantum heat transport for non-equilibrium steady state (NESS) exhibits a characteristic turnover effect, where the heat current reaches a maximum and subsequently declines as system-bath coupling increases. Although numerically exact methods can simulate this non-monotonic behavior, they offer limited information on the thermal state of the heat baths. Here, we introduce a frequency-selective thermometric protocol to probe the baths sustaining an NESS. By extracting a frequency-resolved effective temperature spectrum using a tunable two-level probe, we demonstrate that spectral dispersion serves as a direct witness for the non-equilibrium state of the heat baths. To demonstrate the protocol, we applied the hierarchical equations of motion to spin-boson and two-qubit models, though any exact method can be used. For both models, the turnover effect can be explained by how the thermal state of the heat baths evolves as the system-bath coupling strength increases.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces a frequency-selective thermometric protocol using a tunable two-level probe to extract a frequency-resolved effective temperature spectrum of heat baths sustaining a non-equilibrium steady state. This spectral dispersion directly witnesses the baths' non-equilibrium character, and is used to explain the heat current turnover effect in terms of bath thermal state evolution with increasing system-bath coupling.
AI.motivation: Numerically exact methods can simulate the non-monotonic heat current turnover effect in quantum heat transport for NESS, but they provide limited information about the actual thermal state of the heat baths. A direct probe of the baths is needed to understand the physical mechanism behind the turnover effect.
AI.method: A frequency-selective thermometric protocol is introduced, where a tunable two-level probe extracts a frequency-resolved effective temperature spectrum from the heat baths. The hierarchical equations of motion (HEOM) are applied to spin-boson and two-qubit models to demonstrate the protocol, though any exact method is applicable.
AI.result: The spectral dispersion of the effective temperature serves as a direct witness for the non-equilibrium state of the heat baths. For both the spin-boson and two-qubit models, the turnover effect is explained by how the thermal state of the heat baths evolves with increasing system-bath coupling strength.
AI.conclusion: The frequency-resolved thermometric protocol offers a fundamental understanding of the turnover effect in quantum heat transport by revealing how the bath thermal states deviate from equilibrium as system-bath coupling increases. This reveals the non-equilibrium character of the baths as the underlying mechanism for the non-monotonic heat current behavior.

title: Autoregressive Projective Quantum Monte Carlo: From a Hermitian to a Non-Hermitian Perspective
summary: Accurately determining the ground-state properties of quantum many-body systems remains a central challenge. In this work, we introduce an autoregressive projective quantum Monte Carlo (PQMC) framework that leverages recurrent neural networks (RNNs) to guide the stochastic dynamics. By incorporating autoregressive sampling into PQMC, we demonstrate substantial improvements in accuracy compared to standard unguided PQMC, while retaining polynomial computational cost. We benchmark our approach against conventional variational RNN ansätze and find that the autoregressive PQMC consistently achieves lower energies and higher fidelity, regardless of system size or whether the Hamiltonian is Hermitian or non-Hermitian. Our results highlight the versatility and power of neural-guided PQMC methods, paving the way for promising scalable simulations of low-energy states in complex quantum many-body systems.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces an autoregressive projective quantum Monte Carlo (PQMC) framework that uses recurrent neural networks (RNNs) to guide stochastic dynamics. The method achieves substantially better accuracy than unguided PQMC at polynomial computational cost, and consistently outperforms variational RNN ansätze in energy and fidelity for both Hermitian and non-Hermitian Hamiltonians across various system sizes.
AI.motivation: Accurately determining ground-state properties of quantum many-body systems remains a central challenge, motivating the need for more powerful and scalable simulation methods.
AI.method: The method combines autoregressive sampling with projective quantum Monte Carlo (PQMC), leveraging recurrent neural networks (RNNs) to guide the stochastic dynamics of the PQMC framework while maintaining polynomial computational cost.
AI.result: The autoregressive PQMC achieves substantially improved accuracy over standard unguided PQMC, and consistently achieves lower energies and higher fidelity than conventional variational RNN ansätze, regardless of system size or whether the Hamiltonian is Hermitian or non-Hermitian.
AI.conclusion: Neural-guided PQMC methods demonstrate versatility and power, paving the way for scalable simulations of low-energy states in complex quantum many-body systems.

title: Genuinely Unextendible Product Bases from Maximum Distance Separable Codes
summary: The existence of genuinely unextendible product bases (GUPBs), incomplete orthogonal sets of fully product states whose orthogonal complements contain no product vector across any bipartition, has remained an open problem. Here we construct GUPBs for any number $N\geq3$ of parties using classical maximum distance separable (MDS) codes. The MDS property imposes a rigidity on the induced product tiling across every bipartition; combined with Fourier mode deletion and a stopper state, this rigidity enforces genuine unextendibility. Consequently, the orthogonal complement of each GUPB is a genuinely entangled subspace whose normalized projector is invariant under partial transposition across every bipartition, yielding an explicit family of multipartite bound entangled states. We further construct GME witnesses that detect these states even though no fully decomposable witness can do so. Moreover, the resulting indistinguishability persists under arbitrary finite tensor powers and measurements separable across any bipartition. These results establish a direct connection between error-correcting codes and multipartite entanglement and provide an algebraic route to certifying genuinely multipartite bound entanglement.

AI.tldr: The paper constructs genuinely unextendible product bases (GUPBs) for any N≥3 parties using classical maximum distance separable (MDS) codes, producing genuinely entangled subspaces whose normalized projectors are invariant under partial transposition across every bipartition. This yields explicit multipartite bound entangled states, non-fully-decomposable genuine multipartite entanglement (GME) witnesses, and indistinguishability that persists under arbitrary finite tensor powers and any separable bipartition measurements, establishing a direct link between error-correcting codes and multipartite entanglement.
AI.motivation: The existence of genuinely unextendible product bases (GUPBs)—incomplete orthogonal sets of fully product states whose orthogonal complements admit no product vector across any bipartition—has been an open problem. Constructing such objects is important for understanding the structure of product-state orthogonality, quantum indistinguishability, and bound entanglement in multipartite settings.
AI.method: The construction uses classical maximum distance separable (MDS) codes. The MDS property imposes rigidity on the induced product tiling across every bipartition. Combined with Fourier mode deletion and a stopper state, this rigidity enforces genuine unextendibility of the resulting product basis.
AI.result: GUPBs are constructed for any number of parties N≥3. Their orthogonal complements are genuinely entangled subspaces with projectors invariant under partial transposition across every bipartition, yielding explicit multipartite bound entangled states. Genuine multipartite entanglement witnesses that detect these states are constructed even though no fully decomposable witness can detect them. The associated indistinguishability persists under arbitrary finite tensor powers and measurements separable across any bipartition.
AI.conclusion: The work establishes a direct connection between error-correcting codes and multipartite entanglement, providing an algebraic route to certifying genuinely multipartite bound entanglement and opening a new pathway for constructing and verifying GUPBs and bound entangled states.

title: Gate-based emulation of boson sampling using photonic qubits
summary: Boson sampling arising from multiphoton interference in linear-optical networks is a prominent non-universal model for quantum computation. Here, by encoding the multi-qubit state to bosonic Fock state, we present a scalable quantum-circuit framework for simulating boson sampling on a universal quantum computing platform. Beginning with balanced beam-splitter transformations on the single- and two-photon sectors, we derive equivalent quantum-circuit implementations and unify them within a common Hilbert-space representation using an ancilla-assisted encoding. This construction is then generalized to arbitrary interferometers by replacing each optical beam splitter with a repeating quantum-circuit unit that selectively acts only within the relevant local interference subspace, requiring $N+1$ qubits for a two-photon $N$-mode interferometer and a linear-overhead subspace-identification procedure. Using this framework, gate-based quantum circuit for a four-mode boson-sampling circuit is developed and experimentally implemented on a four-qubit gate-based photonic qubit system. The qubit framework for emulating boson sampling of $n-$photons in $m-$mode will be useful to solve a broad class of sampling complexity problem on a gate-based quantum computers.

AI.tldr: This paper presents a scalable quantum-circuit framework for simulating boson sampling on universal gate-based quantum computers by encoding multi-qubit states into bosonic Fock states. The framework uses ancilla-assisted encoding to map beam-splitter transformations to quantum-circuit equivalents, generalized to arbitrary interferometers via repeating circuit units that act only within relevant local interference subspaces. The framework requires N+1 qubits for a two-photon N-mode interferometer and was experimentally demonstrated on a four-qubit gate-based photonic system for a four-mode boson-sampling circuit.
AI.motivation: Boson sampling is a prominent non-universal model for quantum computation, but simulating it on universal gate-based quantum computers lacks a scalable framework. The authors aim to bridge the gap between boson sampling and universal quantum computation by developing a scalable circuit-level encoding that maps the optical interference problem onto qubit-based quantum circuits.
AI.method: The method starts with balanced beam-splitter transformations on single- and two-photon sectors, deriving equivalent quantum-circuit implementations unified via an ancilla-assisted encoding in a common Hilbert space. This is generalized to arbitrary interferometers by replacing each optical beam splitter with a repeating quantum-circuit unit that selectively acts only within the relevant local interference subspace. The approach requires N+1 qubits for a two-photon N-mode interferometer and employs a linear-overhead subspace-identification procedure. A four-mode boson-sampling circuit was experimentally implemented on a four-qubit gate-based photonic qubit system.
AI.result: A scalable gate-based quantum-circuit framework for emulating boson sampling was developed and experimentally validated on a four-qubit photonic system implementing a four-mode boson-sampling circuit.
AI.conclusion: The qubit framework for emulating n-photon m-mode boson sampling will be useful for solving a broad class of sampling complexity problems on gate-based quantum computers, providing a practical bridge between photonic boson sampling and universal quantum computing platforms.

title: Faster Algorithms for Multimarginal Optimal Transport
summary:
