We study algorithms for approximating the multimarginal optimal transport (MOT) distance, a generalization of the classic optimal transport distance, between $m$ discrete probability distributions each supported on at most $n$ points. We give a classical algorithm that computes a coupling between these marginals whose expected transportation cost is within an additive $\varepsilon > 0$ of the MOT distance in time $O(m^2 n^m \varepsilon^{-1}\mathrm{polylog}(m,n,\varepsilon^{-1}))$. This is, to our knowledge, the first bound for general MOT problems with simultaneous linear dependence on the dimension $n^m$ and on the accuracy parameter $\varepsilon^{-1}$, improving the prior state of the art.
  On the quantum side, we give two algorithms that achieve speedups in dimension, though with worse accuracy dependence than classical approaches. First, we construct a quantum projected subgradient method for estimating the MOT distance within an additive $\varepsilon >0$ with runtime $O( m^3 n^{\frac{m}{2}+1} \varepsilon^{-2} \mathrm{polylog}(m,n,\varepsilon^{-1}))$. This algorithm works with the linear programming dual of the MOT problem, and does not return a coupling. We also give a quantum multimarginal Sinkhorn algorithm for entropy-regularized MOT. This algorithm returns an implicit description of an approximately optimal coupling with runtime $O(m^8n^{\frac{m+1}{2}} \varepsilon^{-5} \mathrm{polylog}(m,n,\varepsilon^{-1})))$ after the usual reduction from entropic MOT to unregularized MOT. We also record query lower bounds: for any precision $\varepsilon<1/2$, randomized classical algorithms require $Ω(n^m/(1+\varepsilon n))$ queries and quantum algorithms require $Ω(\sqrt{n^m/(1+\varepsilon n)})$ queries.

AI.tldr: This paper studies classical and quantum algorithms for approximating the multimarginal optimal transport (MOT) distance between m discrete distributions on at most n points. They give a classical algorithm with O(m²n^m ε⁻¹ polylog) runtime—the first with simultaneous linear dependence on n^m and ε⁻¹—and two quantum algorithms achieving speedups in dimension (n^{m/2+1} and n^{(m+1)/2}) at the cost of worse ε-dependence, plus matching query lower bounds for both classical and quantum settings.
AI.motivation: Multimarginal optimal transport is a generalization of classical OT with broad applications, but general MOT problems are computationally expensive due to the n^m dependence on dimension. The goal is to design faster approximation algorithms for MOT, both classically and quantumly, while also understanding the fundamental query complexity limits.
AI.method: The paper proposes: (1) a classical algorithm achieving simultaneous linear dependence on both n^m and ε⁻¹, improving prior state-of-the-art; (2) a quantum projected subgradient method operating on the linear programming dual of MOT with better dimension scaling (n^{m/2+1}) but worse ε-dependence; (3) a quantum multimarginal Sinkhorn algorithm for entropy-regularized MOT, returning an implicit coupling description with runtime O(m⁸ n^{(m+1)/2} ε⁻⁵ polylog), after the standard entropic-to-unregularized reduction. The paper also establishes query lower bounds for both randomized classical (Ω(n^m/(1+εn))) and quantum (Ω(√(n^m/(1+εn)))) algorithms.
AI.result: The classical algorithm runs in O(m²n^m ε⁻¹ polylog(m,n,ε⁻¹)), marking the first bound with simultaneous linear dependence on n^m and ε⁻¹. The quantum projected subgradient method runs in O(m³ n^{m/2+1} ε⁻² polylog) and does not return a coupling. The quantum Sinkhorn runs in O(m⁸ n^{(m+1)/2} ε⁻⁵ polylog) and returns an implicit coupling. Query lower bounds match (up to the ε factor) for both classical and quantum settings, showing the dimension-speedup is essentially optimal.
AI.conclusion: The paper establishes a new classical state-of-the-art for MOT approximation and demonstrates that quantum algorithms can achieve dimension speedups (roughly from n^m to n^{m/2}) at the cost of worse precision dependence. The query lower bounds confirm the quantum dimension speedup is near-optimal given the problem structure.

title: Compound beams for direct experimental comparison of quantum operations
comment: Photon addition and subtraction are systematically compared across twin-beam, thermal, and sub-Poissonian states at varying intensities over two orders in magnitude
summary: Compound beams composed of simple experimental blocks (detected in simultaneous detection windows) that form specific quantum-correlated structures are suggested for simulating the properties of different quantum operations used for creating highly nonclassical and entangled multi-mode states needed in quantum communication, metrology, and information protocols. Qualitative and quantitative comparison of multi-photon addition and subtraction in compound multi-mode thermal as well as sub-Poissonian beams and multi-mode twin beams with their intensities extending over two orders in magnitude is provided. Adding and subtracting up to twenty photocounts, optimal conditions for the generation of experimental nonclassical states are identified. In general, photon addition is identified as advantageous over photon subtraction for the multi-mode thermal and sub-Poissonian beams: It induces (enhances) the nonclassicality in the former (latter) state. Contrary to this, photon subtraction outperforms photon addition in the multi-mode twin beams. Moreover, exploiting temporal photon-pair correlations in compound twin beams when post-selecting, nearly ideal experimental photon(s) addition is demonstrated.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes using compound beams made of experimental blocks with quantum-correlated structures to simulate quantum operations for generating nonclassical and entangled multi-mode states. It compares photon addition and subtraction in multi-mode thermal, sub-Poissonian, and twin beams, finding photon addition is superior for thermal/sub-Poissonian beams while photon subtraction outperforms for twin beams, and demonstrates near-ideal photon addition via temporal photon-pair correlations.
AI.motivation: To identify optimal experimental conditions and operations for generating highly nonclassical and entangled multi-mode states needed for quantum communication, metrology, and information protocols.
AI.method: Compound beams composed of simple experimental blocks detected in simultaneous detection windows are used to simulate quantum operations. Qualitative and quantitative comparison of multi-photon addition and subtraction is performed across multi-mode thermal, sub-Poissonian, and twin beams, with intensities spanning two orders of magnitude and up to twenty photocounts added/subtracted.
AI.result: Photon addition is advantageous over photon subtraction for thermal and sub-Poissonian beams, inducing or enhancing nonclassicality. For multi-mode twin beams, photon subtraction outperforms photon addition. Nearly ideal experimental photon addition is demonstrated by exploiting temporal photon-pair correlations in compound twin beams with post-selection.
AI.conclusion: The optimal operation for generating nonclassical states depends on the beam type: photon addition is preferred for thermal and sub-Poissonian beams, while photon subtraction is preferred for twin beams. Temporal photon-pair correlations enable near-ideal photon addition in twin beams.

title: Quantum Coordination and Nonlocal Games: Theory and Applications
summary:
Coordination is a fundamental primitive in communication and information theory, in which distributed systems must collectively generate correlated behavior rather than merely exchange messages. In quantum networks, the nature of entanglement, quantum measurements, and nonclassical correlations introduces coordination possibilities unavailable classically. This article reviews recent advances in coordination over classical and quantum communication networks, focusing on empirical and strong coordination in multi-user settings.
  We consider the implications of coordination for nonlocal games, showing how it provides a natural framework for understanding the correlations that enable spatially separated players to improve their probability of winning. We present a unified framework for coordination using classical or quantum communication and pre-shared correlation resources. The review covers simulation of both entanglement and separable correlations across a variety of network architectures, including two-node, cascade, broadcast, and multiple-access networks. We study the operational differences between empirical and strong coordination, and the tradeoffs between communication and correlation resources, such as pre-shared randomness and entanglement.
  Coordination plays a major role in device-independent quantum key distribution (DI-QKD) schemes, in which parties can generate a secret key even if the devices used in the process have been prepared by an adversary. Furthermore, we examine the role of coordination in quantum repeaters, where distributed entanglement serves as a resource for long-distance quantum communication. The review highlights connections between coordination theory and applications such as distributed quantum systems, quantum internet architectures, and future communication networks.

AI.tldr: This paper reviews recent advances in coordination over classical and quantum communication networks, covering empirical and strong coordination in multi-user settings, their implications for nonlocal games, simulation of entanglement and separable correlations across various network architectures, and the role of coordination in DI-QKD and quantum repeaters.
AI.motivation: Coordination is a fundamental primitive in communication theory where distributed systems must generate correlated behavior beyond simple message exchange. Quantum networks introduce coordination possibilities unavailable classically, and a unified review of these advances is needed to understand the interplay between coordination theory and emerging quantum applications.
AI.method: The paper presents a unified framework for coordination using classical or quantum communication and pre-shared correlation resources. It reviews empirical and strong coordination across various network architectures (two-node, cascade, broadcast, and multiple-access networks) and analyzes tradeoffs between communication and correlation resources such as pre-shared randomness and entanglement.
AI.result: The review demonstrates how coordination provides a natural framework for understanding correlations in nonlocal games, shows operational differences between empirical and strong coordination, establishes coordination's central role in DI-QKD and quantum repeaters, and highlights connections between coordination theory and distributed quantum systems, quantum internet architectures, and future communication networks.
AI.conclusion: Coordination theory serves as a unifying lens for understanding both classical and quantum network communication, with significant implications for security protocols like DI-QKD, long-distance quantum communication via repeaters, and the design of future quantum internet architectures.

title: Conditional non-Hermitian acceleration of multiphoton atomic transitions
summary: Continuous monitoring can convert a dissipative channel into a resource for accelerating otherwise slow multiphoton transitions. We consider a three-level atom in a $Λ$ configuration and condition the evolution on the absence of photon emission through an auxiliary monitored decay channel. The resulting no-jump dynamics is governed by a non-Hermitian Rabi-type Hamiltonian. Using Floquet theory and Brillouin--Wigner projection-operator perturbation method, we derive effective two-state descriptions of odd-multiphoton resonances in the semiclassical and quantum Rabi models. The effective population-transfer rate, defined as the inverse of the time required for the first complete transfer between the atomic states, is maximized at an exceptional point, where its enhancement factor approaches $π/2$, corresponding to an approximately $57\%$ increase over the Hermitian value. Numerical results for three- and five-photon resonances closely reproduce the analytical transition times and yield non-negligible postselection probabilities. By contrast, the complete unconditioned dissipative evolution does not exhibit the same population-transfer enhancement. These results demonstrate a speed--success trade-off for measurement-conditioned multiphoton state transfer.

AI.tldr: Measurement-conditioned no-jump dynamics in a monitored decay channel converts a dissipative channel into a resource that accelerates multiphoton transitions. Using Floquet theory and Brillouin-Wigner perturbation methods, the authors show that odd-multiphoton resonances in semiclassical and quantum Rabi models are optimally enhanced at an exceptional point, achieving a ~57% increase in population-transfer rate over the Hermitian limit.
AI.motivation: To investigate whether continuous monitoring of a dissipative channel can be exploited as a resource to accelerate otherwise slow multiphoton transitions, rather than treating dissipation purely as a decoherence source.
AI.method: Conditioning the three-level Λ-atom evolution on no photon emission through an auxiliary monitored decay channel yields non-Hermitian Rabi-type dynamics. Floquet theory combined with Brillouin-Wigner projection-operator perturbation theory is used to derive effective two-state descriptions of odd-multiphoton resonances in both semiclassical and quantum Rabi models.
AI.result: The effective population-transfer rate is maximized at an exceptional point with an enhancement factor approaching π/2 (~57% over the Hermitian value). Numerical simulations for three- and five-photon resonances match analytical transition times with non-negligible postselection probabilities. Unconditioned dissipative evolution shows no such enhancement.
AI.conclusion: The results establish a speed-success trade-off for measurement-conditioned multiphoton state transfer, showing that conditioned monitoring can accelerate quantum state transfer at the cost of postselection success probability.

title: A Highly Accurate Fast Decoding Framework for QLDPC codes Accelerated by Noise Perturbation and Ensemble Decoding
summary: A well-balanced decoder has been central to the development of modern fault-tolerant quantum computing. However, the inherent topologies of quantum error correcting codes can limit the performance of many well-studied decoding algorithms. In this work, we introduce Noise Assisted Ensemble Decoding (NAED), a highly accurate decoding framework with a significant advantage in real-time speed. NAED constructs an ensemble of Tanner forests, obtained as acyclic subgraphs of the original Tanner graph, and performs exact inference on each Tanner forest using a lightweight dynamic programming algorithm. The forest construction is guided by synthetic soft information derived jointly from the measured syndrome and channel statistics, with controlled noise perturbations generating diverse yet informative decoding matrix column orderings for the Tanner forest construction across the ensemble. Our benchmark results show that the proposed synthetic soft information-driven construction and inference on the Tanner forests can achieve improved or comparable decoding performances to the state-of-the-art decoding solutions, such as BP+OSD$0$, while also providing orders-of-magnitude improvements in per-round decoding speed under circuit-level noise.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces Noise Assisted Ensemble Decoding (NAED), a fault-tolerant quantum decoding framework that constructs an ensemble of Tanner forests from the code's Tanner graph, performs exact inference on each using dynamic programming, and achieves performance comparable to BP+OSD0 while being orders of magnitude faster under circuit-level noise.
AI.motivation: The inherent topologies of quantum error correcting codes can limit the performance of many well-studied decoding algorithms, despite the need for a well-balanced decoder being central to modern fault-tolerant quantum computing. Real-time decoding speed and accuracy are both critical but often trade off against each other in existing approaches.
AI.method: NAED constructs an ensemble of Tanner forests (acyclic subgraphs of the original Tanner graph) and performs exact inference on each using a lightweight dynamic programming algorithm. The forest construction is guided by synthetic soft information derived jointly from the measured syndrome and channel statistics, with controlled noise perturbations generating diverse column orderings across the ensemble for building informative Tanner forests.
AI.result: Benchmark results show NAED achieves improved or comparable decoding performance to state-of-the-art decoders such as BP+OSD0, while providing orders-of-magnitude improvements in per-round decoding speed under circuit-level noise.
AI.conclusion: NAED offers a highly accurate and real-time-fast decoding framework by leveraging ensemble decoding over Tanner forests, bridging the gap between decoding accuracy and computational speed for fault-tolerant quantum computing.

title: Time Dilation and center of Mass Normalization in the Page-Wootters Formalism
summary: In this work, we study the emergence of relativistic effects in a composite quantum clock within the Page-Wootters relational formulation of quantum mechanics. We consider a system with internal and center-of-mass degrees of freedom and analyze the conditioned evolution of the center-of-mass relative to the internal system treated as an internal clock. We show that the internal sector exhibits an effective time dilation. Retaining the full mass-energy structure of the composite particle, a back-reaction of the internal energy on the center-of-mass sector appears through an operator-valued normalization factor. As a direct consequence of the back-reaction, the conditioned center-of-mass dynamics is governed by a Schroodinger equation that is non-local in the clock time, with an effective temporal non-locality of the order of the Compton time of the composite system. Applying the formalism to a center-of-mass momentum superposition, we find that the interferometric visibility acquires a correction that is quadratic in the internal energy, and therefore depends on the absolute distribution of clock energies rather than only on the energy gaps that control the standard time-dilation dephasing. Although this correction is parametrically small, it is a generic feature of relativistic composite clocks and can, in principle, be isolated through a differential visibility measurement comparing clocks with equal transition frequency but different mean internal energies.

AI.tldr: This paper studies relativistic effects in a composite quantum clock within the Page-Wootters relational formulation of quantum mechanics, showing that the internal clock sector exhibits effective time dilation and that back-reaction of internal energy on the center-of-mass sector leads to non-local dynamics (at the Compton time scale) and a visibility correction quadratic in internal energy.
AI.motivation: To understand how relativistic effects emerge in composite quantum systems treated relationally (via the Page-Wootters formalism), particularly how internal energy back-reacts on center-of-mass dynamics and produces observable signatures beyond standard time-dilation dephasing.
AI.method: The authors adopt the Page-Wootters relational formulation, treat the internal degrees of freedom as an internal clock, and analyze the conditioned evolution of the center-of-mass. They retain the full mass-energy structure of the composite particle, leading to an operator-valued normalization factor that induces back-reaction. They apply this to a momentum superposition and compute the interferometric visibility, comparing clocks with equal transition frequency but different mean internal energies.
AI.result: The conditioned center-of-mass dynamics obeys a Schrödinger equation that is non-local in clock time with temporal non-locality of order the Compton time. The interferometric visibility acquires a correction quadratic in internal energy, depending on the absolute distribution of clock energies, not only energy gaps. This correction is parametrically small but generic, and can be isolated via differential visibility measurements.
AI.conclusion: Relativistic composite clocks exhibit generic back-reaction effects of internal energy on center-of-mass dynamics, yielding quantum corrections (quadratic in internal energy) to interferometric visibility that are in principle detectable through differential measurements, even though they are parametrically small.

title: A Design Space Study of Density Matrix Parameterizations for Diffusion-Based Quantum State Tomography
summary: Diffusion-based quantum state tomography (QST) has shown promising results, but all existing methods implicitly adopt a single parameterization---typically Cholesky---without systematic evaluation. We present a design space study of density matrix parameterizations for diffusion QST, introducing a geometric framework based on the Jacobian Gram matrix $\mathbf{J}^\top\mathbf{J}$ that quantifies two competing criteria: isometric conditioning and physical constraint satisfaction. Our calibration of seven parameterizations at 2- and 3-qubit scales reveals three key findings. First, isometry and constraints are orthogonal criteria---no single parameterization optimizes both. Second, theoretical elegance does not predict geometric quality: the exponential map exhibits a spectral range of $149\times$ at 2 qubits and $75\,658\times$ at 3 qubits, while simpler parameterizations remain well-conditioned. Third, geometric conditioning alone does not fully predict end-to-end performance: without classifier-free guidance (CFG), Hermitian direct outperforms Bloch despite worse local isometry; under CFG, the ranking reverses due to amplified boundary effects. End-to-end training confirms that better-conditioned parameterizations converge faster and achieve higher fidelity in the absence of CFG. We provide actionable selection guidelines to guide future QST method design.

AI.tldr: This paper presents a systematic design space study of density matrix parameterizations for diffusion-based quantum state tomography (QST), introducing a geometric framework based on the Jacobian Gram matrix to quantify isometric conditioning and physical constraint satisfaction. The study evaluates seven parameterizations at 2- and 3-qubit scales, finding that isometry and constraints are orthogonal criteria, that theoretical elegance does not predict geometric quality (with the exponential map showing spectral ranges up to 75,658× at 3 qubits), and that geometric conditioning does not fully predict end-to-end performance under classifier-free guidance. The authors provide actionable selection guidelines for QST method design.
AI.motivation: All existing diffusion-based QST methods implicitly adopt a single parameterization (typically Cholesky) without systematic evaluation, leaving a critical gap in understanding how different density matrix parameterizations affect diffusion QST performance.
AI.method: The authors introduce a geometric framework based on the Jacobian Gram matrix J^T J to quantify two competing criteria: isometric conditioning and physical constraint satisfaction. They calibrate seven parameterizations at 2- and 3-qubit scales, and evaluate end-to-end performance with and without classifier-free guidance.
AI.result: Three key findings: (1) isometry and constraints are orthogonal criteria with no single parameterization optimizing both; (2) theoretical elegance does not predict geometric quality—the exponential map has a spectral range of 149× at 2 qubits and 75,658× at 3 qubits while simpler parameterizations remain well-conditioned; (3) geometric conditioning alone does not fully predict end-to-end performance—Hermitian direct outperforms Bloch without CFG despite worse isometry, but the ranking reverses under CFG. Better-conditioned parameterizations converge faster and achieve higher fidelity without CFG.
AI.conclusion: The paper provides actionable selection guidelines for choosing density matrix parameterizations in diffusion QST, highlighting the need to consider both geometric properties and downstream application context (e.g., CFG usage) when designing QST methods.

title: Conditions for implementing projective measurements through continuous monitoring
summary: Projective measurements are foundational for quantum physics in general and quantum information tasks in particular. However, their direct implementation is often not warranted. Here, we investigate under what conditions continuous monitoring that manifests in quantum jump trajectories realises projective measurements over time. Considering finite-dimensional quantum systems and single, diagonalisable jump operators, we show if and how the detected quantum jump statistics force, and allow inferring, the convergence of individual quantum trajectories towards eigenstates of an observable in the long-time limit. We identify a necessary non-degeneracy condition that is related to the presence of a strong symmetry with non-degenerate symmetry sectors. We derive analytical expressions for the rate of convergence and the time-error relationship in finite-time measurements. Our results provide a transparent framework for understanding the emergence of projective measurements from continuous monitoring, with direct implications for the optimisation of quantum measurement protocols in experiments.

AI.tldr: This paper investigates when continuous monitoring via quantum jump trajectories can realize projective measurements over time in finite-dimensional quantum systems with single, diagonalizable jump operators.
AI.motivation: Projective measurements are fundamental to quantum physics and quantum information, but their direct implementation is often impractical. Understanding how continuous monitoring can effectively realize projective measurements over time would enable more feasible quantum measurement protocols.
AI.method: The authors analyze finite-dimensional quantum systems with single, diagonalizable jump operators, examining whether and how detected quantum jump statistics force individual quantum trajectories to converge towards eigenstates of an observable in the long-time limit. They identify a necessary non-degeneracy condition related to strong symmetry with non-degenerate symmetry sectors, and derive analytical expressions for convergence rates and time-error relationships.
AI.result: They identify a necessary non-degeneracy condition (related to strong symmetry with non-degenerate symmetry sectors) for projective measurement realization via continuous monitoring, and provide analytical expressions for convergence rates and finite-time measurement error bounds.
AI.conclusion: The work provides a transparent framework for understanding the emergence of projective measurements from continuous monitoring, with direct implications for optimizing quantum measurement protocols in experiments.

title: QSVM-RQNN: Low-Qubit Recurrent Quantum Similarity Learning for Condition Monitoring and Fault Classification
summary: In the Noisy Intermediate-Scale Quantum (NISQ) era, limited qubit availability and hardware noise constrain the practical deployment of quantum machine learning (QML). Existing quantum neural network (QNN) and quantum convolutional neural network (QCNN) architectures often require increasing quantum resources as the input dimension grows, limiting scalability on near-term devices. We propose QSVM-RQNN, a low-qubit framework integrating centroid-based Quantum Support Vector Machine (QSVM) similarity learning with Recurrent Quantum Neural Networks (RQNNs) for fault classification. The framework reduces the feature space using principal component analysis (PCA), partitions the reduced representation into sequential timesteps, and processes them using a compact three-qubit recurrent quantum architecture with shared parameters. Two complementary variants are developed: QSVM-RQNN-V1 performs class-conditioned joint quantum encoding of input and centroid segments, whereas QSVM-RQNN-V2 performs recurrent learning over timestep-wise quantum similarity representations. Experimental evaluation on multiple fault diagnosis datasets shows competitive and, in several cases, state-of-the-art performance compared with QSVM, QNN, QCNN, QSVM-QNN, QSVM-QCNN, and RQNN models. The proposed architectures provide favorable performance-efficiency trade-offs, improved recall, and enhanced fault detection on highly imbalanced datasets. These results demonstrate that integrating centroid-based quantum similarity learning with low-qubit recurrent representation learning provides an effective and scalable approach to condition monitoring and fault classification on resource-constrained NISQ devices.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes QSVM-RQNN, a low-qubit quantum machine learning framework that integrates centroid-based Quantum Support Vector Machine similarity learning with Recurrent Quantum Neural Networks for fault classification. The framework uses PCA for dimensionality reduction, partitions data into sequential timesteps, and processes them with a compact three-qubit recurrent architecture. Two variants (V1 and V2) are evaluated on multiple fault diagnosis datasets, achieving competitive or state-of-the-art performance against existing QML models while maintaining favorable performance-efficiency trade-offs on resource-constrained NISQ devices.
AI.motivation: Existing QNN and QCNN architectures scale poorly in qubit requirements as input dimensionality grows, limiting their practical deployment on NISQ devices that have limited qubit availability and hardware noise. There is a need for a scalable, low-qubit quantum learning framework that can handle high-dimensional data such as fault classification tasks without exhausting quantum resources.
AI.method: The framework first reduces the feature space using principal component analysis (PCA), then partitions the reduced representation into sequential timesteps. These are processed by a compact three-qubit recurrent quantum architecture with shared parameters. Two variants are introduced: QSVM-RQNN-V1 performs class-conditioned joint quantum encoding of input and centroid segments, while QSVM-RQNN-V2 performs recurrent learning over timestep-wise quantum similarity representations derived from centroid-based QSVM similarity learning.
AI.result: Experimental evaluation on multiple fault diagnosis datasets shows that QSVM-RQNN achieves competitive and, in several cases, state-of-the-art performance compared with QSVM, QNN, QCNN, QSVM-QNN, QSVM-QCNN, and RQNN baselines. The proposed architectures demonstrate favorable performance-efficiency trade-offs, improved recall, and enhanced fault detection on highly imbalanced datasets.
AI.conclusion: Integrating centroid-based quantum similarity learning with low-qubit recurrent representation learning provides an effective and scalable approach to condition monitoring and fault classification on resource-constrained NISQ devices, addressing the scalability bottleneck of existing QML architectures.

title: A Domain-Specific Language for Formulating Hybrid Quantum-Classical Meta-Solver Strategies
comment: 13 pages, 3 figures, preprint of a paper that was accepted at the GI Quantum Computing Workshop 2026
summary: A key challenge when designing hybrid quantum-classical workflows is the identification of quantum candidates, that is, determining for which specific problems quantum advantages could potentially be achieved. When choosing between several candidates, it is crucial to consider the characteristics specific to the problem, as these can fundamentally determine how successful quantum or classical approaches will be. This implies that specialized expertise is needed to use hybrid quantum-classical workflows successfully. To address this challenge, we propose a domain-specific language (DSL) to express best-practices in solution strategies using a universal representation that is easy to use and share. This DSL provides a flexible approach to design hybrid quantum-classical workflows and to automate decisions for a wide range of problems, supporting decisions down to problem-specific details while remaining technically independent. Furthermore, we propose a framework that is built around our DSL that enables the execution of defined workflows using the ProvideQ toolbox as an orchestration layer. All contributions from this publication are open source.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes a domain-specific language (DSL) and framework for designing hybrid quantum-classical workflows, enabling the identification of quantum candidates and automating decision-making across a wide range of problems while remaining technically independent. The framework is built around the DSL and uses the ProvideQ toolbox as an orchestration layer, with all contributions made open source.
AI.motivation: The key challenge in hybrid quantum-classical workflows is identifying which specific problems could benefit from quantum advantages. This requires specialized expertise because problem characteristics fundamentally determine the success of quantum vs. classical approaches. There is a need for a universal, easy-to-use representation to express best-practices and share solution strategies.
AI.method: The authors propose a domain-specific language (DSL) that expresses best-practices in solution strategies using a universal representation. The DSL provides a flexible approach to design hybrid quantum-classical workflows and automates decisions down to problem-specific details while remaining technically independent. A framework is built around the DSL using the ProvideQ toolbox as an orchestration layer to enable execution of defined workflows.
AI.result: The paper presents an open-source DSL and accompanying framework that enables the design and execution of hybrid quantum-classical workflows, supporting automated decision-making for a wide range of problems with problem-specific granularity.
AI.conclusion: The DSL and framework address the expertise barrier in hybrid quantum-classical workflow design by providing a universal, shareable representation of solution strategies, with the open-source ProvideQ-based orchestration enabling practical execution.

title: Memory-, Circuit-, and Ansatz-Efficient VQLS for CFD on Hybrid Quantum-HPC Systems
summary: Fluid dynamics workloads are dominated by repeated solves of large, structured linear systems, motivating the search for quantum acceleration. The Variational Quantum Linear Solver (VQLS) is a leading near-term candidate, but practical deployment on hybrid quantum--high--performance computing (HPC) systems faces three persistent challenges: (i) the linear-combination-of-unitaries (LCU) encoding of the system matrix explodes in memory and runtime as the problem size grows, (ii) ansatz selection is largely empirical, with no clear link between standard circuit metrics and solver convergence, and (iii) end-to-end VQLS pipelines have rarely been exercised on production HPC hardware at non-trivial qubit counts. This work addresses these challenges through three contributions. First, we benchmark four matrix-encoding strategies---naive LCU, PennyLane-integrated, Fast Walsh--Hadamard Transform (FWHT)-based parallel Pauli decomposition, and an singular value decomposition (SVD)-based two-term LCU---and show that the FWHT approach reduces peak memory by up to $1298\times$ on an $11\times 11$ Hele--Shaw grid, while the SVD-based coherent VQLS delivers over $10{,}000\times$ per-iteration speedup over standard Pauli-based VQLS at 8 qubits. Second, we evaluate 11 ansatz families with gradient-free and gradient-based optimizers on canonical Hele--Shaw flow, and find that expressibility and entanglement metrics correlate only weakly with VQLS convergence, motivating problem-aware ansatz design. Third, we deploy the full workflow on the OLCF Frontier supercomputer and successfully simulate a 15-qubit tridiagonal Toeplitz system on a single node. Together, these results establish a practical baseline for VQLS in hybrid quantum--HPC computation fluid dynamic (CFD) workflows and identify the remaining bottlenecks for larger problems.

AI.tldr: This work addresses three practical challenges in deploying Variational Quantum Linear Solvers (VQLS) for fluid dynamics on hybrid quantum-HPC systems: LCU matrix encoding memory/runtime explosion, empirical ansatz selection, and lack of end-to-end deployment on production HPC hardware. Contributions include benchmarking four matrix-encoding strategies (FWHT achieving up to 1298x memory reduction, SVD-based coherent VQLS achieving >10,000x per-iteration speedup at 8 qubits), evaluating 11 ansatz families (finding weak correlation between expressibility/entanglement metrics and convergence), and successfully deploying a 15-qubit tridiagonal Toeplitz system on the OLCF Frontier supercomputer.
AI.motivation: Fluid dynamics requires repeated solves of large structured linear systems, and VQLS is a promising near-term quantum candidate. However, practical deployment faces three persistent challenges: LCU encoding explodes in memory/runtime, ansatz selection lacks principled guidance, and end-to-end pipelines have rarely been exercised on production HPC hardware at non-trivial qubit counts.
AI.method: Three contributions: (1) benchmark four matrix-encoding strategies (naive LCU, PennyLane-integrated, FWHT-based parallel Pauli decomposition, SVD-based two-term LCU); (2) evaluate 11 ansatz families with gradient-free and gradient-based optimizers on canonical Hele-Shaw flow, analyzing correlations between circuit metrics (expressibility, entanglement) and solver convergence; (3) deploy the full VQLS workflow on the OLCF Frontier supercomputer simulating a 15-qubit tridiagonal Toeplitz system on a single node.
AI.result: FWHT encoding reduced peak memory by up to 1298x on an 11x11 Hele-Shaw grid. SVD-based coherent VQLS delivered over 10,000x per-iteration speedup over standard Pauli-based VQLS at 8 qubits. Expressibility and entanglement metrics correlated only weakly with VQLS convergence across 11 ansatz families. A 15-qubit tridiagonal Toeplitz system was successfully simulated on a single node of the OLCF Frontier supercomputer.
AI.conclusion: The results establish a practical baseline for VQLS in hybrid quantum-HPC CFD workflows, demonstrate that efficient encoding strategies (FWHT and SVD-based) are critical for scalability, highlight the need for problem-aware ansatz design rather than relying on generic circuit metrics, and identify remaining bottlenecks for scaling to larger problems.

title: Characterising the set of deterministic quantum correlations in prepare-and-measure scenarios
summary: Correlations that do not admit a deterministic explanation are a central feature of quantum theory and a key resource for quantum information processing. Identifying and certifying such correlations, however, remains a fundamental challenge. In this work, we advance on this problem by considering deterministic correlations in the prepare-and-measure scenario consistent with a wide range of communication restrictions. To certify correlations incompatible with such deterministic models, we ask whether they admit a scenario in which measurement outcomes can be perfectly predicted by an adversary equipped with classical side-information. We show the usefulness of this approach and propose semidefinite programming relaxations tailored to three representative communication restrictions: fixed ensemble, bounded overlaps and restricted observables.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces a framework to certify quantum correlations that cannot be explained by deterministic models in prepare-and-measure scenarios under various communication restrictions, using semidefinite programming relaxations and an adversary-with-classical-side-information perspective.
AI.motivation: Identifying and certifying correlations that do not admit deterministic explanations is a central challenge in quantum theory and crucial for quantum information processing, yet remains fundamentally difficult.
AI.method: The authors propose asking whether correlations admit a scenario where an adversary equipped with classical side-information can perfectly predict measurement outcomes, and develop semidefinite programming relaxations tailored to three communication restrictions: fixed ensemble, bounded overlaps, and restricted observables.
AI.result: The approach is shown to be useful for certifying correlations incompatible with deterministic models across the three considered communication restrictions.
AI.conclusion: The proposed framework provides a practical tool for certifying non-deterministic correlations in prepare-and-measure scenarios under various communication constraints.

title: Microscopic QED origin of spin entanglement
summary:
We study effective spin interactions arising from quantum electrodynamics (QED) scattering between localized fermionic spins. By integrating out photon and mediator fields, the dynamics reduce to an effective spin Hamiltonian.
  For two qubits in the nonrelativistic regime, the resulting interaction takes a tensor dipolar form with an asymptotic decay proportional to \(R^{-3}\). We obtain analytical expressions for the entanglement negativity, highlighting its dependence on coupling strength and spatial configuration.
  We then examine a setup in which two bath spins interact via a sequential exchange with an intermediate fermionic mediator. At the perturbative order considered, the mediator remains unentangled and induces an effective bath--bath interaction with stronger spatial suppression than in the photon-mediated case.
  Extending the construction to an \(N\)-spin setting yields an effective interaction network mediated by virtual exchange processes, which can support the generation of multipartite entanglement across the system.

AI.tldr: This paper studies effective spin interactions arising from QED scattering between localized fermionic spins, deriving an effective spin Hamiltonian by integrating out photon and mediator fields. For two qubits in the nonrelativistic regime, the interaction takes a tensor dipolar form decaying as R^{-3}, with analytical expressions for entanglement negativity obtained. A sequential exchange setup with an intermediate fermionic mediator induces a bath-bath interaction with stronger spatial suppression, and extension to N spins yields an effective interaction network supporting multipartite entanglement.
AI.motivation: To understand how effective spin interactions emerge from QED scattering processes and to characterize the resulting entanglement properties, both for two-qubit systems and for larger spin networks, in regimes where photon and mediator degrees of freedom can be integrated out.
AI.method: The authors integrate out photon and mediator fields from QED scattering between localized fermionic spins to reduce the dynamics to an effective spin Hamiltonian. They analyze the two-qubit case in the nonrelativistic regime (identifying a tensor dipolar form with R^{-3} decay), derive analytical expressions for entanglement negativity, and extend the analysis to sequential exchange via a fermionic mediator and to N-spin configurations through perturbative calculations.
AI.result: The two-qubit interaction exhibits a tensor dipolar form with R^{-3} asymptotic decay. Entanglement negativity depends on coupling strength and spatial configuration. The bath-bath interaction via an intermediate fermionic mediator shows stronger spatial suppression than photon-mediated interactions, while the mediator itself remains unentangled at the perturbative order considered. The N-spin extension yields an effective interaction network via virtual exchange processes capable of generating multipartite entanglement.
AI.conclusion: QED-mediated effective spin interactions provide a framework for generating both bipartite and multipartite entanglement in localized spin systems, with the nature and spatial scaling of the interactions tunable by the choice of mediator (photon vs. fermionic) and the system geometry.

title: Phase-error estimation for quantum key distribution with leaky receivers
summary: Practical quantum key distribution (QKD) receivers may leak information about their measurement outcomes and settings to the channel (e.g., through detector backflashes or back-reflected Trojan-horse light) that could compromise the protocol's security. Here we present a simple finite-key security proof based on phase-error estimation for prepare-and-measure QKD in the presence of either a priori information leakage about the basis choices and/or a posteriori information leakage about the measurement outcomes. The proof requires only a bound on the distinguishability of the side-channel states. Furthermore, the analysis is modular and compatible with existing security proofs that address detector and source imperfections, making it applicable to a wide range of practical QKD implementations.

AI.tldr: A finite-key security proof for prepare-and-measure QKD protocols based on phase-error estimation, addressing both a priori basis-choice leakage and a posteriori measurement-outcome leakage through side channels. The proof requires only a bound on side-channel state distinguishability and is modular, compatible with existing security proofs for detector and source imperfections.
AI.motivation: Practical QKD receivers can leak information about measurement outcomes and settings to the channel through physical side channels such as detector backflashes or back-reflected Trojan-horse light, which could compromise protocol security. Existing proofs did not adequately address these realistic leakage scenarios.
AI.method: The authors present a simple finite-key security proof based on phase-error estimation for prepare-and-measure QKD. The proof handles two types of leakage: a priori information leakage about basis choices and a posteriori information leakage about measurement outcomes. It requires only a bound on the distinguishability of the side-channel states, and is designed to be modular so it can be combined with existing security proofs addressing detector and source imperfections.
AI.result: A modular finite-key security proof is obtained that is compatible with existing security proofs for detector and source imperfections, requiring only a bound on side-channel state distinguishability, making the analysis applicable to a wide range of practical QKD implementations.
AI.conclusion: The proposed security proof addresses realistic side-channel information leakage in practical QKD receivers in a modular and broadly applicable way, enhancing the practical security guarantees of QKD implementations.

title: An Efficient Explicit Implementation of a Quantum Algorithm with Quantum Advantage for Nonlinear Scalar Conservation Laws
summary: Quantum algorithms for nonlinear partial differential equations remain challenging because nonlinear dynamics are not directly amenable to unitary quantum simulation. Building on the level-set formulation, we construct a quantum algorithm and provide an explicit gate-level implementation for solving scalar conservation laws. The nonlinear equation is first lifted to a linear Liouville equation, discretized by finite differences, and then embedded into a unitary evolution through Schrödingerisation. We further develop quantum procedures for estimating relevant observables from the evolved state. Error bounds and gate-complexity estimates are established for the complete algorithm. The resulting complexity comparison demonstrates a quantum advantage for observable estimation in sufficiently high spatial dimensions, under standard assumptions on state preparation and oracle access. Finally, numerical experiments validate the accuracy, multidimensional applicability, and predicted scaling of the proposed method.

AI.tldr: The paper presents a quantum algorithm for solving scalar conservation laws (nonlinear PDEs) by lifting the nonlinear equation to a linear Liouville equation via the level-set formulation, discretizing it with finite differences, and embedding it into unitary evolution using Schrödingerisation. The authors provide explicit gate-level implementations, quantum procedures for observable estimation, error bounds, and gate-complexity estimates, demonstrating quantum advantage for observable estimation in sufficiently high spatial dimensions. Numerical experiments validate accuracy and predicted scaling.
AI.motivation: Nonlinear partial differential equations are challenging for quantum computing because nonlinear dynamics cannot be directly simulated with unitary quantum operations, and existing approaches lack rigorous end-to-end complexity guarantees. The authors aim to overcome this fundamental obstacle by providing a complete quantum algorithm with explicit implementation and provable quantum advantage for a practically important class of nonlinear PDEs—scalar conservation laws.
AI.method: The approach proceeds in three stages: (1) the nonlinear scalar conservation law is reformulated using the level-set formulation, lifting it to a linear Liouville equation; (2) the linear equation is discretized by finite differences and embedded into a unitary evolution via the Schrödingerisation technique; (3) quantum procedures are developed to estimate relevant observables from the evolved quantum state. Error bounds and gate-complexity estimates are established for the full algorithm, and numerical experiments verify the method.
AI.result: The complete algorithm yields rigorous error bounds and gate-complexity estimates. A complexity comparison shows quantum advantage for observable estimation when the spatial dimension is sufficiently high, assuming standard state-preparation and oracle-access conditions. Numerical experiments confirm the accuracy, multidimensional applicability, and predicted scaling of the proposed method.
AI.conclusion: The level-set-based Schrödingerisation framework provides a viable and rigorous route to quantum simulation of scalar conservation laws, achieving provable quantum advantage for observable estimation in high dimensions. This establishes a template for handling broader classes of nonlinear PDEs on quantum computers.

title: Collective-dissipation-induced dark and metastable-like states for enhanced quantum battery performance
comment: This work has been submitted as a preprint on arXiv and is intended for future publication in a peer-reviewed journal. The authors retain all rights for formal publication
summary: We investigate the role of symmetry-protected dark states and metastable-like frozen states in the autonomous charging dynamics of open quantum batteries described by a transverse-field Ising model. By comparing local and collective dissipation over a range of system sizes, temperatures, and magnetic phases, we demonstrate that collective dissipation generates symmetry-protected dark states together with a much larger set of frozen (metastable) states, forming an extended protected Hilbert space. We derive the multiplicity of the collective dark sector analytically, showing that it follows the Catalan sequence for even system sizes, while such states are absent for odd sizes. Our results show that collective dissipation can enhance ergotropy and charging power, with its advantage depending on temperature, magnetic phase, and system size. While the number of dark and frozen states is identical in the ferromagnetic and antiferromagnetic phases, the achievable ergotropy differs substantially because of the different spectral locations of these protected states. In particular, the antiferromagnetic configuration exhibits considerably larger extractable work owing to the favorable positioning of the protected subspaces within the many-body energy spectrum. Finally, we analyze the active Hilbert-space fraction and show that metastable protection provides an effective mechanism for suppressing dissipative losses while preserving efficient charging pathways. These results establish the dark-state and frozen-state sectors as key resources for optimizing the performance of open quantum batteries through engineered dissipation.

AI.tldr: This paper analyzes how symmetry-protected dark states and metastable frozen states affect autonomous charging of open quantum batteries modeled by a transverse-field Ising model with collective dissipation. It shows collective dissipation creates an extended protected Hilbert space whose dark-state multiplicity follows the Catalan sequence for even system sizes (absent for odd sizes), enhances ergotropy and charging power, and that antiferromagnetic configurations yield significantly more extractable work due to favorable spectral positioning of protected subspaces.
AI.motivation: To understand how engineered dissipation and symmetry-protected quantum states can be leveraged as resources for optimizing the performance of open quantum batteries, particularly by suppressing dissipative losses while preserving efficient charging pathways.
AI.method: The authors study autonomous charging dynamics in a transverse-field Ising model open quantum battery, comparing local versus collective dissipation across varying system sizes, temperatures, and magnetic phases. They derive the multiplicity of the collective dark sector analytically, showing it follows the Catalan sequence for even system sizes. They analyze ergotropy, charging power, active Hilbert-space fraction, and spectral locations of protected states in both ferromagnetic and antiferromagnetic phases.
AI.result: Collective dissipation produces symmetry-protected dark states plus a larger set of frozen (metastable) states forming an extended protected Hilbert space. Dark-state multiplicity follows the Catalan sequence for even N (absent for odd N). Collective dissipation enhances ergotropy and charging power, though the advantage depends on temperature, magnetic phase, and system size. While the number of protected states is identical in both magnetic phases, the antiferromagnetic configuration yields substantially larger extractable work due to favorable spectral placement of protected subspaces. Metastable protection effectively suppresses dissipative losses while preserving charging efficiency.
AI.conclusion: Dark-state and frozen-state sectors constitute key resources for optimizing open quantum batteries through engineered dissipation, with the antiferromagnetic phase being particularly advantageous due to its favorable protected-subspace spectral positioning. This establishes a framework for using symmetry-protected states to enhance quantum battery performance.

title: Spread of Entanglement in Generalized Kicked Ising Chain
summary: We investigate the dynamics of entanglement in a generalized version of the kicked Ising chain, extending the model from the standard qubit case (local dimension $q=2$) to higher local dimensions ($q > 2$). We identify the existence of ''dual-unitary'' points where the model's space-time duality allows for exact analytical solutions. Our analysis reveals that while a few unique dual-unitary points exist analytically for systems with local dimensions $q=3$ and $q=4$, such points do not exist for $q \ge 5$ due to the lack of a unique kicking strength that satisfies the required matrix element conditions. Utilizing the transfer matrix method and a replica trick specifically adapted for higher dimensions, we derive exact expressions for the growth of entanglement entropy in the $q=3$ (kicked Potts-type) model starting from a class of solvable initial states. Our results demonstrate that at the dual-unitary point, both Rényi and von Neumann entanglement entropies grow linearly with time until reaching a maximum value determined by the subsystem size.

AI.tldr: This paper generalizes the kicked Ising chain to higher local dimensions (q>2) and identifies dual-unitary points where exact analytical solutions are possible. Dual-unitary points exist only for q=3 and q=4, but not for q>=5. For the q=3 (kicked Potts-type) model, exact expressions for entanglement entropy growth are derived via transfer matrix and replica trick methods, showing linear growth with time at the dual-unitary point.
AI.motivation: To extend the study of dual-unitary quantum circuits and exactly solvable entanglement dynamics beyond the standard qubit (q=2) case to higher local dimensions, and to determine whether such special solvable points persist in generalized kicked Ising chains.
AI.method: The authors generalize the kicked Ising chain to local dimensions q>2, search for dual-unitary points satisfying specific matrix element conditions, and use the transfer matrix method combined with a replica trick adapted for higher dimensions to derive exact entanglement entropy growth expressions for the q=3 case from solvable initial states.
AI.result: Analytical dual-unitary points exist for q=3 and q=4 but not for q>=5 due to the absence of a unique kicking strength satisfying the matrix element conditions. For the q=3 kicked Potts-type model, both Rényi and von Neumann entanglement entropies grow linearly with time at the dual-unitary point, saturating at a value determined by the subsystem size.
AI.conclusion: The existence of dual-unitary points in generalized kicked Ising chains is limited to low local dimensions (q=3,4). For q=3, the model remains exactly solvable at these points, exhibiting characteristic linear entanglement growth, demonstrating that higher-dimensional generalizations of dual-unitary dynamics are possible but constrained by algebraic conditions on the kicking parameters.

title: State Diagnostics of Complexity in Open Quantum Systems
summary: We study the emergence of complexity in finite-size quantum systems as their dynamics transition from closed and coherent evolution to interacting and effectively open behavior. Using a state-based geometric framework, we represent mixed quantum states as probability measures on complex projective Hilbert space. This representation allows us to track how interactions reshape the underlying pure-state geometry. We introduce two complementary diagnostics: a distinguishability measure, based on the Wasserstein distance between probability-measure representations of mixed states, that quantifies sensitivity to initial states, and a state-space coverage index that measures long-time exploration of the subsystem state space. These diagnostics provide a geometric perspective on the emergence and evolution of quantum dynamical complexity. When applied to the quantum kicked top, both diagnostics generally increase with interaction strength. Their dependence on environment size is structured by parity symmetry, with integer-spin systems often exhibiting greater sensitivity and state-space coverage than half-integer-spin systems. These results highlight finite-size quantum effects and provide a geometric approach to quantifying dynamical complexity deep in the quantum regime

AI.tldr: This paper introduces a state-based geometric framework for quantifying dynamical complexity in finite-size quantum systems, using probability measures on complex projective Hilbert space. Two diagnostics are proposed—a Wasserstein-based distinguishability measure and a state-space coverage index—both applied to the quantum kicked top, showing that complexity generally increases with interaction strength and is structured by parity symmetry.
AI.motivation: To understand how quantum dynamical complexity emerges as finite-size quantum systems transition from closed, coherent evolution to open, interacting dynamics, and to provide quantitative geometric tools that work deep in the quantum regime where classical notions of chaos may not directly apply.
AI.method: Represent mixed quantum states as probability measures on complex projective Hilbert space. Introduce a distinguishability diagnostic based on the Wasserstein distance between probability-measure representations (quantifying sensitivity to initial states) and a state-space coverage index (quantifying long-time exploration), then apply these to the quantum kicked top across varying interaction strengths and system sizes.
AI.result: Both diagnostics generally increase with interaction strength in the quantum kicked top. The dependence on environment size is structured by parity symmetry: integer-spin systems often show greater sensitivity and state-space coverage than half-integer-spin systems, highlighting finite-size quantum effects.
AI.conclusion: The geometric framework provides a viable approach to quantifying dynamical complexity deep in the quantum regime, revealing finite-size effects and symmetry-structured behavior that enrich our understanding of complexity emergence in quantum systems.

title: Magic State Distillation via Codes over Binary Extension Fields
summary: Fault-tolerant quantum computation architectures are frequently bottlenecked by the overhead of producing high-fidelity magic states. In this work, we use algebraic geometric techniques to construct codes over binary extension fields $\mathbb{F}_{2^s}$, thus discovering new protocols for the distillation of qubit magic states, where our focus is on the regime of practical qubit-based quantum computing architectures. To do this, we show that multi-qubit gates of interest such as $\text{CS}$, $\text{CCZ}$, and $\text{TOF}\# = \text{CCZ}_{123}\text{CCZ}_{345}$, can be packaged into simple gates over the larger fields, and we derive simple algebraic conditions in the extension fields allowing the distillation of these gates. Because they are derived from Galois qudits, the corresponding qubits codes naturally handle the correlated errors present on such multi-qubit states. Moreover, the protocols we discover are extremely compact; for example, we show that 4 $\text{CS}$ states can be distilled to 1 $\text{CS}$ state at distance 2, using only 4 logical qubits. For a case study, we consider the distillation of $\text{CS}$ and $\text{CCZ}$ states from injected $\text{T}$ and $\text{CS}$ states. When optimized for magic state production per unit time, or logical spacetime volume, we find that our protocols outperform the state-of-the-art in almost every situation, both at input error rates $10^{-3}$ (direct injection), and $10^{-6}$ (allowing some cultivation pre-injection).

AI.tldr: This paper uses algebraic geometric techniques to construct codes over binary extension fields F_{2^s}, yielding new magic state distillation protocols for qubit-based quantum computing. The authors package multi-qubit gates (CS, CCZ, TOF#) into simple gates over larger fields and derive algebraic conditions enabling distillation. Their compact protocols (e.g., 4 CS states distilled to 1 at distance 2 using only 4 logical qubits) outperform state-of-the-art methods in almost every scenario for both CS and CCZ distillation from T and CS states at error rates 10^-3 and 10^-6.
AI.motivation: Fault-tolerant quantum computation is bottlenecked by the high overhead of producing high-fidelity magic states, which are essential for enabling non-Clifford operations. Finding more efficient distillation protocols that reduce this overhead is critical for practical quantum computing architectures.
AI.method: The authors employ algebraic geometric techniques to construct codes over binary extension fields F_{2^s}. They show that multi-qubit gates (CS, CCZ, TOF#) can be packaged into simple gates over the larger fields and derive simple algebraic conditions in the extension fields that enable distillation of these gates. Because the codes derive from Galois qudits, they naturally handle correlated errors on multi-qubit states. The protocols are optimized for magic state production per unit time and logical spacetime volume.
AI.result: The protocols are extremely compact—for example, 4 CS states can be distilled to 1 CS state at distance 2 using only 4 logical qubits. When optimized for magic state production per unit time or logical spacetime volume, the protocols outperform state-of-the-art methods in almost every situation, both at input error rates 10^-3 (direct injection) and 10^-6 (with cultivation pre-injection), for distillation of CS and CCZ states from injected T and CS states.
AI.conclusion: Algebraic geometric codes over binary extension fields provide a powerful new framework for magic state distillation, yielding compact and efficient protocols that outperform existing state-of-the-art approaches across most operating regimes. This work demonstrates that leveraging Galois qudit structure can significantly reduce the overhead bottleneck in fault-tolerant quantum computation.

title: Aicir: A Full-Stack Quantum Circuit Simulator with AscendNPU Support
summary: Quantum computing is a promising way to study problems that are difficult for classical methods, but current quantum hardware still faces limits in scale, noise, and fidelity. Running quantum algorithms on physical machines can also be costly. Quantum circuit simulators therefore remain important because they let researchers design and test algorithms on classical computers before using quantum hardware. Most high-performance simulators provide GPU backends, while few offer native support for NPUs. This gap limits the computing platforms available for quantum-algorithm research. We developed Aicir to provide a full-stack quantum circuit simulator with a native Huawei Ascend NPU backend. Aicir connects circuit construction, several state representations, measurement, differentiation, variational algorithms, quantum machine learning, and quantum architecture search through one programming model. It also supports noise simulation, tensor-network and matrix-product-state engines, and distributed state simulation. On the NPU, paired real tensors, fixed-rank gate views, and hardware-specific formulas keep the tested simulation paths on the device. The same representation lets Aicir partition a state across $2^{p}$ NPUs while retaining reverse-mode differentiation. We validated native execution with CPU fallback disabled and checked distributed communication and gradients on 2, 4, and 8 NPUs. For the tested fused layered circuits, Aicir's CPU runtime is within $0.97$--$1.28\times$ that of Qiskit Aer and $0.76$--$1.10\times$ that of Cirq. These results place its CPU execution in the same range as established simulators for this workload, while the NPU tests establish correct native execution rather than CPU-to-NPU speedup.

AI.tldr: Aicir is a full-stack quantum circuit simulator with a native Huawei Ascend NPU backend, supporting state representations, variational algorithms, QML, noise simulation, tensor-network engines, and distributed state simulation across 2^p NPUs with reverse-mode differentiation. Its CPU runtime is comparable to Qiskit Aer and Cirq for fused layered circuits, and NPU execution is validated for correctness.
AI.motivation: Most high-performance quantum circuit simulators provide GPU backends but few offer native NPU support, limiting the computing platforms available for quantum algorithm research. This gap motivates the development of Aicir to expand simulation platform options.
AI.method: Aicir is built as a full-stack simulator with a native Huawei Ascend NPU backend. It employs paired real tensors, fixed-rank gate views, and hardware-specific formulas to keep simulation on-device. The same representation enables partitioning a quantum state across 2^p NPUs while supporting reverse-mode differentiation. It integrates circuit construction, multiple state representations, measurement, differentiation, variational algorithms, QML, quantum architecture search, noise simulation, tensor-network/MPS engines, and distributed state simulation into one programming model.
AI.result: Native NPU execution with CPU fallback disabled was validated, including distributed communication and gradients on 2, 4, and 8 NPUs. For fused layered circuits, Aicir's CPU runtime is within 0.97-1.28x of Qiskit Aer and 0.76-1.10x of Cirq. NPU tests confirmed correct native execution rather than demonstrating CPU-to-NPU speedup.
AI.conclusion: Aicir achieves CPU performance on par with established simulators like Qiskit Aer and Cirq while providing a native NPU backend for broader compute-platform coverage. NPU execution is validated for correctness, positioning Aicir as a viable cross-platform quantum circuit simulator.

title: Quantized Stabilizer-Rényi Boundary Response across Fermionic SPT Transitions
summary: Open boundaries host symmetry-protected Majorana modes, yet their imprint on the stabilizer Rényi entropy is obscured by a nonuniversal volume law. At Rényi index $α=1/2$, we isolate a bulk-subtracted boundary response in free-fermion BDI chains using exact finite-open-chain relations, large-$L$ Pfaffian evaluations, and direct positive-weight checks. Across a mass inversion, this response approaches $|Δω|\ln 2$, where $Δω$ is the change in winding number. The response survives primitive bulk deformations, the tested local boundary perturbations, and broken bulk duality. Thus, for the families studied here, the boundary response counts the Majorana channels that change the fermionic SPT index.

AI.tldr: The paper studies how symmetry-protected Majorana modes at open boundaries imprint on the stabilizer Rényi entropy in free-fermion BDI chains. Using exact finite-open-chain relations and Pfaffian evaluations at Rényi index α=1/2, the authors isolate a bulk-subtracted boundary response that approaches |Δω|ln2 across a mass inversion, robustly counting the Majorana channels that change the fermionic SPT index.
AI.motivation: While open boundaries host symmetry-protected Majorana modes, their signature in the stabilizer Rényi entropy is masked by a nonuniversal volume-law contribution, making it difficult to extract boundary information from this entanglement-like measure. The authors seek to isolate the boundary contribution to characterize topologically nontrivial Majorana modes.
AI.method: The authors work with free-fermion BDI chains at Rényi index α=1/2. They use exact finite-open-chain relations, large-L Pfaffian evaluations, and direct positive-weight checks to define and compute a bulk-subtracted boundary response in the stabilizer Rényi entropy. They test robustness against primitive bulk deformations, local boundary perturbations, and broken bulk duality.
AI.result: Across a mass inversion (where the winding number changes), the bulk-subtracted boundary response approaches |Δω|ln2, namely the change in winding number times ln2. The result survives primitive bulk deformations, the local boundary perturbations tested, and scenarios with broken bulk duality, indicating that the boundary response counts the Majorana channels that change the fermionic SPT index.
AI.conclusion: The stabilizer Rényi entropy at α=1/2, after removing the bulk contribution, provides a genuine boundary diagnostic that quantitatively counts the number of Majorana channels associated with a change in the fermionic SPT (winding number) index in free-fermion BDI chains, robust to various perturbations.

title: Security of quantum key distribution with passive basis choice and detection-efficiency mismatch for a realistic satellite setup
summary: Detection-efficiency mismatch is a common problem in realistic quantum key distribution (QKD) systems. The existing security proofs for the case of the passive basis choice provide a nonzero secret key rate only for a small detection-efficiency mismatch. Unfortunately, in realistic setups, the detection-efficiency mismatch can be significant. Here we present a more precise estimation of the secret key rate for the BB84 protocol with the passive basis choice, which accounts for the detection-efficiency mismatch between four threshold detectors as well as an adaptation of the decoy-state method. The suggested approach is used to estimate the secret key rate in a QKD experiment between the Micius satellite and the Zvenigorod ground station.

AI.tldr: This paper presents a more precise estimation method for the secret key rate in BB84 QKD with passive basis choice, accounting for detection-efficiency mismatch between four threshold detectors and adapting the decoy-state method. The approach is applied to a real QKD experiment between the Micius satellite and the Zvenigorod ground station.
AI.motivation: Detection-efficiency mismatch is a common problem in realistic QKD systems, but existing security proofs for passive basis choice only provide a nonzero secret key rate for small mismatch values. In realistic setups, however, the mismatch can be significant, so a more precise estimation method is needed.
AI.method: The authors develop a refined estimation of the secret key rate for the BB84 protocol with passive basis choice that explicitly accounts for detection-efficiency mismatch among four threshold detectors, and integrates an adaptation of the decoy-state method.
AI.result: The suggested approach successfully estimates the secret key rate in a real QKD experiment between the Micius satellite and the Zvenigorod ground station, demonstrating applicability under realistic significant detection-efficiency mismatch.
AI.conclusion: The proposed method extends secure QKD operation to realistic setups with significant detection-efficiency mismatch, and is validated on an actual satellite-to-ground QKD link.

title: From Barren Plateaus to SPSA Optimization in Variational Quantum Eigensolvers
summary: The barren plateau (BP) phenomenon poses a fundamental challenge to the trainability of variational quantum eigensolvers (VQEs) by causing exponentially vanishing gradients as the system size increases. While extensive studies have investigated the geometric origins of BP, its impact on the optimization dynamics and complexity of practical algorithms under finite-shot measurements remains poorly understood. In this paper, we develop a theoretical framework that characterizes how the BP affects the optimization dynamics of the Simultaneous Perturbation Stochastic Approximation (SPSA) algorithm and quantifies the resulting iteration complexity and measurement budget. We derive non-asymptotic bias and variance characterizations of the SPSA gradient estimator, introduce a signal-to-noise ratio analysis to quantify gradient reliability, and establish convergence guarantees for SPSA under finite-shot measurements. Our results show that the exponentially decaying gradient energy associated with BP leads to an exponential increase in the number of iterations required to achieve a fixed relative optimization accuracy, which in turn results in an exponential increase in the total measurement budget.

AI.tldr: This paper develops a theoretical framework to analyze how the barren plateau phenomenon affects the optimization dynamics, iteration complexity, and measurement budget of the Simultaneous Perturbation Stochastic Approximation (SPSA) algorithm in variational quantum eigensolvers under finite-shot measurements.
AI.motivation: While the geometric origins of the barren plateau phenomenon have been extensively studied, its impact on the optimization dynamics and algorithmic complexity of practical variational quantum eigensolvers under finite-shot measurements remains poorly understood.
AI.method: The authors derive non-asymptotic bias and variance characterizations of the SPSA gradient estimator, introduce a signal-to-noise ratio analysis to quantify gradient reliability, and establish convergence guarantees for SPSA under finite-shot measurement settings.
AI.result: The analysis shows that the exponentially decaying gradient energy associated with barren plateaus causes an exponential increase in the number of iterations needed to reach a fixed relative optimization accuracy, which consequently leads to an exponential growth in the total measurement budget.
AI.conclusion: The barren plateau phenomenon not only causes vanishing gradients geometrically but also imposes exponential complexity costs on the optimization dynamics and measurement resources of practical VQE algorithms using SPSA.

title: Quantum Information Flow under String-Diagram Rewriting
summary:
We revisit the notion of ``quantum information flow'' introduced in Bob Coecke's early work and seek to give it an explicit string-diagrammatic formalization. Given a semantics preserving string-diagram rewriting sequence, we first distinguish apparent through-paths, which depend on the current graphical presentation, from genuine through paths, which can be compatibly inherited through successive rewrites to a terminal decoupled bare wire factor. We then formally define a ``Coecke flow line'' in terms of this compatible inheritance relation.
  In particular, we use the ZX calculus, i.e., the ZX string diagram rewriting system, to illustrate the resulting formalism. In the physical setting of quantum protocols, a Coecke flow can be interpreted as a constrained, quasi-local, line-like presentation of a target bare wire morphism factor within the protocol string diagram.

AI.tldr: This paper formalizes the notion of "quantum information flow" from Bob Coecke's early work using string-diagrammatic methods. It distinguishes apparent through-paths (dependent on graphical presentation) from genuine through-paths (compatibly inherited through rewrites to a terminal decoupled bare wire factor), then defines a "Coecke flow line" via this compatible inheritance relation. The formalism is illustrated using the ZX calculus, and in quantum protocols a Coecke flow is interpreted as a constrained, quasi-local, line-like presentation of a target bare wire morphism factor.
AI.motivation: The paper revisits Coecke's early notion of quantum information flow and aims to give it a rigorous, explicit string-diagrammatic formalization, which was previously lacking.
AI.method: The authors analyze semantics-preserving string-diagram rewriting sequences, distinguishing apparent versus genuine through-paths based on compatibility of inheritance through successive rewrites to a terminal decoupled bare wire factor. They define a Coecke flow line in terms of this compatible inheritance relation and use the ZX calculus as the illustrative rewriting system.
AI.result: A formal definition of Coecke flow lines is provided, grounded in the compatible inheritance of genuine through-paths across diagram rewrites, with the ZX calculus used to demonstrate the resulting formalism.
AI.conclusion: In the physical setting of quantum protocols, a Coecke flow can be interpreted as a constrained, quasi-local, line-like presentation of a target bare wire morphism factor within the protocol string diagram.

title: An upper bound for the purity of absolutely positive partial transpose states
summary: A quantum state is called absolutely separable (resp. absolutely positive partial transpose (APPT)) if it remains separable (resp. positive partial transpose (PPT)) under any global unitary transformation. It is known that the set of all absolutely separable states is a subset of the set of all APPT states. Moreover, these two sets are identical for qubit-qudit systems. In this note, we give an upper bound for the purity of APPT bipartite states (and therefore for the purity of absolutely separable bipartite states).
