For qubit-qudit systems, this upper bound becomes the maximum purity of APPT (and absolutely separable) states.

AI.tldr: The paper provides an upper bound on the purity of absolutely positive partial transpose (APPT) bipartite states, which also applies to absolutely separable states. For qubit-qudit systems, this bound is shown to be tight, achieving the maximum purity of both APPT and absolutely separable states.
AI.motivation: To characterize the geometric properties (specifically purity) of absolutely separable and APPT quantum states, which are important classes of quantum states invariant under global unitary transformations.
AI.method: The authors derive a mathematical upper bound for the purity of APPT bipartite states, and demonstrate that for qubit-qudit systems this bound coincides with the maximum achievable purity.
AI.result: A generic upper bound on the purity of APPT bipartite states is obtained, which is proven to be tight for qubit-qudit systems, where it equals the maximum purity of both APPT and absolutely separable states.
AI.conclusion: The upper bound provides a quantitative characterization of these state classes, and the exactness for qubit-qudit systems confirms the known equivalence of these sets in that case.

title: Tensor network methods for non-perturbative dynamics of open quantum systems
summary: The description of open quantum system dynamics beyond the perturbative treatment (usually associated with Markovian master equations) is a computationally challenging task due to the unfavorable exponential scaling of memory kernels. Developed over recent decades in the context of quantum information and condensed matter, tensor networks provide both a new formalism and a toolbox for overcoming previous computational bottlenecks. This framework enables the formulation of non-perturbative, numerically exact methods for describing the dynamics of open quantum systems to controllable numerical accuracy. In this review, we present these methods and discuss their commonalities and differences to paint a comprehensive view of the field.

AI.tldr: This review paper discusses tensor network methods as a new formalism and toolbox for non-perturbative, numerically exact simulation of open quantum system dynamics, overcoming the computational challenges associated with memory kernel scaling in beyond-Markovian treatments.
AI.motivation: Describing open quantum system dynamics beyond perturbative/Markovian master equation treatments is computationally challenging due to the exponential scaling of memory kernels, motivating the need for more efficient computational approaches.
AI.method: The paper presents tensor network methods developed in quantum information and condensed matter contexts as a framework for formulating non-perturbative, numerically exact methods for open quantum system dynamics, and compares these methods to identify commonalities and differences.
AI.result: The framework enables controllable numerical accuracy in simulating open quantum systems, and the review provides a comprehensive comparison of various tensor network-based approaches.
AI.conclusion: Tensor networks provide a powerful toolbox that overcomes previous computational bottlenecks in open quantum system dynamics, offering a unified perspective on non-perturbative numerical methods in this field.

title: From Nonlinear Stochastic Differential Equations to Quantum Channels: The Kolmogorov--Lindblad Mapping
summary: Nonlinear stochastic differential equations (SDEs) underlie molecular modeling and drug discovery, quantitative finance, stochastic learning, and uncertainty quantification. Their expectations, event probabilities, and time correlations are therefore natural targets for quantum computation, but nonlinear drift and averaging over noise realizations obstruct a direct quantum representation. We develop an exact \emph{Kolmogorov--Lindblad mapping} (KLM) at the level of the probability law, encoded natively as a trace-one quantum density operator. For each Brownian realization, the pathwise density admits a half-density whose evolution is a stochastic Schrödinger equation. Averaging the associated pure states yields a Lindblad equation for $Γ(t)$ whose diagonal kernel is exactly the Fokker--Planck density, $p(t,x)=Γ(t;x,x)$, with classical diffusion represented by decoherence through Hermitian jump operators. Statistical observables become quantum expectations without the unknown time-dependent normalization introduced by direct amplitude encoding of the density, and classical two-time correlations admit an exact quantum regression formula. A structure-preserving Galerkin projection retains the Lindblad form at finite dimension, placing classical SDEs and open quantum dynamics on the same quantum-native computational footing. Numerical experiments for double-well Langevin dynamics and noisy Lorenz--63 exhibit rapid convergence of statistical observables. KLM thus provides a mathematically controlled path from general nonlinear stochastic dynamics to quantum channels, while isolating function approximation and coherent operator access as the remaining determinants of algorithmic efficiency.

The goal is to find a mathematically exact path to encode such classical stochastic dynamics onto quantum hardware.

title: Surface passivation for narrowing optical linewidth of silicon T centers in nanophotonic devices
summary: Silicon T centers are promising spin-photon interfaces in solid-state platforms for telecom-compatible, scalable quantum information technologies. A major challenge for T centers in nanophotonics is spectral diffusion, where fluctuations in the local electric-field environment from surface and bulk charge states broaden the optical transition and reduce photon indistinguishability. Strategies that directly suppress spectral diffusion are therefore critical for improving T-center-based quantum photonic devices. Here, we use atomic-layer-deposited Al2O3 to passivate the silicon surface and demonstrate a systematic narrowing of T center optical linewidths. Across our measurements, Al2O3 passivation reduces the T center emission linewidth by up to 57%. Complementary above-bandgap illumination and spectral hole burning measurements show that the remaining linewidth contains a significant spectral-diffusion component caused by adjacent charge traps, while placing an upper bound of approximately 75 MHz on the homogeneous linewidth. This work provides a CMOS-compatible path toward generating indistinguishable photons from silicon T centers for scalable quantum photonic applications.

AI.tldr: The paper demonstrates that atomic-layer-deposited Al2O3 passivation of silicon surfaces reduces spectral diffusion in T centers, narrowing emission linewidths by up to 57%. Complementary measurements place an upper bound of ~75 MHz on the homogeneous linewidth, providing a CMOS-compatible path to indistinguishable single photons for scalable quantum photonic applications.
AI.motivation: T centers in silicon are promising spin-photon interfaces for telecom-compatible quantum technologies, but spectral diffusion caused by fluctuating local electric fields from surface and bulk charge states broadens optical transitions and reduces photon indistinguishability. Direct suppression of spectral diffusion is critical for improving T-center-based quantum photonic devices.
AI.method: The authors use atomic-layer-deposited Al2O3 to passivate the silicon surface. They systematically measure T center optical linewidths before and after passivation, and employ complementary above-bandgap illumination and spectral hole burning measurements to separate spectral-diffusion and homogeneous linewidth contributions.
AI.result: Al2O3 passivation reduces T center emission linewidth by up to 57%. Above-bandgap illumination and spectral hole burning show a significant remaining spectral-diffusion component from adjacent charge traps, while establishing an upper bound of approximately 75 MHz on the homogeneous linewidth.
AI.conclusion: Al2O3 passivation provides a CMOS-compatible approach to suppress spectral diffusion in silicon T centers, improving optical linewidths and moving toward indistinguishable photon generation for scalable quantum photonic technologies.

title: Learning Clifford-structured quantum unitaries and Hamiltonians
summary: Learning algorithms for structured quantum unitaries and Hamiltonians have primarily considered classes of processes that are local or sparse in the Pauli basis. We turn our attention to learning $n$-qubit quantum unitaries $U$ and Hamiltonians $H$, given query access to $U$ or the unitary evolution of $H$, that may be dense in the Pauli basis but still admit concise Clifford decompositions. Specifically, we consider unitaries (or Hamiltonians) of the form $U = \sum_i α_i C_i$ over Cliffords $C_i$ with bounded Clifford extent $\sum_i |α_i|$. To extract this Clifford structure, we introduce an agnostic tomography protocol for Clifford unitaries that given query access to an unknown unitary $U$ with optimal Clifford fidelity $\textsf{opt}$, outputs a Clifford unitary witnessing fidelity $\geq \textsf{opt} - \varepsilon$ for some error $\varepsilon > 0$, in time $\textsf{poly}(n,(1/\varepsilon)^{\log(1/\varepsilon)})$. We then apply this protocol to obtain tomography protocols for unitaries and Hamiltonians that have bounded Clifford extent. This extends learnability of Hamiltonians from those with sparse Pauli decompositions to those that are dense (i.e., has sparsity $Ω(2^n)$) in the Pauli basis but are Clifford structured.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces learning algorithms for n-qubit quantum unitaries and Hamiltonians that may be dense in the Pauli basis but admit concise Clifford decompositions. The authors propose an agnostic tomography protocol for Clifford unitaries that outputs a Clifford unitary near-optimal in fidelity, running in poly(n, (1/ε)^{log(1/ε)}) time, and apply it to learn unitaries and Hamiltonians with bounded Clifford extent.
AI.motivation: Existing learning algorithms for structured quantum unitaries and Hamiltonians focus on classes that are local or sparse in the Pauli basis. The authors aim to extend learnability to a broader class of processes that are dense in the Pauli basis (with sparsity Ω(2^n)) but still have concise structure when decomposed into Cliffords, thereby generalizing prior Hamiltonian learning results.
AI.method: The paper introduces an agnostic tomography protocol for Clifford unitaries. Given query access to an unknown unitary U with optimal Clifford fidelity opt, the protocol outputs a Clifford unitary with fidelity ≥ opt − ε in time poly(n, (1/ε)^{log(1/ε)}). This Clifford tomography protocol is then used as a subroutine to design tomography protocols for unitaries and Hamiltonians expressible as U = Σᵢ αᵢ Cᵢ over Cliffords Cᵢ with bounded Clifford extent Σᵢ |αᵢ|.
AI.result: The authors obtain tomography protocols for unitaries and Hamiltonians with bounded Clifford extent, extending the learnability of Hamiltonians from those with sparse Pauli decompositions to those that are dense (sparsity Ω(2^n)) in the Pauli basis yet admit Clifford structure.
AI.conclusion: The work broadens the landscape of efficiently learnable quantum processes by showing that dense-in-Pauli but Clifford-structured unitaries and Hamiltonians are learnable, demonstrating that structural sparsity in alternative bases (beyond Pauli) suffices for efficient quantum tomography.

title: From Koszul-Complex Stabilizer Models to Superselection Profiles: Topological Rigidity and Nonsplit Extensions
summary: Koszul-complex stabilizer models unify the toric-code hierarchy and bivariate-bicycle codes in one homological framework. To study translation-symmetry-enriched topological (SET) phases in these models and, more generally, in translation-invariant Calderbank-Shor-Steane (CSS) codes with stabilizer maps $(\varphi_X,\varphi_Z)$, we introduce the associated topological superselection profile $\mathscr S_σ:=τ_{\geq1}\mathbf R\!\operatorname{Hom}_R(\overline{\operatorname{coker}\varphi_σ},R),\ σ=X,Z$. Its cohomology layers $E_σ^\ell:=H^\ell(\mathscr S_σ)\cong_R\operatorname{Ext}_R^\ell(\overline{\operatorname{coker}\varphi_σ},R)$ encode sectors, fusion, and translation action. When finite, the $\ell=1,2,\ldots$ layers describe pointlike, looplike, and higher-dimensional excitations; $\mathscr S_σ$ retains inter-layer gluing. For regular Koszul models, we compute $E_σ^\ell$ explicitly, find $\mathscr S_σ$ single-layer, and obtain finite-size $Z$-logicals from $\operatorname{Tor}$. Single-layer means that at most one positive-degree layer $E_σ^\ell$ is nonzero. Our matrix-level Schanuel-lemma method proves rigidity: under a finite-resolution hypothesis, the nonzero layer and degree uniquely determine a topological CSS code's translation SET order at the stable translation-invariant Clifford level. For prime qudits the hypothesis is automatic, and a finite layer's translation kernel gives the exact minimal coarse graining to a toric-code stack. We realize admissible single-layer data. Beyond this regime, split and nonsplit extensions of 3D qubit toric codes yield eight models sharing all identical $E_σ^\ell$ layers with trivial translation action but having distinct size-dependent ground-state degeneracies, hence distinct translation SET phases. Thus inter-layer gluing carries SET data invisible to individual layers.

AI.tldr: The paper unifies toric-code hierarchy and bivariate-bicycle codes via Koszul-complex stabilizer models within a homological framework. It introduces the topological superselection profile S_σ (with cohomology layers E_σ^ℓ = Ext^ℓ) to study translation-symmetry-enriched topological (SET) phases in translation-invariant CSS codes. For regular Koszul models, layers are computed explicitly, and a matrix-level Schanuel-lemma method establishes rigidity of SET order. Beyond this regime, split and nonsplit extensions of 3D qubit toric codes yield eight models with identical layers but distinct SET phases, showing inter-layer gluing carries SET data invisible to individual layers.
AI.motivation: To systematically study translation-symmetry-enriched topological phases in a broad class of topological stabilizer codes, unifying the toric-code hierarchy and bivariate-bicycle codes under one homological framework, and to understand what data determines the SET order and ground-state degeneracy of such codes.
AI.method: The authors associate to a translation-invariant CSS code with stabilizer maps (φ_X, φ_Z) the topological superselection profile S_σ := τ_≥1 R Hom_R(coker φ_σ, R), whose cohomology layers E_σ^ℓ = Ext^ℓ encode sectors, fusion, and translation action. For regular Koszul models, they compute E_σ^ℓ explicitly and establish single-layer structure. They use a matrix-level Schanuel-lemma method to prove rigidity of the translation SET order from the nonzero layer and degree, under a finite-resolution hypothesis (automatic for prime qudits). They also construct examples realizing admissible single-layer data and analyze split/nonsplit extensions of 3D qubit toric codes.
AI.result: For regular Koszul models the layers E_σ^ℓ are computed explicitly, S_σ is single-layer, and finite-size Z-logicals follow from Tor. A rigidity theorem shows the nonzero layer and degree uniquely determine the translation SET order at the stable translation-invariant Clifford level, with the translation kernel of a finite layer giving the exact minimal coarse graining to a toric-code stack for prime qudits. In the non-regular regime, eight models built from split and nonsplit extensions of 3D qubit toric codes share all identical layers with trivial translation action yet have distinct size-dependent ground-state degeneracies, hence distinct SET phases.
AI.conclusion: The superselection profile S_σ, including inter-layer gluing, provides a complete homological invariant for translation-SET phases in translation-invariant CSS codes. Individual layer data (Ext groups) is insufficient in general; inter-layer gluing carries essential SET data invisible to individual layers. The framework unifies toric-code and bivariate-bicycle families and yields concrete rigidity results for Koszul models and prime qudit systems.

title: Decoupling 2D translation-invariant topological CSS codes
summary: Two-dimensional translation-invariant topological CSS codes on qubits are known to be locally equivalent, after coarse-graining, to stacks of toric codes. However, existing constructions generally break more translation symmetry than is required to remove anyon-permuting translations, leaving open whether any further obstruction exists. We prove that no such obstruction occurs: after passing to the maximal anyon-preserving superlattice, every such code admits a local unitary decoupling into toric codes and product states. We further provide an efficient algorithm for explicitly constructing the decoupling map, together with bounds on the required supercell size and operator spreading. The decoupling requires no additional ancillas in generic cases and extends to finite systems with suitable boundary conditions.

AI.tldr: Translation-invariant topological CSS codes on qubits can always be locally decoupled into stacks of toric codes and product states after passing to the maximal anyon-preserving superlattice, with an efficient explicit algorithm and no further obstructions.
AI.motivation: While 2D translation-invariant topological CSS codes are known to be locally equivalent to stacks of toric codes after coarse-graining, existing constructions break more translation symmetry than necessary to remove anyon-permuting translations. This leaves open whether any residual obstruction to decoupling exists beyond those symmetries.
AI.method: The authors prove that after passing to the maximal anyon-preserving superlattice, every such code admits a local unitary (LU) decoupling into toric codes and product states. They provide an efficient algorithm for explicitly constructing the decoupling map, along with bounds on the required supercell size and operator spreading. The construction requires no additional ancillas in generic cases and extends to finite systems with appropriate boundary conditions.
AI.result: No further obstruction exists beyond anyon-permuting translations; all translation-invariant topological CSS codes can be fully decoupled into toric code stacks and product states on the maximal anyon-preserving superlattice, with efficient algorithmic construction.
AI.conclusion: The maximal anyon-preserving superlattice is sufficient to enable complete local unitary decoupling of 2D translation-invariant topological CSS codes, settling the question of whether additional obstructions exist.

title: A Quantum Coherence Microscope in the Hubbard Regime
summary: Quantum coherence underlies collective quantum phenomena and emerging quantum technologies. Quantum gas microscopes have transformed quantum simulation by providing projective snapshots of many-body states with single-atom resolution, but spatially resolved measurements of off-diagonal correlations have remained elusive. Here, using the Talbot effect, we introduce a quantum coherence microscope that maps off-diagonal correlations onto site-resolved density signals with near-single-site resolution. We use this technique to locally probe the superfluid-Mott transition in a layer of a three-dimensional optical lattice and to measure coherence beyond nearest neighbors in an engineered potential landscape. By mapping off-diagonal correlations onto density signals through controlled Talbot evolution, this work opens new possibilities for accessing observables beyond the density basis through tailored matter-wave evolution and recapture.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces a quantum coherence microscope that uses the Talbot effect to map off-diagonal correlations (quantum coherence) onto site-resolved density measurements in quantum gas microscopes, enabling spatially resolved probing of the superfluid-Mott transition and long-range coherence in optical lattices.
AI.motivation: Quantum gas microscopes can provide projective snapshots of many-body states with single-atom resolution, but spatially resolved measurements of off-diagonal correlations (quantum coherence) have remained elusive, limiting access to important observables beyond the density basis.
AI.method: The technique exploits the Talbot effect to map off-diagonal correlations onto site-resolved density signals with near-single-site resolution, achieved through controlled matter-wave Talbot evolution and recapture in optical lattices.
AI.result: The quantum coherence microscope was used to locally probe the superfluid-Mott transition in a layer of a three-dimensional optical lattice and to measure coherence beyond nearest neighbors in an engineered potential landscape.
AI.conclusion: By mapping off-diagonal correlations onto density signals through controlled Talbot evolution, this work opens new possibilities for accessing observables beyond the density basis through tailored matter-wave evolution and recapture.
